The Euclid Collaboration prepares to read the cosmos with care in this 2026 paper. Euclid is a space telescope built to survey galaxies. Its spectroscopic data will map how galaxies cluster in space. To read that map, scientists must model redshift-space distortions. These distortions arise because galaxy motions stretch the map along the line of sight.

Accurate models are essential to squeeze full value from the data. The team tests three approaches to modeling the effect. They apply them to the power spectrum multipoles of mock galaxies. The mock galaxies emit the H-alpha line, a standard marker. The study is groundwork for the real survey analysis. It helps ensure that Euclid's map of the universe is read without bias.
arxiv-2601-21026:
Louis Grenioux and Maxence Noble explore generators that sample matter at thermal balance. Their 2026 paper studies diffusion-based annealed Boltzmann generators. Sampling such states is a central challenge in statistical physics. Boltzmann generators pair a generative model with a Monte Carlo fix-up step. The fix-up yields unbiased samples from an unnormalized target. Most such generators use classic fix-ups, such as importance sampling.

Those fix-ups carry two burdens. They need tractable likelihoods from the base model. And they scale poorly in high-dimensional, multi-modal targets. The authors weigh the benefits and pitfalls of a diffusion-based design. Annealing eases the path from noise to target in steps. The paper is candid about hopes and limits. It guides physicists who simulate molecules and materials.
arxiv-2601-21526:
Alireza Nadafian, Alireza Mohammadshahi, and Majid Yazdani present a framework that writes and improves programs on its own. Given a goal in plain words and a way to score results, the system cycles through stages. It drafts ideas, writes code, runs it, scores it, and learns from the outcome.

Each loop aims to push a working artifact closer to the stated goals. Grounding the loop in outside knowledge keeps the search from wandering. A modular build lets teams swap parts for their own tasks. The framework targets research and engineering chores where the target is clear enough to measure.
arxiv-2601-21626:
Jinhao Zhang, Yunquan Zhang, Zicheng Yan, Boyang Zhang, Jun Sun, and Daning Cheng fix a paradox in compressing language models. Post-training quantization shrinks models by rounding their numbers. It often shows low rounding error yet high loss, which seems contradictory.

The cause lies in the shape of the loss landscape. A few high-curvature directions are extremely sensitive to small nudges. Errors there cost far more than errors elsewhere. Their method conditions the problem using that curvature map, so rounding avoids the fragile directions. Steadier compression keeps small models accurate enough for real use on modest hardware.
arxiv-2601-21926:
Jinhao Zhang and co-authors try to slim down the networks that teach robots to move. Diffusion-based visuomotor policies learn complex skills from three-dimensional visual input, and they perform strongly. But most designs use an oversized denoising decoder, the part that turns noise into action.

The authors note that more capacity can help denoising, yet evidence suggests it also adds redundancy and noise in the middle feature blocks. Their 2026 preprint uses information filtering, guided by variational regularization, to strip out what the policy does not need. Leaner policies would run faster on robot hardware and react quicker, which matters when a robot arm must correct itself mid-motion.
arxiv-2601-22026:
Constantin Kleinbeck and co-authors render medical volumes fast enough for immersive use. Three-dimensional scans hold rich information about disease, but flat slices force clinicians to rebuild anatomy mentally. Direct volumetric path tracing in virtual reality gives true spatial understanding, yet it is computationally expensive.

The team's 2026 preprint mixes two techniques. Sharp path tracing covers the fovea, the center of vision where detail matters, while smooth Gaussian representations fill the periphery, where the eye notices less. That hybrid foveated approach targets immersive anatomy viewers that stay fluid on real hardware. Better spatial views could help surgeons plan operations and students learn anatomy from real patient data.
arxiv-2601-22226:
Edoardo Latini, Fausto Rossi, and Fabrizio Dolcini set out a new way to build a qubit, the basic unit of a quantum computer. Their 2026 preprint uses the edge states of a thin material that acts as a topological insulator. A Josephson junction and added magnetic atoms complete the setup.

The team shows that spin states in this setup can form a working qubit. They also show that pulses of microwave light can steer the qubit through shifts in its spin states. The plan gives labs a fresh route to test. It may aid work on small, stable quantum parts.
arxiv-2601-22826:
Dart-yin A. Soh builds a model for how photons can create vector mesons, heavy particles of light-matter interaction. The model rests on Regge theory and a soft dipole Pomeron, a tool for describing high-energy scattering. It handles photons with any kind of polarization, round or linear.

The model fits three kinds of data at once: total rates, momentum patterns, and spin patterns for one key meson. Fitting all three pins down its twenty free settings with care. Good models of this process help plan and read particle physics experiments.
arxiv-2601-23026:
Hendrik Suhr, David Kaltenpoth, and Jilles Vreeken separate two kinds of anomaly that are usually lumped together. A value may look wrong because it was recorded badly, while the real process ran fine. Or the process itself may have changed, shifting how data are generated.

Root cause methods that ignore this split can blame the wrong features. Their causal characterization distinguishes measurement errors from mechanism shifts. The distinction matters in factories and hospitals, where a sensor fault and a real failure demand opposite responses. Measurement anomalies and mechanism shifts demand different remedies, which is why telling them apart is operationally valuable.
arxiv-2601-23126:
Pascal Lenzner and Paraskevi Machaira study routing games where each sender sees only its local network. Modern networks mix many autonomous entities, from smart devices to parts of AI systems. Each has a local view and must rely on a local protocol to forward packets.

The authors analyze when greedy routing, always forwarding toward the target, can reach its destination. Selfish local choices can loop or stall in the worst case. Understanding reachability helps design protocols that work without central control. Local views are the realistic constraint, since no device in a vast network can hold the whole map.
arxiv-2603-01526:
Adapting one large model to many tasks at once often works at small scale, then collapses as tasks pile up. Zichen Tian, Antoine Ledent, and Qianru Sun diagnose that collapse in this 2026 study of low-rank adaptation. They trace it to clashes between task updates and to blurred traits that routing needs.

The team finds that shared knowledge sits in strong components, while uniform rules force those parts apart. Working at block level, rather than on small pieces, cuts gradient clashes a lot with fewer settings. Their fix, mtLoRA, guards strong parts, adapts by blocks, and routes with fine per-dimension weights. Across vision and language suites with many tasks, it beat top rivals while using fewer settings and less training time.
arxiv-2603-01626:
Xinxun Zhang, Pengfei Jiao, Mengzhou Gao, and colleagues help graph models cope when data patterns shift over time. Their 2026 work studies dynamic graphs, where nodes and links evolve, in fields from social feeds to traffic. Most models assume test data matches training data, yet real streams drift in ways that break that match.

Their model, DyCIL, hunts for steady causal patterns inside the changing graph. A generator first pulls out dynamic subgraphs that carry the causal core of each change. An attention module then reads how those core patterns evolve through space and time. A third part invents varied shift settings, so training sees more kinds of drift. Tests on real and synthetic dynamic graphs beat top baselines under distribution shift.
arxiv-2603-02226:
Bojian Yin, Shurong Wang, Haoyu Tan, and colleagues rethink how recurrent networks handle long signals in this 2026 paper. Audio and video hold brief key moments inside long stretches of quiet or noise. Standard recurrent networks update their memory at every step, even when nothing changes. That habit erases old memory and blocks learning from distant events.

Their network, the suRNN, gives each neuron a switch that opens only for useful input. During dull stretches, memory stays exactly as it was, untouched. Learning signals can then flow straight back across long gaps. On long-range tests and text data, suRNNs matched or beat far larger models. They did so while staying much cheaper for long-term storage of past events.
arxiv-2603-02426:
Leo Muxing Wang, Pengkun Yang, and Lili Su study cooperative learning across agents in this 2026 paper. Each agent faces its own environment and learns its own value function. A shared linear representation links them, with personal weights lying in one unknown subspace. Borrowing from personalized federated learning, agents jointly estimate that subspace and their local parts.

The single-timescale method runs all updates together, without nested loops. Splitting shared and personal parts filters out conflicting signals between agents. Misaligned signals otherwise drag learning in wrong directions. The analysis proves a linear speedup from cooperation. Challenges include agent differences, Markovian sampling, and tightly coupled error dynamics. Experiments on a broader control problem confirm the shared-structure gains.
arxiv-2603-02526:
Yi Zhang, Yichao Wang, Wei Xiao, and colleagues protect automated vehicles from data attacks in this 2026 paper. Connected automated vehicles share roads with human drivers whose behavior is uncertain. False data attacks can corrupt acceleration inputs with growing, unbounded fakes. Safety methods assume honest data, while resilient methods often ignore crash risk.

Their event-driven framework fuses both concerns into one controller. Barrier functions enforce safety and Lyapunov functions enforce stability, both checked at events, not constantly. Adaptive control absorbs attack effects, and human driver behavior is estimated from data. The test case is lane changing amid unpredictable human drivers. Simulations show crash-free maneuvers and stable speed under attack. The method beat conventional safety-only controllers in their comparisons.
arxiv-2603-02926:
Qiming He, Jing Li, Tian Guan, and colleagues train a foundation model devoted to the kidney's tiny filtering units. GloPath, presented in 2026, learned from over a million glomeruli drawn from more than fourteen thousand biopsy samples. These structures vary widely, and their fine lesion patterns drive diagnosis and prognosis in kidney disease.

Across three separate cohorts and dozens of tasks, from lesion grading to few-shot sorting, GloPath beat leading methods in most head-to-head tests. A large real-world study confirmed strong accuracy for lesion recognition in routine practice. The model also linked measurable tissue traits to clinical indicators across hundreds of trait pairs. The authors present it as a scalable, readable platform for kidney pathology and discovery.
arxiv-2603-03126:
Jonas Wilinski assembles nearly three hundred million papers into one searchable lake. Scholarly records sit scattered across siloed databases with clashing metadata and missing links. His 2026 Science Data Lake unifies eight open sources, from Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex to Retraction Watch and Crossref, on a single local setup.

Records join through normalized DOIs while each source keeps its own schema, stored as plain files a single drive can hold. An embedding-based alignment maps thousands of topics onto thirteen scientific ontologies with strong measured accuracy, beating classic text-matching baselines. Ten automated checks and cross-source citation comparisons validate the merge. Four showcase analyses demonstrate questions no single database could answer alone.
arxiv-2603-03226:
Enea Monzio Compagnoni and four colleagues compare training methods that protect privacy in the data they learn from. Differential privacy adds noise so no single example can be picked out, but that noise interacts with the optimizer, the rule that updates the model. Their 2026 paper gives the first analysis of private optimizers using stochastic differential equations, a tool for tracking noisy change over time.

Two methods face off: standard private gradient descent and an adaptive sign-based variant. With fixed settings the adaptive method wins clearly in high-privacy regimes, and its best learning rate barely changes as privacy tightens, so settings transfer without retuning. Experiments back the theory and extend the advantage to a private form of the popular Adam optimizer.
arxiv-2603-03326:
Florian Hoppe and three colleagues give language models personality sliders that users can adjust directly. Setting a persona today usually means costly fine-tuning, with a separate trained model for every personality profile. Steering the model's internal activations at run time is cheaper, but pushing several traits at once makes the steering signals interfere and garble the result.

Their 2026 method, Sequential Adaptive Steering, fixes the interference. Each new steering direction is trained on the model's internal state after earlier adjustments, so the directions stay compatible and reusable. Users then blend traits by turning coefficients up or down, with no change to the model's weights. Tested on the Big Five personality traits, the approach beat naive steering on both hitting the target personality and keeping replies coherent.

arxiv-2605-09126: DiLoCo trains models across scattered workers that drift out of sync — staleness is the enemy. Vatsal Shah and Jiahao Sun propose Cosine-Gated Adam-Decay, a drop-in staleness-aware outer optimizer for the decoupled variant. The 2026 paper keeps distributed training honest when workers lag behind.
arxiv-2605-09326: Magnetically arrested disks — MADs — are black holes choked by their own magnetic fields, cooled by radiation into filaments. Akshay Singh, Damien Bégué, and Asaf Pe'er characterize their scale height and filamentary structure. The 2026 paper is high-energy astrophysics on nature's most extreme engines.
arxiv-2605-09526: Klein surfaces generalize Riemann surfaces to allow non-orientability; their moduli space is a counting ground. N. K. Chidambaram, E. Garcia-Failde, A. Giacchetto, and K. Osuga refine lattice point counting on it. The 2026 paper is geometry meets number theory.
arxiv-2605-09626: Rectifiable curves — those with finite length — in the plane seem elementary, yet old questions linger stubbornly alongside new ones. Boris Shapiro and Guillaume Tahar survey the landscape, old and new. The 2026 paper is a geometric tour from classical results to current frontiers.
arxiv-2605-09726: Testing whether an jamming model is correctly specified — via exposure mappings — turns out to be impossible in general. Chao Gao, Christopher Harshaw, Fredrik Sävje, and Yitan Wang prove the impossibility tightly. The 2026 paper is a sobering negative result in causal read.
arxiv-2605-09826: Theory of mind — modeling what others believe and want — matters for embodied agents acting in the physical world. Gurusha Juneja, Dylan Lu, Saaket Agashe, and others build EnactToM: an evolving benchmark for functional theory of mind. The 2026 paper tests whether agents can read minds.
arxiv-2605-10026: 3D object detection for autonomous driving must adapt across domains, data sources, and modalities — without labels. bailey-epicurus-extant-remains-1926:
Epicurus taught in his Athens garden in the early third century BCE and wrote a great deal, yet almost all of it is lost. Cyril Bailey gathered all that survives into one Oxford volume in 1926. His edition gives the Greek text with his own English version, along with notes and a critical apparatus.

Inside are three letters, to Herodotus, Pythocles, and Menoeceus, that sum up his physics and his ethics. Next come the Principal Doctrines, forty short sayings, and the Vatican Sayings, found in a single manuscript. Bailey's notes explain the hard points. For English readers of its day, this volume was the standard Epicurus.
barrett-besterman-divining-rod-1926:
William F Barrett, a physicist, and Theodore Besterman published The Divining Rod in 1926, after years of study for the Society for Psychical Research. Their subject was dowsing, the old practice of finding water or metal with a forked rod that twists in the hands. Many well diggers swore by it.

Field tests, case reports, and past records fill the book, along with a study of how the rod moves. The authors looked for trickery, chance, and knowledge of the land that a dowser might not know he had. Their inquiry, among the last big SPR field studies, treats a folk craft with full scientific care.
bernier-travels-mogul-empire-vol1-1826:
François Bernier, a French doctor, spent twelve years in India and served at the court of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb. Volume One of his Travels, in Brock's 1826 translation, reports what he saw between 1656 and 1668. It is the classic European account of Mughal India.

Bernier describes the war of succession among Shah Jahan's sons, the wealth of Delhi, and the habits of the court. He writes as a trained observer of medicine, trade, and religion. His letters home shaped how Europe pictured India for a century. Few early travelers match his mix of access and clear prose.
bernier-travels-mogul-empire-vol2-1826:
Volume Two of Bernier's Travels in the Mogul Empire continues his account of India under Aurangzeb. The French physician had traveled with the court and seen the empire at close range. Brock's translation completes the work in this volume.

The highlight is Bernier's trip to Kashmir with the emperor's camp, a rare early picture of that valley. He also writes on the Ganges delta, Hindu customs, and the burning of widows, which he condemns. His remarks on trade and land rent drew later thinkers on Asia. Together the two volumes remain a prime source on seventeenth-century India.
bible-tyndale-new-testament-1526:
William Tyndale put the New Testament into English and saw it printed in 1526, the first printed English New Testament. He worked from Greek, not Latin, and paid for the work with exile. Church leaders banned his text, yet copies spread fast across England.

Readers get the four Gospels, Acts, the letters of Paul and others, and Revelation. Tyndale wrote in plain, strong English that later Bibles kept. Much of the King James wording starts here. His version changed how English people read Scripture and how English prose sounds. Its cadence rings through church and school to this day.
black-tertiary-man-asia-choukoutien-1926:
Davidson Black, a Canadian anatomist working in China, announced the Choukoutien discovery in Science in 1926. Fossil teeth had come from a cave deposit near Peking, now Beijing. Black saw them as evidence of very early humans in Asia.

He argues Asia may have been a center from which humans spread. The announcement launched the excavations that soon produced Peking Man. Those fossils, later classed as Homo erectus, became world famous. The originals were lost during wartime, adding mystery to the story. Black's short paper opened one of paleoanthropology's great chapters.
bolivian-constitution-1826:
Bolivia's first constitution was adopted in 1826, and it came almost straight from Simón Bolívar's own hand. The Liberator had freed the country that took his name. A congress in Chuquisaca asked him for a charter, and he sent his draft with a famous speech.

The text creates a president who holds office for life, with the right to name his successor. Beside him sit three chambers, including censors charged with guarding morals and the constitution itself. Bolívar argued that a new nation, torn by war, needed a fixed point of authority to survive. Chuquisaca adopted the charter, and Sucre became the first president under it. The lifetime presidency scared many, and the charter lasted only a few years. It remains Bolívar's political last will, written into law.
cather-my-mortal-enemy-1926:
My Mortal Enemy, published in 1926, is Cather's short, pitiless novella of Myra Henshawe, remembered by a younger woman who knew her in youth and in ruin. Myra had given up a fortune to elope with Oswald Henshawe for love.

Years later the couple live poor and diminished, and Myra's bitterness turns on the man she chose. Her dying words name him her mortal enemy. Cather strips the elopement romance to the bone in barely a hundred pages. The late style here is bare, hard, and unforgettable, among the most perfect things she wrote in fiction.
churchward-lost-continent-mu-1926:
Colonel James Churchward claimed a lost continent, Mu, once filled the Pacific Ocean. His 1926 book The Lost Continent of Mu calls it the motherland of man. He said old tablets in India taught him its story.

Churchward describes a rich, wise land that sank in a great quake. Its people, he argues, seeded Egypt, India, and the Americas. Maps, symbols, and stone marks serve as his proof. Scholars reject the tale for lack of hard evidence. Yet the book became a fringe classic, still read by seekers of lost worlds.
cia-0000009726:

Enemy publications became unlikely sources for the prisoner accounting. A photograph in a propaganda sheet could prove a man alive and held. Analysts therefore read the other side's press with close, hostile care. This file records that practice: a weekly bulletin mined for names, faces, and dates the enemy never meant to give.

Construction reports revealed the prison system's growth from the ground up. New bunkers also signaled where bombing could endanger the very men it meant to pressure. Officials logged the site for both reasons. This file preserves the building report as received, an entry in the strange architecture of captivity in the war's last year.

The mid-fifties balance it strikes set a baseline for a generation of defense planning. It measures the bear's strength at the Cold War's heightening. For readers, the estimate shows the superpower contest being priced, in forces and intentions, by the men charged with knowing.

clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-1:
Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, was Charles I's closest adviser through the English Civil War. His History of the Rebellion tells that war from inside the king's council. The history was published in 1702 to 1704, after his death. Volume one here opens the Oxford edition of 1826, which runs to eight volumes.

Clarendon blends memoir with history: he knew the actors, sat in their councils, and weighed their characters. His portraits of the age's great men remain famous for their shrewdness and grace. The royalist cause has no fuller or finer advocate. Volume one begins the grandest English narrative of the civil wars.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-2:
Volume two continues Clarendon's History of the Rebellion in the Oxford edition of 1826. Edward Hyde wrote the history from his own years at the heart of royalist power, and it was published in 1702 to 1704. The work runs to eight volumes in this edition, each thick with council, camp, and character.

Clarendon's strength is the portrait: friend and foe alike stand forth as living men with mixed motives. He defends the king's cause while blaming royal errors with striking candor. The narrative carries the war's early campaigns in stately, rolling prose. For the inner story of Charles I's court at war, no source stands beside Clarendon. Volume two deepens that story.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-3:
The Oxford edition of Clarendon's History of the Rebellion reaches volume three of eight. Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, had served Charles I as chancellor and chief counselor before exile and disgrace. His history, published in 1702 to 1704, grew from notes and memory gathered across a lifetime in high politics.

Volume three holds the war's middle passage, where negotiation and battle chased each other year by year. Clarendon writes with a minister's grasp of paper, money, and men. His judgments on the great figures of the age shaped how later centuries saw them. The book is at once a royalist brief and a work of literature, and this volume keeps both alive.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-4:
Volume four of Clarendon's History of the Rebellion follows the Oxford edition of 1826, though this volume comes from the 1827 printing of the same edition. Edward Hyde wrote the history from his place in Charles I's council, and it was published in 1702 to 1704 in eight volumes. The 1826 scan from Toronto could not be had, so the matched 1827 printing serves.

The fourth volume stands mid-war, where Clarendon's double gift shows best: narrative of events and portraits of the men who drove them. His account of the king's cause is partisan, learned, and deeply felt. No other royalist history matches its access or its art. The set reads whole with this volume in its proper place.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-5:
Volume five continues the 1826 Oxford Clarendon, the History of the Rebellion and Civil Wars in England. Edward Hyde wrote the work across his years of power and exile, and it appeared in 1702 to 1704 in eight volumes in this edition. Few historians have written about events in which they played so large a part.

That nearness gives the narrative its weight: decisions of the king's council are told by a man who sat in it. Clarendon's measured prose hides strong feeling for the lost royalist cause. His character sketches, generous and severe by turns, remain models of the art. Volume five carries the war toward its end, with the council chamber always in view.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-6:
Clarendon's History of the Rebellion moves through volume six of the Oxford edition of 1826. Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, began the history during the war itself, at the urging of friends who saw it slipping into legend. The published work of 1702 to 1704 fills eight volumes in this edition.

The later volumes trace the royalist cause through defeat, exile, and the long wait for restoration. Clarendon never writes as a mere partisan: he scores his own side's blunders with care. His great gift, the lifelike portrait, stays sharp to the end. Readers meet the English Civil War here as tragedy told by a chief actor. Volume six keeps that telling grave and full.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-7:
Volume seven of the 1826 Oxford edition brings Clarendon's History of the Rebellion near its close. Edward Hyde wrote the history as the chief minister and counselor of Charles I, and its publication ran from 1702 to 1704. The eight-volume Oxford set is the classic form of the work.

In these later pages the war's outcome is sealed, and Clarendon turns to judgment: of men, of measures, of the causes that ruined a kingdom. His prose keeps its stately balance even in bitterness. No other royalist source matches his access to the king's mind and councils. Volume seven holds the penultimate share of the greatest memoir-history of the English civil wars.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-8:
Volume eight completes the Oxford edition of 1826 of Clarendon's History of the Rebellion and Civil Wars in England. Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, wrote the work from inside Charles I's council, and it was published in 1702 to 1704. Eight volumes hold the whole of his vast, personal history.

The closing volume ends the story of a kingdom torn apart and a cause lost and, in time, restored. Clarendon's portraits and judgments set the terms in which the civil wars were debated for two centuries. His book stands as the great royalist memoir-history, literary and documentary at once. To close volume eight is to finish the fullest inside account of England's great rebellion.
constitution-barbados-2026: Barbados' Constitution, reformed toward republic status, frames its island state. It cut the Crown in 2021. The Tower library holds the full text. It crowned a republic. Queen left. President rose. People chose. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-kazakhstan-2026: Kazakhstan's 1995 Constitution, amended through 2026, frames its republic. It renamed the capital twice. The Tower library holds the full text. It ordered the steppe. Soviets left. Oil flowed. Power centered. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
cooper-last-of-the-mohicans-1826:
James Fenimore Cooper published The Last of the Mohicans in 1826, the second Leatherstocking tale and his most famous book. Cooper set it in 1757, during the French and Indian War, around the fall of Fort William Henry. He claimed the story grew from a visit to Lake George with British tourists.

Hawkeye, the white scout raised beside the Mohicans Chingachgook and his son Uncas, guides two sisters through a war-torn forest. The Huron villain Magua pursues them with patience and hatred. Captures, rescues, and massacres follow across glens and caverns Cooper made iconic. The title's tragedy gathers force as the old order of the forest dies with Uncas. The novel became the archetypal American adventure and the most translated early American book.
cross-true-masonic-chart-1826:
Jeremy L Cross published The True Masonic Chart in 1826, and it became a well known American guide to lodge ritual. Cross was a traveling Masonic teacher who helped spread a shared form of work across many lodges. His chart used pictures as memory aids for members.

Rows of symbols, tools, and scenes, called hieroglyphic emblems, helped Masons recall the lessons of each degree. The text around them gave the order and sense of the ritual without printing every secret word. For historians, the chart shows how American Masonry taught itself, and how pictures carried meaning that words alone were not meant to hold.
cummings-is-5-1926:
E. E. Cummings published is 5 in 1926, his second major collection of poems. By then his experiments with broken lines, scattered type, and lowercase letters were becoming famous. He divided the book into sections that move from satire to love poems.

The best-known piece here, anyone lived in a pretty how town, tells a whole life in a few musical, looping lines. Other poems mock politicians and professors, then soften into tender songs about lovers and seasons. Cummings plays with grammar the way jazz musicians play with rhythm. The collection shows him at his most beloved and most daring at once.
defoe-history-of-the-devil-1726:
Daniel Defoe, the English writer of Robinson Crusoe, published his History of the Devil at London in 1726. The full title adds 'as well ancient as modern,' and the book runs in two parts. Defoe treats Satan as a figure with a long public career.

He traces the devil through the Bible, Milton's Paradise Lost, the Crusades, and the age of witch trials. Then he jokes that Satan has moved on to softer prey: fine ladies, wits, and fools of fashion. The result is part history, part satire, and pure Defoe.
defoe-political-history-of-the-devil-172:
Daniel Defoe, the novelist of Robinson Crusoe, published The Political History of the Devil in 1726. The book traces Satan's career from the Fall through the witchcraft panics of Defoe's own recent past. It is the great Augustan synthesis of demonology and skepticism, belief and doubt in one shrewd mind.

Defoe mocks credulous tales of pacts and apparitions while still treating the Devil as a real political schemer in human affairs. He sorts scripture, history, and street gossip with a journalist's nose for a weak story. The result reads like a skeptical sermon, funny and unsettling by turns.
doe-osti-17154913-petsc-tao-users-manual: PETSc/TAO users got their revision 3.26, and this manual updates the documentation. The pages explain the solvers. The computational scientists get their reference. The revision was 3.26. The solvers were PETSc. The scientists got references. The manual was revision. The docs were solver.

doe-osti-3374174-science-amp-technology-: Tsunamis got science-reviewed, and this DOE June 2026 predicts tsunamis. The pages detail the technology findings. The scientists get their data. doe-osti-3375711-mod-amp-system-design-s: MOD-Amp got spring-designed, and this DOE Spring 2026 covers Georgetown systems. The pages detail the design findings. The students get their data. doe-osti-3376038-energy-technology-provi: Proving Ground got FY-2026-planned, and this DOE Rev.1 covers program plans. The pages detail the energy findings. The energy folks get their data. The plan was technology. The data were energy. The FY-2026 were ground. The program were plan.
doe-osti-3451869-ornl-hep-self-appraisal: ORNL HEP got FY2026-appraised, and this DOE self-appraisal covers the year. The pages detail the appraisal findings. The physicists get their data. The appraisal was self. The data were physicist. The FY2026 were appraisal. The ORNL were self.
doyle-land-of-mist-1926:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote The Land of Mist in 1926. Doyle gave his last years to the spirit creed and its cause. The tale brings back Professor Challenger, now old and fierce in grief. His child Enid and a young news man lead the tale's probe.

Seances, spirit guides, and tales of the dead fill the crew's path. Challenger fights the creed at first, then falls to its proofs one by one. Doyle meant the tale as a plea for faith in life past death. It is his clear creed told in the dress of a tale.
dunsany-charwomans-shadow-1926:
Dunsany turned to comedy in The Charwoman's Shadow, his novel of 1926. A young lord trades his shadow to a magician for gold to win his love. The lighter twin of the Elfland book, it completes his great fantasy run of the 1920s.

The lost shadow draws the hero into a Spain of enchantment, bandits, and a scheming mage. A charwoman's own shadow holds a key to the cure, as the title hints. The book charms where its mate awed, and its wit is warm. It shows Dunsany could laugh in the worlds he made grave.
eichendorff-aus-dem-leben-eines-taugenic:
A miller's son with a fiddle, no money, and no plan walks out of his father's mill to seek his fortune. Eichendorff's Aus dem Leben eines Taugenichts, published in 1826 and given here in German, made that good-for-nothing the most beloved figure of German Romanticism. Adventures, mistaken identities, and romantic Italy crowd his road.

The Taugenichts drifts through gardens, castles, and a countess's household, lucky where others would starve. Poetry and song save him as often as wit does. Lazy, lyrical, and eternal, he embodies the Romantic hunger for the open road. No German book captures that wanderlust more perfectly. Readers have been packing his knapsack in their imaginations for two hundred years.
elements-of-phrenology-1826: Elements of Phrenology, 1826. The phrenological elements. This book preserves that work. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it.
engels-peasant-war-germany-olgin-1926:
Engels wrote The Peasant War in Germany in 1850, on the great revolt of 1525. Moissaye J. Olgin translated it for International Publishers in 1926. German peasants had risen against lords and princes three centuries earlier. Thomas Munzer, the radical preacher, leads the most daring wing in Engels's account.

Engels reads the revolt through class struggle, the first such Marxist history. Peasants, burghers, and nobles act from their place in the order of the day. Defeat, he argues, came from division among the rebels. The book set a pattern for Marxist history writing. It also rescued Munzer as a hero of the left. The narrative moves fast and hard.
europmc-pmc10353926:
Ballester and a large team counted heat deaths in Europe in the summer of 2022. That summer was the hottest on record for the region. The team used death counts from 823 areas in 35 nations, for over 543 million people. They sought the burden of heat, 19 years after the deadly summer of 2003.

The team put heat deaths at 61,672 for late May to early September. Italy had the most deaths, at 18,010, then Spain and Germany. Per million people, Italy, Greece, Spain, and Portugal had the worst rates. Women faced 56% more heat deaths than men. Ballester calls for stronger heat watch systems and better long-term plans.
europmc-pmc10427426:
Mosele and a large team ran the DAISY trial in 2023 on a breast cancer drug that pairs an antibody with a cell poison. The drug seeks HER2, a growth protein on some cancer cells. Patients fell into three groups by HER2 level: high, low, and none. All had cancer that had spread.

Response rates split sharply by HER2 level. Mosele reports shrinkage in 70.6% of the high group and 37.5% of the low group. Even the no-HER2 group hit 29.7%, a surprise result. Stain tests showed the drug reached tumours in line with HER2 level. The team argues that HER2 guides the drug, but other paths may add to its effect. No new safety flags arose.
europmc-pmc10453126:
Caturano and co-authors reviewed in 2023 how cell stress from oxygen harms people with type 2 diabetes. The stress grows when reactive oxygen, unstable bits that attack cells, outruns the body's shields. High blood sugar and faulty cell power units both raise that load. The load then damages cells across many organs.

Stress harms the cells that make insulin and blunts the body's response to it. Caturano links it to eye, kidney, and nerve damage, and to disease of the heart and vessels. Fixes range from strict sugar control to diet and lifestyle shifts. Drugs that soak up reactive oxygen form a further line of work. Proof of their worth in patients is still thin, the authors note.
europmc-pmc10635526:
Tang and co-authors built SRplot in 2023, a free web tool for drawing science charts. Charts sum up complex data in most research papers. Past tools demand coding skill, cost money, or tie users to one system. SRplot runs in any web browser with no install.

Users paste data into a text box in a set format. Tang stocked the tool with over a hundred chart types used in labs. Edits show at once, and charts export in print-grade forms, from PNG to PDF. The charts have appeared in more than 500 peer-reviewed papers. The team updates the site fast in reply to user feedback.
europmc-pmc11026526:
Xia, Sun, Huang, and Jin review the reuse of approved drugs as cancer treatments in this 2024 paper. Cancer care has improved with surgery, radiation, and immune therapy, yet drug therapy stays central. Its power is often curbed by resistance and harsh side effects. Finding new uses for drugs already approved offers a shortcut, since their safety is known.

The review sorts the methods used to spot such second uses. It details how candidate drugs attack cancer traits inside tumour cells and in the tissue around them. Pairing this reuse with modern data tools is treated as a rising strategy. The authors note the cost and speed gains: known drugs skip years of safety testing. They frame reuse as a practical complement to new drug discovery, not a replacement for it.
europmc-pmc1175026:
Le Maitre, Freemont, and Hoyland test whether a cytokine drives human spinal disc degeneration in this 2005 study. Intervertebral discs are the cushions between spine bones, and their degeneration causes much back pain. The cytokine IL-1 is a potent inflammatory signal. The team hypothesised that disc cells make IL-1 locally and that it then induces the cell and matrix changes of degeneration.

Staining of human discs located five IL-1 family members in the tissue, they report. Native disc cells from both healthy and degenerate discs produced the agonists, the antagonist, the active receptor, and the converting enzyme. Positivity for most of these proteins increased with severity of degeneration. Treating cultured disc cells with IL-1 shifted expression of matrix-degrading enzymes and matrix proteins. The findings support IL-1 as a local driver of degeneration.
europmc-pmc11927026:
Markus and Brainin gave a global view on COVID-19 and stroke in 2020. They wrote for the World Stroke Organization. Stroke patients seem prone to severe infection and poor outcomes. At the same time, the pandemic reshaped how stroke care runs.

Hospitals first saw a sharp fall in stroke arrivals. Services worldwide reported strain and delays. Infection itself was also described as a stroke risk factor. Markus highlights remote care as a bright spot with lasting value. Protecting staff and patients at once became a core challenge. Telemedicine use grew fast during the same period.
europmc-pmc1240126:
Laden, Neas, Dockery, and Schwartz linked air particles to daily deaths in 2000. Fine particles in city air come from several sources. Past work tied total fine particle mass to daily mortality. Which sources drove the harm stayed open.

Chemical fingerprints split particles into source groups for six cities. Groups included soil dust, vehicle exhaust, and coal burning. Death records were matched to daily levels of each group. Models adjusted for weather and time trends. Laden shows source-specific risks, not just total mass, matter for health. Death counts came from national health statistics records.
europmc-pmc1247526:
Gong and colleagues followed aflatoxin exposure and child growth in Benin in 2004. Aflatoxins are mold poisons in food that can cause liver cancer. They also stunt growth in animals. Human growth evidence was thin despite high West African exposure.

Two hundred toddlers from four villages were followed for eight months. Blood markers of aflatoxin rose sharply from February to October. Rises were largest in the higher-exposure villages. Fully weaned children carried higher blood markers than breastfed peers. Growth measures were tracked at three visits. Gong links postweaning diet to impaired growth with direct data.
europmc-pmc1310926:
Ward and co-authors reported a workgroup review of nitrate in drinking water in 2005. Human activity has steadily raised nitrate in water resources. Legal limits were set to protect infants from a blood disorder. Some scientists called the limit too strict, citing only acute effects.

An August 2004 symposium weighed chronic outcomes against the limit. Focus fell on nitrate feeding formation of N-nitroso compounds inside the body. Certain groups form those compounds at higher rates. Health effects depend on intake, co-factors, and medical conditions together. Ward lists research needed before loosening standards.
europmc-pmc1334226:
Chi and co-authors profiled gene programs under low oxygen across cell types in 2006. Low oxygen, or hypoxia, reshapes cell behavior in health and disease. A factor called HIF directs much of that response. How the response varies by cell type was little known.

Four human cell types were tracked over time on DNA chips. Kidney tubule cells mounted the largest transcriptional response. Their height linked to uniquely high levels of the HIF-1alpha protein. Breast, muscle, and vessel cells each showed distinct programs. Chi connects those programs to cancer prognosis in the analysis.
europmc-pmc1367826:
Hardman reviewed quantum dot toxicity and its governing factors in 2006. Quantum dots are engineered nanoscale crystals with wide uses. Medicine, electronics, energy, and aerospace all employ them. The nano economy was projected near one trillion dollars by 2012.

Not all quantum dots are alike, the review stresses. Engineered dots cannot be treated as one uniform substance. Absorption, distribution, and breakdown vary with physical chemistry. Surroundings change toxicity as much as the dots themselves. Hardman organizes evidence dot property by dot property. Safety testing must specify exact materials and conditions. Dose and coating change the risk a lot. Dots can be made in more than one size and with more than one coat. Each change can shift how they act in the body.
europmc-pmc1413526:
Genes that switch on together often work together. Carlson and co-authors mapped those links in yeast in 2006, using many gene activity data sets. They built webs where each gene is a point and strong shared activity forms a tie. Some genes, called hubs, hold far more ties than most.

Hub genes were more likely to be vital for yeast survival. Their DNA also changed less over time than that of loosely tied genes. Carlson found the webs break into modules, groups with tight inner ties. Inside rich modules, tie counts could flag which genes matter most for a given task.
europmc-pmc1463026:
Genes rich in the DNA letters G and C speak louder than genes poor in them. Kudla and co-authors proved that in 2006 by a clean test. They built rich and poor versions of three genes, keeping the protein code the same. Each pair sat behind the same switch and flanks in mammal cells.

The rich versions made far more protein, up to a hundred times more. The gap came from higher RNA levels, not faster protein building or slower RNA decay. Kudla concludes that silent letter choices, which leave proteins unchanged, still steer how much RNA a gene yields. That fact matters for gene design.
europmc-pmc1481526:
Root fungi that feed plants need a signal that a host is near. Besserer and co-authors found that signal's effect in 2006. Roots release strigolactones, compounds also known for waking parasitic weed seeds. In earlier work, one such compound made fungus branches sprout.

Treating fungus spores with strigolactones sparked fast cell growth at tiny doses. Within an hour, the cells' power plants, mitochondria, grew dense and changed shape and motion. Two other fungus species woke as well, breathing faster. Besserer concludes these plant signals start the partnership before roots and fungi touch. The same cue betrays the plant to parasitic weeds.
europmc-pmc1888726:
Melov, Bush and co-authors tested in 2007 whether oxidative stress inside mitochondria can set off a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease. That hallmark is excess phosphate tagging of tau, a protein that then tangles inside brain cells. Mice lacking the protective enzyme SOD2 suffer severe mitochondrial oxidative stress and die young unless given catalytic antioxidants.

With low antioxidant doses the mice lived longer but revealed brain pathology. Their tau carried strikingly high phosphate levels at sites tied to Alzheimer's, including the spot numbered Ser-396. A higher antioxidant dose, already known to prevent the brain damage, blocked that excess tagging. The team also bred the enzyme defect into an Alzheimer's model to extend the test. The dose pattern makes a causal case: mitochondrial oxidative stress drives tau hyperphosphorylation, and quenching it prevents the change.
europmc-pmc1925126:
Munro, Volmink and co-authors reviewed in 2007 the qualitative research on why tuberculosis patients do or do not finish treatment. TB is a major global disease burden, tightly linked with HIV in poorer countries. Courses last months, and stopping early breeds relapse and drug resistance, yet programs lacked a full picture of the barriers.

The team searched 19 databases covering 1966 to early 2005 for studies reporting the views of patients, caregivers, and health workers. Citation chasing and expert contacts added more. Each included study was quality-checked with a set list, and two reviewers pulled the data separately onto a standard form. The synthesis followed an established method for pooling qualitative findings. The aim was a holistic account that programs could act on, spanning money, services, knowledge, and social pressures.
europmc-pmc1963326:
Cohen reviewed Sweet's syndrome in 2007, a rare skin disease also called acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis. Its signature bundle is fever and a high count of neutrophil white blood cells. Tender red skin papules, nodules, and plaques complete the picture. Under the microscope, mature neutrophils pack the upper skin layer. Several hundred cases had been published by then.

The syndrome appears in three settings. The classical form mostly strikes women aged 30 to 50, often follows a chest infection, and links to bowel inflammation and pregnancy, with about a third of patients relapsing. A second form rides alongside cancer, most often acute myelogenous leukemia, and can precede the cancer diagnosis, making it a warning sign. A third form is drug-induced. The review gathers diagnostic criteria and course for all three.
europmc-pmc1971126:
Hunt-Newbury, Moerman and co-authors built in 2007 living reporter worms to show where and when nearly two thousand genes switch on. Knowing a gene's expression pattern is often the key to its function. The team worked in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, a transparent worm whose cells can be watched directly.

They fused the control DNA in front of each gene to a green fluorescent protein gene, making worms glow wherever that gene is active. The set covers 1,886 genes, about ten percent of the worm's total. Animals were examined at every stage from embryo to adult, and control regions were found for 38 cell and tissue types. Some switches work in all cells, others in one tissue, a tissue mix, or a single cell. Most studied genes have human counterparts, and all images went to public worm atlases.
europmc-pmc2125226: A medical paper on the cultivation of human sarcomatous tissue in vitro. The cancer flesh. This article preserves that oncology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2131226: A medical paper on the relative reaction within living mammalian tissues, factors determining. The tissues' chemistry again. This article preserves that physiology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2364126:
Andreyev and a worldwide group pooled data on ras gene faults in colorectal cancer in 2001. The study, called RASCAL II, gathered records from 42 centres in 21 countries. An earlier round had shown that different faults in the same gene can affect patients differently, a first for a common cancer.

After exclusions, 3,439 patients entered the final analysis. Of 12 possible faults at two spots, codons 12 and 13, of the Kirsten ras gene, only one mattered clearly. Changing glycine to valine at codon 12, found in 8.6% of patients, worsened both survival and time without cancer return. Its harm was strongest in Dukes' C cancers, which had spread to lymph nodes, with a hazard ratio near 1.5 there. The authors said this fault may mark tumors primed for aggressive behaviour.
europmc-pmc2394426:
Rubino and co-authors studied second cancers after thyroid cancer treatment in 2003. Many thyroid patients receive radioiodine, a radioactive form of iodine that concentrates in the thyroid. Whether the radiation raises the risk of later, separate cancers was unclear, since single centres treat few patients.

Pooling Swedish, Italian, and French cohorts gave 6,841 patients, diagnosed between 1934 and 1995, of whom 62% received radioiodine. In all, 576 patients developed a second primary cancer, 27% more than expected from general rates. Risk rose with the total radioiodine dose given. Each gigabecquerel of activity, a unit of radioactivity, added an excess of 14.4 solid cancers per 100,000 person-years in their scaling, plus a smaller leukaemia excess. Bone, soft tissue, bowel, and salivary gland cancers were specifically linked, so the authors urged tighter targeting of treatment.
europmc-pmc2639426:
Jaureguy and colleagues surveyed in 2008 the E. coli bacteria that had entered the blood of patients in two French hospitals. These infections are a heavy burden, yet doctors knew little about how varied the blood-invading strains are. The team collected 161 samples in a row over one year, along with details of each patient's illness.

Gene typing showed the strains were highly varied, spread across five major family lines of the species. Two strain groups stood out for coming from urine infections more often than chance would suggest. No group, though, was linked to worse illness or death. A deeper gene scan of chosen strains then found DNA regions that marked those two urine-linked groups. Variety, not one super-strain, was the main picture.
europmc-pmc2646326:
Minne and co-authors reviewed in 2008 how well scores based on organ failure predict death in intensive care patients. The score, called SOFA, rates how badly six organ systems are working. Doctors hoped daily scores could forecast who will live and who will die, but studies used the score in many different ways.

The reviewers kept 18 studies that met their standards. Methods varied so widely that direct comparison was hard. Scores taken at admission forecast death a little worse than two older scoring systems built for that purpose. Scores tracked over days did better: the worst score reached, and the change from the first score, separated survivors from those who died more clearly. Only five of the ten studies that built forecast models tested them on fresh patients, a gap the authors flag.
europmc-pmc2698926:
Robroek, van Lenthe, van Empelen, and Burdorf reviewed in 2009 who actually joins workplace health programs, and why others stay away. Employers widely offer exercise and diet programs, and research had judged whether they work. Almost no one had asked the prior question: who signs up at all, without which the programs cannot help.

Twenty-three studies met the review's rules. Joining rates ranged from 10 to 64 percent of staff, with a middle value near a third. Women joined more than men overall, though not when the offer was simply access to a fitness center. Beyond sex, the picture blurred: age, health, and job traits showed no consistent pull. How the program was built and sold mattered, with personal invitations and on-site convenience lifting turnout. Recruiting the reluctant, the authors argue, deserves the same design care as the program itself.
europmc-pmc2717326:
Lansink and co-authors recorded in 2009 how two rat brain areas replay place and reward memories during sleep. The hippocampus holds place cells that fire at set locations, while the ventral striatum, a reward area, fires for expected treats. Learning where a reward sits needs both kinds of signal to join into one memory.

Recording both areas at once in waking and sleep, they found the patterns returned together after behavior. Hippocampal replay came first, shortly before striatal replay of reward traces. That lead supports the idea that the hippocampus drives the pairing, helping bind where a reward was found to the reward itself during sleep consolidation, when memories settle.
europmc-pmc2793426:
Miller, Doyle, and Terstappen reviewed in 2010 how counting tumor cells in blood can track cancers that have spread. Their CellSearch system counts these circulating tumor cells, meaning cancer cells shed into the blood, from a small vein sample of seven and a half milliliters.

The review compared three large multi-center studies in breast, colorectal, and prostate cancer that had spread to other body parts. Counts taken at any point during care predicted how patients fared and how long they lived. Because the test needs only a blood draw and gives a number rather than an image, it offers a repeatable way to judge whether treatment is holding the disease back.
europmc-pmc2797026:
Close and a large team built fast DNA testing tools for barley in 2009, aimed at breeders who track thousands of markers at once. The markers are SNPs, single-letter DNA differences between plants. Error-filled marker sets had long warped plant genetic maps, stretching distances and scrambling marker order.

From gene reads the team found about twenty-two thousand candidate markers and tested over four thousand in pilot assays. They then picked just over three thousand reliable ones for two shared production assays offered to all barley researchers. Mapping several breeding populations gave a joint map of nearly three thousand marker spots. Comparing that map with rice showed large gene blocks locked near chromosome centers, where swapping is rare.
europmc-pmc2803126:
Chen and co-authors described MolProbity in 2010, a web service that checks the quality of molecule shapes solved by crystallography, the method that reads shapes from crystal X-ray patterns. A flawed shape can mislead every study built on it, so checks at the level of single atoms matter.

The service adds hydrogen atoms, corrects common side-chain flips, then tests shapes for atoms squeezed too close, bad angles, and unlikely backbone shapes. Results come back as summary scores, charts, and three-dimensional views that mark each problem spot. The authors argue this kind of check can catch most local errors in a structure and guide the fixes, improving the shared databases other scientists rely on.
europmc-pmc2876926:
Kadam and Bhalerao explained in 2010 how to calculate sample size, the number of participants a clinical study needs before it starts. A sample is a smaller group drawn to stand for a whole population, and its members must be chosen randomly so results can be generalized. Choosing the size upfront is a basic guard against biased reading of results.

Too few participants leave a study unable to detect real effects or support broad claims, while too many waste money and expose extra people needlessly. The authors walk through the ingredients of the calculation, including the effect size worth catching, acceptable error rates, and expected variation. Worked reasoning shows how each choice moves the final number, giving new researchers a practical recipe.
europmc-pmc2879426:
Brodeur, Dionne-Dostie, Montreuil, and Lepage released in 2010 the Bank of Standardized Stimuli, a set of four hundred eighty photographs of everyday objects for use in mind and language experiments. Each photo comes with measured norms, reference ratings that let researchers control or study a property. The norms cover how often the object's name is used, what category it belongs to, and how familiar it feels.

Ratings also capture how visually complex each object looks, whether viewers agree on its name and viewpoint, and how easily a hand could act on it. The set ships in color, grayscale, blurred, scrambled, and line-drawn versions for flexible designs. Freely shared norms help labs pick pictures that differ only in the feature under test.
europmc-pmc2889826:
Torgerson and co-authors produced in 2010 the first global estimate of alveolar echinococcosis, a slow, tumor-like disease caused by a fox tapeworm larva. The disease is common in some rural Chinese communities and rare but scattered elsewhere in the northern hemisphere. Data quality varied so much by country that the team modeled uncertainty with probability methods instead of forcing one standard review.

Their estimate lands near eighteen thousand new cases a year worldwide, with a wide uncertainty range reflecting the patchy data. Most cases concentrate in China and Central Asia among herding communities. Converting cases into disability-adjusted life years shows a burden rivaling better-known tropical diseases. That measure combines early death with years lived ill. The authors use it to argue for surveillance and control funding.
europmc-pmc2981526:
Jones and a very large team mined genome-wide association data for Alzheimer's disease in 2010, asking which biological processes the risk genes collectively implicate. The disease is the leading cause of dementia, and fresh risk genes had just emerged from big scans.

Applying a pathway mining tool to the largest dataset, then checking a second one, they found association signals crowded in two process groups: cholesterol handling and immune response. Both had been suspected from tissue and population studies, but it was unclear whether they caused disease or followed it. Converging genetic evidence now places them near the start.
europmc-pmc2988826:
Leung and co-authors tested whether a surface marker called CD44 picks out stem-like cells in non-small cell lung cancer in a 2010 study. The cancer stem cell idea holds that a small hardy set of cells keeps a tumour going.

Screening ten lung cancer lines for five stem markers pointed to CD44. Cells carrying it formed floating spheres, started tumours in mice repeatedly across transplant rounds, and regenerated mixed tumours containing both marked and unmarked cells. They switched on core stemness genes and shrugged off the chemotherapy drug cisplatin better than unmarked cells, matching the stem-like profile.
europmc-pmc3027626:
Lee and colleagues followed in this 2011 study whether low levels of long lasting pollutants in blood predict later weight gain and metabolic trouble. The chemicals included old pesticides and industrial compounds that linger in body fat for years. Ninety adults who stayed free of diabetes were tracked for close to two decades, with blood drawn near the start.

Higher early levels of several compounds predicted higher body weight, worse blood fats, and stronger insulin resistance at the final check, even after accounting for starting values. The strongest links often appeared at low doses and faded at the highest doses, forming an upside down U shape. One old pesticide breakdown product showed the most consistent pattern. The authors suggest everyday exposure may help drive obesity and the conditions that precede diabetes.
europmc-pmc3062526:
Taylor, Perrais, and Merrifield filmed in 2011 the molecular choreography by which living animal cells pull material inward through coated pits. This intake route, built around the protein clathrin, is how cells import nutrients and signals and recycle their surface. Earlier movies of the process blurred fast steps together. New imaging gave the team roughly ten times finer timing than before.

With that sharper view they mapped the order and duration of the protein arrivals that bend the membrane, pinch off a bubble, and haul it inside. The sequence proved more orderly and stereotyped than fuzzy earlier records suggested. Precise timing exposes which steps can stall or fail, which matters for diseases where intake goes wrong. The survey sets a reference timeline for the best studied intake pathway in cell biology. Other labs can now test their mutants against hard numbers.
europmc-pmc3077926:
Daw, Gershman, Seymour, Dayan, and Dolan reported in 2011 that the brain's reward signal blends two kinds of learning that textbooks had kept apart. One kind learns by trial and error from past payoffs. The other plans ahead using a mental model of how choices lead onward. The team built a multi step decision game where the two styles predict different choices, then scanned players' brains during play.

Choices clearly carried both influences, in proportions that varied by person. A signal in the ventral striatum tracked a blend of both prediction errors, in the same proportions as behavior. That signal had long been labeled as purely trial and error. The result challenges the idea of a sealed, model free learner in the human brain. The authors argue for one integrated system that mixes habit and planning throughout.
europmc-pmc3094326:
Kao, Chang, Hsu, and Huang showed in 2011 that sorting breast cancers by their gene activity patterns can guide which chemotherapy each patient should get, beyond the usual risk scores. They profiled tumors from more than three hundred patients with complete treatment and outcome records, and defined six molecular subtypes with distinct biology and behavior. The subtypes partly matched the known intrinsic types, but cut the pie differently.

One subtype did equally well on a gentler drug mix as on a stronger one. Another shrugged off the gentler mix yet thrived on the stronger, apparently because of low levels of a gene tied to sensitivity to one drug in the mix. A fifth subtype did so well on hormone therapy alone that added chemotherapy gave early stage patients nothing. Patients sharing one commercial risk score were scattered across subtypes needing different care. The authors argue subtyping can personalize treatment now.
europmc-pmc3098226:
Hughes, Koga, Xue, Fukatsu, and Rasgon tested in 2011 whether inherited bacteria that protect other insects could also block malaria inside its main mosquito carrier. The bacteria, Wolbachia, do not naturally infect Anopheles mosquitoes, and permanent infections there had failed. The team used temporary body infections of two contrasting strains to learn what stable infections might do.

One strain spread through the mosquito's body but avoided the gut and ovaries. It first provoked, then suppressed, the mosquito's immune genes as it multiplied. Both strains sharply reduced the malaria parasite's cyst stage in the gut. The aggressive strain also turned deadly for about a day after the mosquito drank blood, then left survivors unharmed. The authors say the results justify pressing on toward stable infections as a malaria control strategy.
europmc-pmc3114826:
Tracey Woodruff and colleagues measured chemical exposure in pregnant women across the United States for a 2011 paper in Environmental Health Perspectives. Exposure before birth can raise risks of birth problems and later disease, yet how many chemicals reach pregnant women at once was poorly known. They used a national health survey from 2003 and 2004.

Blood and urine from more than two hundred pregnant women were tested for well over a hundred substances across many chemical families. Several long-banned or restricted chemicals, plus flame retardants, stain repellents, and plastic-related compounds, showed up in nearly every woman. A typical woman carried dozens of detected chemicals at once. Levels were mostly similar to or lower than in non-pregnant women. The authors call for work on sources and health meaning.
europmc-pmc3181226:
Benjamin Toh and colleagues showed that immune cells visiting a tumour teach cancer cells to spread in a 2011 paper in PLoS Biology. Spreading requires a motile form, long blamed on late random mutations, yet cancer cells are now known to leave early. In a mouse melanoma model that spreads on its own, a class of immature immune cells gathered preferentially inside the main tumour.

Those cells release a chemical lure that draws more of their kind in. Once inside, they push tumour cells through the identity switch that makes them mobile, using three known signalling routes. The finding supplies the fast track to spread that early dissemination implied, and it mechanistically ties chronic inflammation to cancer progression, suggesting the visiting immune cells as a target.
europmc-pmc3191826:
Xinrui Tian and colleagues reviewed the molecular glue that seals sheet-like tissues in a 2011 paper in the Journal of Biomedicine and Biotechnology. The partnership between a surface anchor protein and its intracellular partner holds epithelial cells together and maintains the barrier lining organs. Breaking the partnership does more than loosen cells: it also unleashes a growth signalling pathway the partner normally restrains.

Faulty levels of the complex appear across many human cancers and in the scarring diseases that follow a cell-identity switch in organs. The review walks through how the complex assembles, recycles, and talks to the cell skeleton and nucleus. That double life, as both glue and signal brake, likely explains its tumour- and fibrosis-suppressing reputation, and marks its parts as drug targets.
europmc-pmc3201926:
Daniel Goldberg and Summer McGee argued in this 2011 article in BMC Public Health that pain should be treated as a global public health priority. About a fifth of adults worldwide live with pain, and roughly one in ten is newly diagnosed with chronic pain each year. Yet pain has mostly been framed as a private medical problem.

Viewing pain through a public health lens, they argue, shows it as a problem with many causes, including the social conditions people live in. Its burden is growing and falls unevenly across the world. Giving pain proper attention would help governments set priorities and shape policy, and would give health workers a fuller picture of what drives the problem and what responses it needs.
europmc-pmc3303626:
Lushchak reviewed the protective chemical glutathione and how the body keeps its supply in balance, in a 2012 article. Glutathione is a small three part molecule that shields cells from reactive oxygen and nitrogen compounds, which can damage proteins and DNA. It also helps clear toxic substances and keeps metals in check inside cells.

The review covers how glutathione is built, broken down, shared between organs, and used by a family of related enzymes. Separate sections connect its balance to various diseases and describe the tools and drugs researchers use to raise or lower its levels. Plant derived compounds that nudge these processes get special attention, and the author frames the topic as a starting point for new medical strategies.
europmc-pmc3348526:
Kolluru, Bir, and Kevil reviewed how diabetes damages the lining of blood vessels and stalls the growth of new ones, in a 2012 article. Diabetes, marked by high blood sugar from missing or resisted insulin, frequently brings blocked arteries and wounds that will not heal. A healthy vessel lining manages blood flow, repair, and new vessel sprouting, and diabetes undermines all three.

The review gathers evidence on how high sugar and related changes injure lining cells, stiffen the scaffolding around vessels, and cut off local nerve supply. Together these changes choke off the new vessel growth that ischemic tissue and wounds desperately need. Growing replacement vessels on purpose remains an attractive therapy for diabetic complications. The authors argue that past clinical disappointments may stem from narrow drug targets and weak testing in animal models that truly mimic the disease.
europmc-pmc3358326:
Calderone tracked eighteen years of United States farm data to measure how much crops rely on insect pollinators. Covering 1992 to 2009, the study split crops that need insects outright, such as apples, almonds, and blueberries, from crops grown from insect-pollinated seed, such as legume hays and onions.

The area and output of the first group grew through the nineteen-nineties and held near those levels. Pollination was worth roughly fifteen billion dollars by 2009, most of it credited to honey bees. Crops in the second group shrank in area. Calderone concludes that growers still need pollinators badly, and that losing them would put much of this output at risk.
europmc-pmc3359326:
Kidd, Piantadosi, and Aslin tested how babies choose what to look at, proposing that infants prefer information pitched at an intermediate level of complexity. Material that is too predictable teaches nothing new, while material that is too surprising cannot be absorbed, so efficient learning should favour the middle ground.

In two experiments with seven- and eight-month-old babies, the researchers measured looking behaviour toward event sequences whose complexity was scored by an ideal learner model. Babies were most likely to look away from sequences rated either very simple or very complex, and kept attention on the intermediate ones. The authors call this Goldilocks pattern a general principle guiding infant attention.
europmc-pmc3366926:
Meng and D'Arcy reviewed whether schooling protects against dementia, testing the cognitive reserve idea. That idea holds that people with more schooling, higher IQ, or demanding jobs can bear more brain damage before symptoms show, because their brains cope better with harm.

Searching five databases for studies from 1980 to 2011, they gathered 133 articles covering over four hundred thousand subjects. Pooled results showed low schooling roughly doubled the odds of dementia, and studies of new cases pointed the same way. Other evidence added that well-schooled patients decline faster once symptoms begin, in line with greater hidden damage. The authors conclude the idea enjoys robust support.
europmc-pmc3384226:
Belzung and Lemoine revisited in 2011 how to judge whether an animal model of mental illness is any good. Models of anxiety and depression are usually scored on three tests set out by Willner: likeness, prediction, and underlying sameness. The authors trace the history of those tests and find them too loose.

They propose five sharper criteria, some with sub-parts. A model should use the right species and strain, be produced in a way that mirrors how illness develops, and share the brain mechanisms at fault. It should also look right in behavior and body markers, and respond to triggers and treatments as patients do. The scheme gives researchers a stricter checklist.
europmc-pmc3387626:
Otto and colleagues charted the course of severe sepsis in 2011 across nearly a thousand intensive care patients, looking for a dangerous late phase. Newer models suggested the immune system may shut down as sepsis drags on, but hard clinical data were missing. The team split the illness into three phases by its death peaks.

Three peaks of death appeared, around days two, seven, and seventeen. Nearly two thirds of deaths came after the early phase. Blood cultures turned positive again late, at rates matching the first days, and the germs found shifted toward opportunists and Candida fungi. The late rebound in hard-to-treat germs, the authors warn, deserves targeted study.
europmc-pmc3464226:
Amman and a large team investigated Marburg virus in Egyptian fruit bats in Uganda for a 2012 PLoS Pathogens paper. The virus causes severe bleeding fever in people, and bats in caves and mines were the prime suspects as its natural home. The study centered on Python Cave, where two tourists had caught the virus in separate visits.

Over fifteen months the team caught and tested more than sixteen hundred bats from the cave's huge colony. A small share carried active virus, and infection rose sharply in young bats about six months old, just after the twice-yearly birthing seasons. Amman's group matched past human spillover cases against those pulses and found most fell inside them. The pattern points to clear seasons of higher risk for people.
europmc-pmc3464626:
Dos Santos and colleagues surveyed microbial genomes for the genes behind nitrogen fixation in BMC Genomics in 2012. Only some microbes can turn nitrogen gas from the air into a form life can use, and lab tests miss many of them. The team set a stricter rule for judging a genome, requiring a minimum set of six key genes.

Applying that rule across all sequenced genomes, they predicted close to one hundred fifty species that can fix nitrogen. Dozens of those had never been known to do so, and seven whole phyla gained their first predicted fixers. Dos Santos also found nitrogenase-like proteins in species that lack the full gene set. Those look-alike proteins may do other, still unknown jobs in the cell.
europmc-pmc3482226:
Tam and colleagues worked out how stressed cells switch on an inflammatory master gene, in a 2012 PLoS ONE paper. When proteins pile up unfolded inside a cell compartment called the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell mounts a rescue response. That response also wakes NF-kB, a factor that drives inflammation, by a route that differed from the usual one.

The team found the waking depends on a standing, low level of activity in an enzyme complex, not on a fresh surge. A stress sensor in the compartment keeps that baseline alive through one of its two tools. A second sensor helps by briefly slowing protein making. Tam's results matter for cancer care: tumors with high baseline activity resist drugs that block the enzyme, since stress revives the factor anyway.

Clinics can put a tool like this to work right away, since the testing is already done.
europmc-pmc9801026: This 2022 research paper covers kaks_calculator 3-0: calculating selective pressure on coding and non-coding sequences. Kaks_calculator 3-0 is an updated toolkit that is capable of calculating selective pressure on both coding and non-coding sequences. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc9825826: Dedrick and co-authors published this research paper in 2023 on phage therapy of mycobacterium infections: compassionate use of phages in 20 patients with drug-resistant mycobacterial disease. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
europmc-pmc9849126: Published in 2023, this research paper takes on finngen provides genetic insights from a well-phenotyped isolated people. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc9935926: A fresh look at low-oxygen microenvironment (the tissue surrounding a tumor) in cancer: mechanisms (the inner workings) and treatment treatments arrived with this 2023 research paper. Having a low-oxygen microenvironment (the tissue surrounding a tumor) is a common and salient feature of most solid tumors. Once the chain of events is mapped, future treatments can be built to break it.
europmc-pmc9963026: Published in 2023, this research paper takes on fibrosis (scarring of tissue): types, effects, markers, mechanisms (the inner workings) for disease progression (worsening), and its relation with oxidative stress. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Pinning down the inner workings gives drug makers a concrete target to aim at.
faulkner-soldiers-pay-1926:
Soldiers' Pay, published in 1926, was the first novel of William Faulkner of Mississippi. Its central figure is Donald Mahon, a young flying officer badly wounded in the First World War. Scarred and nearly blind, Mahon comes home to a small Georgia town that does not know what to do with him.

Around the dying airman gather a kind widow, a cynical veteran, and Mahon's shallow fiancee. Each reacts to his ruin in a different way, from pity to flight. Faulkner writes in a lush, brooding style already marked by his later manner. The novel opened his long study of the South, war, and loss.
fitzgerald-all-sad-young-men-1926:
All the Sad Young Men, published in 1926, is Fitzgerald's third story collection, written at the height of his Jazz Age fame. Its title sets the tone: youth, money, and the sadness underneath both, in America after the war.

'The Rich Boy' studies a wealthy man whose money has deformed his capacity to love. 'Winter Dreams' follows Dexter Green's longing for Judy Jones and the world she stands for, and 'Absolution' turns to a boy and a priest in Minnesota. Fitzgerald's prose is at its most polished here, glamorous and quietly bleak. The stories remain his elegies for a generation.
ford-man-could-stand-up-1926:
A Man Could Stand Up, published in 1926, is the third volume of Ford's Parade's End. It opens on Armistice Day in London, the guns stopped at last, crowds half joyful and half lost, and Christopher Tietjens waiting in a silent office.
