He trained at the Ecole Polytechnique and the artillery school. After reaching captain, he studied at the war college. Staff duty in Paris followed his graduation in 1880.

He commanded an artillery battery from 1884. Two years later he served General Boulanger, then war minister. He rose to lieutenant-colonel in 1898 and colonel in 1902. As colonel he headed the military artillery school. In 1904 he became chief of cabinet at the War Ministry. Brigadier-general rank came in 1905 with new commands. He also received the Legion of Honor that period.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weil-jacob-1482:
Jacob Weil was a German teacher and writer on Jewish rights. He was born at Frankfort in 1792. Isidore Singer and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He died at Frankfort on November 18, 1864. His first work drew fragments from Talmud and rabbis. He taught at Frankfort's Jewish school, the Philanthropin.

From 1818 to 1845 Weil ran his own school institute. In 1816 he voiced hope for Jewish emancipation. He then answered attacks by professors Rühs and Fries. His pamphlet defended Jewish claims to German citizenship. He helped found a group promoting crafts among Jews. He backed Gabriel Riesser and wrote his life story. His essays filled the Frankfort press for years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wilenkin-gregor:
Gregory Wilenkin was a Russian government official. Cyrus Adler wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Tsarskoye Selo on February 22, 1864. His family held landed estates for two centuries. An ancestor, Blema Wilenkin, endowed houses at Minsk and Jerusalem. Her Minsk house still serves as a study hall.

Wilenkin studied law at Dorpat and St. Petersburg. In 1887 he entered the Ministry of Public Instruction. The ministry sent him to England on a study mission. He examined Oxford and Cambridge and Paris schools. France honored his report on its schools. Finance minister Witte then recruited him in 1895. He became assistant financial agent in London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wormser-andre-a:
Andre Alphonse Wormser (born 1851) was a French composer of operas and ballets. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Paris, he trained at the Paris stage music school. His teachers were Bazin and Marmontel, both famed men. In 1875 he won the Prix de Rome for his work.

That prize marked him as a star of his class. He wrote a great store of stage and piano works. The list holds overtures, light operas, and farces. It holds ballets for the Paris stage as well. Two full operas stand at the head of the list. One played at Aix-la-Chapelle in the year 1887. The second, named Rivoli, played at Paris in 1896. The short entry rests on a music word book of 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zeitlin-william:
William Zeitlin was a Russian scholar and maker of book lists. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Homel in the Moghilef state, he lived in the 1800s. His fame rests on one great work of his long life.

That work is the Kiryat Sefer, a list of Hebrew books. It lists new Hebrew books from the age of Mendelssohn. That age runs to the year 1890 in the scope of the list. The work took him twenty years of his life to make. He drew on two great lists made by men before him. He toured the book towns of Wilna and Warsaw for facts. He toured great school towns of Europe for more facts. The list holds notes on the lives of the scribes as well.
journal-of-discourses-vol-26:
Volume Twenty-Six, from 1886, closes the Journal of Discourses for good. Twenty-six volumes span thirty-two years of Tabernacle and frontier preaching. Hundreds of sermons end here, in the set's final gathered book.

The founding generation's voice falls silent as this volume shuts. Apostles who crossed the plains now preach to grandchildren in Zion. Their record covers doctrine, war, law, farming, and the soul's fate. No new faith of the age left so full a firsthand record. Scholars still mine the Journal as Mormonism's great primary source today. Its last pages close an era that print alone could preserve.
kafka-das-schloss-1926:
Franz Kafka left The Castle unfinished at his death in 1924, and it was published in German in 1926. The text here is that first German edition, from Kurt Wolff. No English translation of the book is in the public domain. Its hero, known only as K., arrives in a snowbound village claiming the Castle has hired him as a land surveyor.

The Castle's officials never confirm his post, and every effort to reach them snares him deeper. Clerks, letters, and village rules form a maze with no center in sight. K. fights on with stubborn, comic energy against pure fog. The novel became the classic image of life under faceless power. Its cold absurdity still defines the word Kafkaesque.
lawrence-plumed-serpent-1926:
The Plumed Serpent, published in 1926, is Lawrence's Mexican novel and the most argued-over of all his books. Kate Leslie, an Irish widow of forty traveling in Mexico, is drawn into a movement reviving the cult of Quetzalcoatl, the plumed serpent god.

Its leaders, Don Ramon and Don Cipriano, preach a new-old religion of blood and ritual against church and revolution alike. Kate resists and yields by turns, and the novel never settles whether the cult saves or devours her. Lawrence wrote it out of his own Mexican journeys and longings. The result is powerful, disturbing, and impossible to ignore.
levy-bruhl-how-natives-think-1926:
Lucien Levy-Bruhl, a French philosopher, argued in this famous work that native peoples think in a fundamentally different way from modern Europeans. The authorized English translation by Lilian A. Clare appeared in 1926 and spread his thesis widely.

Levy-Bruhl claimed that collective representations, the beliefs a group shares, bend individual thought toward what he called participation mystique. In that mode, a person can feel one with an ancestor, an animal, or a sacred object. Critics attacked the idea as unfair to native reason, and Levy-Bruhl softened it late in life. The debate it started shaped anthropology for decades.
livy-history-rome-books-9-26:
Livy wrote his monumental History of Rome under Augustus, narrating the republic's rise. D. Spillan and Cyrus Edmonds translated this stretch, covering Books 9 through 26. The Second Punic War dominates the later books here.

Early books here cover Rome's wars with the Samnites and Pyrrhus. Then Hannibal crosses the Alps, wins at Cannae, and nearly breaks Rome. Livy tells the story as patriotic epic, full of speeches and omens. Rome's recovery after Cannae becomes his great theme of resilience. This volume completes the library's main Livy set. Ancient history rarely reads at this scale or with this sweep.
llull-blanquerna-peers-1926:
Blanquerna is the great romance of Ramon Llull, the Catalan thinker of the thirteenth century. E. Allison Peers translated it into English in 1926. Its hero, Blanquerna, climbs step by step through the estates of the world: marriage, the religious life, the bishopric, the papacy, and at last the hermit's cell.

Along the road Llull sets out his whole vision of a reformed Christian world, taught by reason and his famous Art of finding truth. The famous Book of the Lover and the Beloved blooms inside the tale. Blanquerna is part novel, part plan for the church and the schools. It shows medieval Catalonia dreaming of a wiser age.
malinowski-crime-custom-1926:
In 1926 Malinowski returned to the Trobriand Islands in print with a short book on law and custom. Crime and Custom in Savage Society asks how order holds in a land with no courts, police, or written laws. It grew from the same field work as his Argonauts.

Malinowski argues that law lives in daily duty, not in force from above. He shows that custom binds because people depend on each other and fear shame before their neighbors. Gifts, feasts, and duties form a web that no one can lightly break. The book founded the study of law in anthropology and still starts debates about rules without rulers.
malinowski-myth-in-primitive-psychology-:
Malinowski based this short 1926 book on his fieldwork in the Trobriand Islands, where he had lived in a village and learned the language. It states his functionalist view of myth in its clearest form.

A myth, Malinowski argues, is not a bad attempt at science or history. It is a charter: a sacred story that justifies present customs, ranks, and land claims by grounding them in the age of origins. He shows Trobrianders using tales of ancestors to settle real disputes. The book helped move anthropology from the armchair to the field, and its argument still frames debates about myth.
mathnawi-nicholson-vol-2-1926:
Jalal al-Din Rumi, the Persian poet of the 1200s, wrote the Mathnawi, a long poem of Sufi teaching told through stories. R. A. Nicholson spent years turning it into English. His second volume, printed in 1926, gives the English text of the poem's first two books.

Rumi teaches through tales of kings, lovers, merchants, fools, and saints, and each story turns toward a lesson on God and the soul. The tales pile up, short and long, comic and grave, and each one points past itself to truths about prayer, love, and the self. Nicholson's version became the standard English Mathnawi for students of Persian verse.
mcbride-symmes-theory-concentric-spheres:
James McBride, a friend and backer of Symmes in Ohio, gave the hollow earth scheme its first full book in 1826. Symmes had put his claim in short forms, and it drew much scorn. McBride set out to give it a learned, full dress case.

He lays out the spheres within spheres, the polar holes, and the seas and lands inside. He draws on maths, star lore, and the tales of north sea men for his proof. The book is the chief shield of the scheme in its first, bold years.
mirrlees-lud-in-the-mist-1926:
Hope Mirrlees set a prim town by the edge of faerie in Lud-in-the-Mist, her novel of 1926. The town bans all talk of fairy fruit and the wild hills. Yet the fruit slips in. Sons and girls stray, and old rites stir in the calm streets.

The tale blends law, lore, and quiet dread. Mirrlees writes with grace and sly wit. She asks what a town loses when it shuts out awe. The book was long hard to find. Now chief tale-smiths rank it at the top. Mayor Chanticleer, stiff and prim at first, must face his own past. His slow change gives the wild lore a warm, sad human core.
morgan-theory-gene-1926:
Thomas Hunt Morgan led the famous 'fly room' at Columbia, where tiny fruit flies remade biology. His Theory of the Gene, published in 1926, sums up what those flies had taught. Morgan had once doubted Mendel; the flies changed his mind.

Morgan shows that genes sit in a line on chromosomes, like beads on a string. Crossed flies reveal how traits link, swap, and map to fixed places. That mapping let scientists chart heredity with real precision. Morgan won a Nobel Prize, and his book stands as the classic statement of gene theory. Diagrams of fly crosses make the argument easy to follow.
openalex-w1487331926:
Pablo Smircich, Fabiola Holetz, José Sotelo-Silveira, and co-authors wrote this study. It appeared in BMC Genomics in the year 2015. The subject is Trypanosoma cruzi, the Chagas disease parasite. Such parasites barely control genes at transcription, they note. Control after transcription shapes most gene changes instead.

The team used RNA sequencing and ribosome profiling together. They compared non-infective and infective life stages. Transcript levels stayed largely steady between the stages. Translation levels dropped for a large share of genes. Virulence factor translation rose in the infective form. The authors conclude that control of translation drives this change. The paper is open access and free for all to read. Its teams worked in Brazil and in Uruguay, the author notes show.
openalex-w2030126026:
Diego Jarquin, Jose Crossa, Xavier Lacaze and colleagues built a model to predict wheat yield from genes and weather. Their paper appeared in Theoretical and Applied Genetics in 2014. Genes affect traits differently in different environments. Breeders call this gene-by-environment interaction. Modern tools now produce huge gene and weather datasets.

Their reaction norm model uses both kinds of data. It includes main effects of genes and environment. It also includes how the two interact. The model raised prediction accuracy for grain yield. Gains held across environments and within them. Better prediction helps breeders pick lines before field trials end. The method suits other crops with rich data too.
openalex-w2066642526:
D. K. Tiwari, Nabanita Dasgupta-Schubert, Luis Manuel Villasenor Cendejas and colleagues tested carbon nanotubes on maize seedlings. Their paper appeared in Applied Nanoscience in 2014. Tiny carbon tubes had boosted sprouting in some plants. Results were uneven between studies. Factory-made tubes of known quality offered a cleaner test.

At low doses, the tubes improved seedling growth. At higher doses, growth was depressed instead. Better water delivery explained much of the benefit. The tubes also changed mineral nutrient flow to seedlings. Effects differed by nutrient type and tube dose. Two forces competed: water inflow and nutrient holding. The authors discuss what this means for nano-agriculture. Careful dosing is essential for any farm use.
openalex-w2099600826:
Georges Aad and colleagues in the ATLAS Collaboration measured Higgs boson production through its decay into two photons. Their paper appeared in Physical Review D in 2014. The two-photon channel is rare but very clean. It gives a sharp signal above background noise. Data came from two LHC energy runs.

The team counted Higgs decays in the photon channel. They compared counts with standard model predictions. Overall production matched the prediction within errors. They also split results by production route. Each route agreed with expectations within wide uncertainties. A new photon calibration improved the mass precision. No clear deviation from the standard model appeared. The measurement confirms the Higgs picture further.
openalex-w2101094926:
Roderick Escombe, David Moore, Robert Gilman and colleagues measured how infectious TB patients with HIV are. Their paper appeared in PLoS Medicine in 2008. Classic knowledge came from 1950s guinea pig studies. Those studies exposed animals to ward air. The team recreated that model in Lima, Peru.

They used gene fingerprinting to match infections to patients. That let them trace which patient infected which animal. Patients also had HIV alongside tuberculosis. The question was whether HIV changes infectiousness. Ward air exposure ran over long periods. Molecular matching gave a patient-level picture of spread. Such data help hospitals judge isolation needs. They also refine models of TB transmission.
openalex-w2113626726:
Juan Carlos Motamayor, Philippe Lachenaud, Jay Wallace da Silva e Mota and colleagues reclassified the cacao tree using gene data. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2008. Cacao seed collections guide chocolate breeding work. Many collected samples were wrongly labelled, though. Links between wild and farmed trees were poorly understood.

The team checked over a thousand cacao samples. Fine DNA markers covered the species' range widely. Wrongly labelled samples were dropped before the checks. Grouping by gene patterns found ten clusters. Tradition had recognised only two groups before. Each cluster ties to a place of origin. A new scheme for cacao was proposed. Breeders can now use the collections with more trust.
openalex-w2130143426:
G. Aad and colleagues in the ATLAS Collaboration published this search in the Journal of High Energy Physics in 2014. They looked for direct production of three kinds of proposed supersymmetric particles: charginos, neutralinos, and sleptons. The sign they sought was two leptons plus missing sideways momentum, which hints at unseen particles escaping the detector.

The team used proton collision data recorded by ATLAS at the Large Hadron Collider. They found no clear excess beyond what the standard model predicts. Instead, they set limits on the masses these particles could have under several simple model setups. The results were also read against broader versions of the minimal supersymmetric standard model.
openalex-w2150408626:
Arnaldo Dubín, Mario Pozo, Christian Casabella, and colleagues published this study in Critical Care in 2009. In septic shock, doctors raise blood pressure with the drug norepinephrine. The team asked whether pushing pressure higher also improves flow in the tiniest vessels, where oxygen actually reaches tissue.

Twenty ventilated patients were studied as their pressure target rose in steps. Heart output and vessel resistance rose with the higher doses, as expected. Oxygen delivery, oxygen use, and lactate levels stayed unchanged. Direct imaging under the tongue showed tiny-vessel flow and the share of working capillaries also stayed flat. Raising the pressure number, the study concludes, did not improve microcirculatory flow.

Teresa To, Sanja Stanojevic, Ginette Moores, and colleagues published this study in BMC Public Health in 2012. They estimated the global burden of asthma in adults from the World Health Survey. Asthma drives disability and health costs worldwide, yet comparable adult figures across many countries were scarce.

The survey covered more than one hundred seventy-eight thousand adults in seventy countries. About four in a hundred reported doctor-diagnosed or treated asthma, and about nine reported recent wheezing. Rates varied as much as twenty-one fold between countries, with Australia highest. Among people with treated asthma, almost a quarter still smoked, and one in five had never received treatment at all.
openalex-w2260781726:
Gissela Borrego-Soto, Rocío Ortiz-López, and Augusto Rojas-Martínez published this review in Genetics and Molecular Biology in 2015. They discuss radiation-induced DNA injury in breast cancer care. Radiotherapy helps many patients, yet some suffer worse side effects, possibly because their DNA repair machinery is weaker.

Ionizing radiation breaks DNA, most dangerously as double-strand breaks. Cells answer with repair systems, and flaws in those systems also drive inherited breast and ovarian cancer through BRCA gene mutations. Milder variants may shape risk in ordinary cases too. The review covers damage and repair mechanisms, the genes involved, and tests designed or in development to spot patients with raised radiosensitivity before treatment.
openalex-w2482115826: Anthony M. Reilly, Richard Ian Cooper, and Claire S. Adjiman lead the long author list on this 2016 report in Acta Crystallographica Section B. Nothing more about its targets, methods, or findings can be stated from the evidence kept here.

Carlos Rosales reviewed the neutrophil's many faces in Frontiers in Physiology in 2018. Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells in human blood. Bone marrow releases about a hundred billion of them daily, and most live only a day. They patrol for microbes and kill them by eating, by poison release, and by casting DNA traps.

Recent research shows neutrophils do far more than kill germs. They release cytokines and other signals that steer inflammation and shape wider immune responses. They help resolve inflammation too, not just start it. This versatility raises the question in the paper's title: one flexible cell type, or several distinct ones? Rosales surveys the evidence for neutrophil subpopulations and changing states. The answer matters for treating diseases where neutrophils drive damage.
openalex-w2811473826:
Crystian B. Oliveira, Christopher G. Maher, and Rafael Z. Pinto lead this 2018 overview of low back pain rules in the European Spine Journal. Non-specific low back pain fills primary care waiting rooms everywhere. Dozens of guidelines tell doctors how to diagnose and treat it. The team updated their 2010 overview to see what current guidelines say, and what changed.

They found fifteen clinical practice guidelines from 2008 to 2017. For diagnosis, the rules agree: check history and examine for red flags and nerve involvement. Imaging is discouraged unless serious disease is suspected, and psychosocial factors deserve assessment. For acute pain, they advise reassurance, staying active, and short courses of anti-inflammatory drugs. Chronic pain adds exercise therapy, antidepressants, and psychosocial interventions. The overview lets clinicians see the consensus, and guideline writers see the gaps.
openalex-w2929552226:
Gianpiero Manes, Gregorios Paspatis, Lars Aabakken, and colleagues wrote this clinical guideline for the European Society of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy, published in Endoscopy in 2019. It covers stones in the common bile duct and how doctors should find and remove them using endoscopy, a scope passed into the digestive tract.

The guideline advises offering stone removal to all patients with these stones who are fit enough for the procedure, whether or not they have symptoms. It names liver function tests and an ultrasound scan of the belly as the first diagnostic steps. Combined, those tests show how likely a patient is to have bile duct stones. Each advice point is graded by strength and by the quality of evidence behind it.
openalex-w2985579226:
Leticia Arregui, Marcela Ayala, Ximena Gómez-Gil, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in Microbial Cell Factories. It covers laccases, enzymes made by fungi and other organisms, and their promise for cleaning polluted water. Cities and industry keep adding foreign chemicals to water, harming ecosystems and health.

Laccases attack a broad range of compounds and can break down pollutants found in factory and hospital wastewater. Trials with crude or purified enzyme show real potential for water treatment. Large-scale use is held back by the harsh mix, salt levels, and acidity of real waste streams, which can damage the enzyme. The review maps the enzymes' structure and function and the knowledge still needed for wider use.
openalex-w3010629926:
Christian Lieven, Moritz Beber, Brett Olivier, and colleagues described this software in a letter to Nature Biotechnology in 2020. The tool, called MEMOTE, runs standard tests on genome-scale metabolic models. Such models map the full chemistry of a cell and can include thousands of substances and reactions.

Model quality varies widely between collections, the authors show. Models from modern automated pipelines are internally consistent, while an older collection proved inconsistent in up to half its entries. Key gene-to-reaction rules are also often missing. MEMOTE checks these points in a uniform way and scores each model. Shared testing should raise the trust researchers can place in metabolic models.
openalex-w3027520426:
S. Abdollahi, F. Acero, M. Ackermann, and colleagues of the Fermi team published this catalog in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series in 2020. It is the fourth source catalog from the Large Area Telescope aboard the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. Gamma rays are the most energetic form of light.

The catalog rests on the mission's first eight years of science data and is the deepest yet in its energy range. It doubles the exposure of the third catalog and adds several analysis improvements, including a fresher model of our own galaxy's glow. Each listed source is a gamma-ray emitter in the sky, from pulsars to distant galaxies. Astronomers use the catalog as a map for follow-up study.
openalex-w3133277826:
Nikolaos Kyriakidis, Andrés López-Cortés, Jorge Vásconez-González, and colleagues wrote this review in npj Vaccines in 2021. It surveys vaccine strategies against SARS-CoV-2, the virus behind COVID-19, focusing on candidates that had reached final phase three trials. By early January 2021 the pandemic had killed more than one point eight million people.

Most leading candidates aim to raise antibodies that block the viral spike protein and stop it latching onto human cells. Growing evidence on the role of T cells pushed some designs to favor cellular immunity as well. Others use whole killed or weakened virus to draw a broader response. The review compares these platforms, their trial designs, and their early results for readers judging a crowded field.
openalex-w4206133226:
Rainer Bussmann, Narel Paniagua-Zambrana, Inayat Ur Rahman, and colleagues catalogued the food plants and fungi of Georgia. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine in 2021. Georgia sits in the Caucasus biodiversity hotspot, and farming there is at least six thousand years old. The team asked how plant use in home gardens and wild gathering compares with nearby regions.

Between 2013 and 2019 they interviewed more than three hundred eighty people across the country, in their homes and gardens. The interviews, held in many local languages, recorded nearly twenty thousand uses. In all they documented four hundred seventy-four kinds of food plants and fungi. The survey shows deep local knowledge, alongside early signs of knowledge loss.
openalex-w4220969226:
Nsikak Benson, Omowumi Agboola, Omowunmi Fred-Ahmadu, and colleagues review micro- and nanoplastics in water life, in Frontiers in Marine Science in 2022. These tiny plastic particles now appear in rivers, lakes, beaches, and oceans, even near the poles. Wastewater plants can pass them into freshwaters instead of removing them. Their amount in aquatic systems is projected to keep climbing for decades.

The review covers how common these particles are, how they move through food webs, and how toxic they prove to water organisms. Small size lets them enter the bodies of tiny animals at the food web's base. From there they can pass upward to fish and beyond. The authors gather scattered findings into one assessment for researchers and regulators.
openalex-w4411251826:
Asahi Hirata, Miho Sumiyoshi, Hazuki Fujita, and colleagues hunt for rare signalling molecules in Streptomyces bacteria. Their paper appeared in The Journal of Antibiotics in 2025. One strain makes two antibiotics, lankacidin and lankamycin. Small butenolide signals switch that production on.

The team tested more than a hundred other Streptomyces strains for the same signals. Almost none could restart antibiotic output in a signal-less mutant strain. Only one known producer strain succeeded. A related signal from another species also failed, even at high doses. A slightly altered signal molecule proved inactive too. The pattern and the chemistry show these signals are rare and highly specific to each strain.
openalex-w7125123226:
Chinenye Iguh, Edith Nwandiko, Asya Azad, and colleagues study sleep apnoea and hidden heart disease risk in obese adults. Their study appeared in the Juntendo Medical Journal in 2026. It is an international cross-sectional study. Obesity alone affects nearly a quarter of adults worldwide.

Obstructive sleep apnoea repeatedly blocks the airway during sleep. The broken sleep and oxygen dips strain fat tissue and metabolism. Both conditions share pathways toward heart disease. The study examines whether apnoea marks higher risk of subclinical ischemic heart disease. That is heart damage present before symptoms appear. Finding such a link would argue for screening obese patients with apnoea early, while prevention can still change outcomes.
openalex-w7125428726:
Yu Zheng, Yanhui Zhao, and Shunji Takahashi review enzymes that borrow charged transfer RNAs to build natural products. Their review appeared in The Journal of Antibiotics in 2026. Charged tRNAs normally feed amino acids into protein synthesis. Some microbes instead use them as building blocks for other molecules.

The review opens with the making of ascamycin, an antibiotic nucleoside. A key enzyme there was found with an AI-guided prediction approach. The authors then model several enzyme families with modern structure prediction. They detail how each family catalyses its reaction. These enzymes expand the known uses of tRNA in chemistry. Understanding them opens routes to engineered antibiotics and other valuable compounds.
openalex-w7204124426: When antidepressants fail twice, depression is called treatment-resistant, and options narrow. This literature review studies electroconvulsive therapy for such cases: how well it works when drugs do not. The authors weigh the evidence for the much-misunderstood treatment. A psychiatric review that takes ECT seriously as a lifeline.
openalex-w7204549026: Cycling does more than build legs; it rewires nerves, hormones, and immune defenses. This narrative review pulls together studies on how regular riding affects the nervous, hormonal, and immune systems. The authors searched major medical databases to map the adaptations. A sports-medicine overview that gives riders scientific reasons to keep pedaling, beyond fitness alone.
openalex-w7204657526: Rural settlers in western Parana practice politics outside formal channels, and this article studies what that means for democracy. The authors investigate how life in land-reform settlements shapes political engagement and conditional loyalty to republican ideals. Based on field research, it shows citizenship lived informally. A rich sociological portrait of politics beyond the ballot box.
openalex-w7206167326: Brazilian students struggle with applying math and logical reasoning, according to international assessments. This paper tests whether Scratch, the free block-based programming tool, can help high schoolers build computational thinking and math logic. The authors report on using Scratch as a teaching tool and what changed for students. It is a concrete experiment in making abstract reasoning hands-on, aimed at teachers looking for new approaches.
openalex-w7206190426: Anxiety often starts young and can shadow a person for years, so stopping it before it starts matters. This paper sums up systematic reviews, with combined data, on programs meant to prevent first-time anxiety and keep it from coming back. The authors judge which approaches the evidence supports. A careful overview for clinicians and policymakers deciding where prevention money does the most good.

This study follows one public school in Rio Grande do Norte, documenting the challenges teachers face and the practices that work when including students on the autism spectrum. It is grounded in a real school rather than theory alone. The paper offers concrete lessons for making inclusion more than a slogan.

Kaline Sousa dos Santos leads a review on physiotherapy for motor growth in children with autism. Their 2026 review searched health databases in March 2026. Five studies from 2021 to 2026, freely available, made the final sample.

Approaches studied included motor physiotherapy, psychomotor work, structured exercise, and sensory integration. Water therapy and horse-based therapy also appeared. Benefits included better coordination, balance, posture control, and motor planning. Daily life function improved as well, the authors report. They conclude that physiotherapy plays a central part in motor development for these children, supporting greater autonomy and social inclusion over time.

Aniely de Souza dos Santos leads a team on play and the development of neurodivergent children. Their 2026 literature review gathers papers and documents from digital platforms. Neurodiversity is treated as natural variation in brain function, and early childhood schooling is the setting.

Play, when planned with intent, supports cognitive, emotional, and social growth, the results indicate. It encourages communication and peer interaction, strengthens bonds, and promotes emotional self-regulation. Schools and educators should treat play as real pedagogy, the authors argue, not as a pause from it. In inclusive settings above all, play belongs inside educational practice in a significant, deliberate way.
openalex-w7218493526:
Caroline Barros Cordeiro, Taiana Renata Siqueira, and Paloma Tainá França Cardoso Nogueira ran a 2026 systematic review on Pilates as therapy for abdominal diastasis. Diastasis is the separation of the belly's paired muscles along the midline, weakening trunk function and stability. Pilates trains strengthening, control, and stabilization of the trunk muscles, a plausible match. Searching five databases, they included primary studies from 2015 to 2025 and kept four after screening.

Three of the four studies observed a reduction in the gap between the muscles, while one, carried out during pregnancy, found none. Improvements in abdominal strength and endurance and reduced lower back pain also appeared. Pilates looks effective for narrowing the separation in most of the small evidence base. It can be considered an applicable physiotherapy resource, the authors conclude, though the studies differ enough to limit generalization.

In 2026, Luanna Rodrigues de Oliveira and André Manoel Correia dos Santos wrote on functional nutrition against the exposome in adolescence, the total of exposures taken in over a life. Adolescence is a window when the body is highly plastic and the reproductive axis restarts, so food and metabolic factors can interact with pubertal maturation. Their review covers hormone disruptors, gut microbiota, gene switching, and bioactive food compounds.

Xenoestrogens, foreign compounds that mimic estrogen, take center stage, above all zearalenone, a fungal toxin in cereals and products, which binds estrogen receptors. Such disruptors can meet hormonal, metabolic, and neuroendocrine paths of maturing, with gut microbes and epigenetic changes taking part. Parts of food might tune the body's clearance of toxins, its antioxidant response, and metabolic pathways. But current evidence cannot show that steps through food neutralize or prevent these effects; clinical and population studies are still needed.
pero-tafur-travels-letts-1926:
Pero Tafur was a Castilian knight who roamed the late medieval world. His Travels and Adventures cover the years 1435 to 1439 abroad. Malcolm Letts put the old Spanish account into English in 1926.

Tafur visits Constantinople, the Holy Land, Egypt, and the courts of Italy. He notes ships, relics, markets, and the manners of each great city. His eye is curious, shrewd, and often frankly amused by strangers. Few books show the 1400s through one traveler's eyes so well. Readers rank it among the most fun travel works of its century by far. Tafur's voice stays fresh, bold, and plainly human throughout.

Natalay Kouprina, Adam Pavlicek, Ganeshwaran H. Mochida, and their team tracked a brain-size gene in PLOS Biology in 2004. ASPM helps control brain size, and broken copies cause a very small brain at birth. The authors compared ASPM across primates to date its fast evolution.

Their timeline shows the gene's rapid change began before the human brain grew to its modern size. That order matters. It means ASPM was already under strong pressure in earlier primates, not only in our own line. The finding tempers simple stories that tie one gene to one human leap. Brain growth, it hints, was a longer, shared ape story.
plos-pone-0000026:
Ryo Matoba, Hitoshi Niwa, Shinji Masui, and their team profiled embryonic stem cells in PLOS ONE in 2006. The protein Oct3/4 is a master switch that keeps stem cells able to become any cell type. The team measured gene activity as Oct3/4 levels changed, to map the networks it runs.

Lowering the switch lets cells start down paths toward specific tissues. The profiles show which gene groups move first and which hold the stem state. Such maps are the working charts of stem cell biology. They help labs grow pure cell types for study and, in time, for therapy. They also flag genes that might make adult cells revert to a stem-like state.
plos-pone-0000126:
Heidi de Wit, L. Niels Cornelisse, Ruud F. G. Toonen, and colleagues published this neuroscience paper in PLOS ONE in 2006. It studies secretory vesicles, the tiny bubbles inside nerve cells that hold chemical messengers. Before release, a vesicle must dock at the cell surface, and the authors test the role of the protein syntaxin in that step.

Their conclusion is in the title: docking depends on syntaxin. Pinning down which protein does which job matters because every nerve signal rides on this release machinery. The paper adds a precise piece to the chain of events that lets one neuron talk to the next.
plos-pone-0000226:
Stephane Esnault, Ruedi K. Braun, Zhong-Jian Shen, and colleagues published this immunology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Pin1 is an enzyme that tweaks the shape of other proteins after they are made. The authors study how Pin1 modulates the type 1 immune response, the branch of immunity that fights viruses and other invaders inside cells.

A single shape-changing enzyme can tilt the strength of a whole immune program. The paper maps Pin1's influence on that response. Because type 1 responses also drive some inflammatory diseases, the findings matter both for fighting infection and for calming immunity when it overshoots.
plos-pone-0000326:
Rauf Bhat and Carsten Watzl published this immunology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Natural killer cells attack tumor cells without prior training. The authors study serial killing, one killer cell destroying several tumor cells in a row. They report that therapeutic antibodies enhance this serial killing by human natural killer cells.

Antibodies already used in cancer therapy may work partly by coaching killer cells. Showing they boost repeated killing strengthens that account. The finding matters for designing antibody treatments that squeeze the most out of the patient's own immune cells.
plos-pone-0000426:
Jenifer L. Marks and colleagues sequenced growth-signal genes in lung adenocarcinomas, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. They analyzed EGFR and related signaling pathway genes, which drive cell growth and are frequent sources of cancer-causing mutations. Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common form of lung cancer, and its growth genes shape treatment choices.

Alongside known changes, the team identified a novel somatic mutation in the kinase domain of FGFR4, another growth receptor. Somatic means the change arose in the tumor, not in the patient's inherited DNA. Each new mutation of this kind adds a possible drug target and refines how lung tumors are classified at the molecular level.
plos-pone-0000526:
Kegong Tian and colleagues investigated a devastating pig virus outbreak in China, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. PRRS, porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome, took an atypical, fatal turn. The team described the emergence of fatal PRRSV variants and performed molecular dissection of the unique hallmark that set the outbreak strain apart.

A molecular hallmark, a signature change in the virus's genome, lets laboratories identify the dangerous variant quickly. China's 2006–2007 outbreaks killed huge numbers of pigs and shook pork supply. Pinning the variant's distinguishing marks is the first step toward matched vaccines and surveillance.
plos-pone-0000626:
Istvan Molnar-Szakacs, Allan D. Wu, Francisco J. Robles and co-authors asked how brains react to hand gestures from another culture. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study concerns emblems, gestures with fixed meanings that speak without words. People everywhere use their hands to communicate, but each culture sets its own gesture meanings.

The team studied corticospinal excitability, how ready the brain's movement pathways are, while people watched culture-specific gestures. Watching a gesture your own culture taught you may prime your motor system differently from a foreign one. The work speaks to the neural bases of cross-cultural social communication, where a familiar sign can land instantly and an unfamiliar one cannot.
plos-pone-0000726:
Wei Zhao, Bapi Pahar, Juan T. Borda and colleagues tracked immune signals during early infection with a hybrid immunodeficiency virus. The chemokines CCL3, CCL4 and CCL5 can block CCR5-using HIV from entering host cells and suppress viral replication in the lab. What the body's own chemokines do during real infection was incompletely understood.

Their title reports a decline in CCL3-5 gene expression during primary simian-human immunodeficiency virus infection. If natural blockers fall just as the virus establishes itself, that timing could help the virus win. The finding sharpens interest in treatments that sustain or mimic these chemokines during the earliest phase of infection.
plos-pone-0000826:
Abraham Miranda, Meade Morgan, Leda Jamal and colleagues measured whether HIV treatment also slowed tuberculosis in Brazil. HIV fuels TB epidemics around the world. In controlled clinical trials, antiretroviral therapy reduces TB incidence in HIV-infected patients. The open question was whether, under real programmatic conditions, Brazil's policy of universal ART access achieved the same effect between 1995 and 2001.

Trials and national programmes often differ: adherence, supply, and late diagnosis all bite in practice. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study tests the policy at national scale. Evidence that treatment-as-delivered prevents TB strengthens the case for funding universal access, beyond the benefit to each treated patient.
plos-pone-0000926:
Jean-Michel Hougardy, Kinda Schepers, Sammy Place and colleagues tested a blood marker for hidden tuberculosis, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Finding latent TB, infection without illness, is central to controlling the disease. The old skin test misses cases, and newer blood tests rely on the release of a signal protein called interferon gamma.

The team used a TB protein named HBHA to trigger that release. A response to HBHA may mark latent infection more sharply than standard antigens. Better latent tests help doctors treat people before they fall ill or spread the germ. The study adds one more candidate to a busy search.
plos-pone-0001026:
Camila Romano, Fernando de Melo, Marco Corsini and colleagues compared ancient retrovirus families in three primate genomes, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Endogenous retroviruses are old infections written into DNA and passed down. The K family is one of the youngest and most studied of these viral fossils.

The team found nineteen complete ERV-K elements in rhesus monkeys and twelve in chimpanzees, then compared them with fifty-five human copies. Those counts sketch each species' demographic history with the virus family. Viral fossils record infections our ancestors survived. Comparing them across primates shows which copies are shared inheritance and which arrived after the species split.
plos-pone-0001126:
Treating drug-resistant tuberculosis takes many months and often fails. Helen Cox and colleagues reported on a treatment program in Karakalpakstan, Uzbekistan, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The region had very high rates of multidrug-resistant TB, found in 13 percent of new cases and 40 percent of previously treated ones.

A pilot program to treat the disease began there in 2003. The authors describe how treatment worked in practice, what outcomes patients had, and how often extensively drug-resistant TB appeared among those who failed treatment. Their account shows the complexity of curing resistant TB in a high-burden setting.
plos-pone-0001226:
Some lung cancers carry activating mutations in the EGFR gene, and these tumors behave differently from other lung cancers. Kuicheon Choi and colleagues profiled gene activity in such cancer cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The subgroup is non-small cell lung cancer with somatic EGFR mutations, changes acquired by the tumor rather than inherited.

The transcriptional mediators of EGFR's effects in this subgroup had not been fully worked out. Using genetic and pharmacological tools, the authors mapped which genes switch on downstream of the mutant receptor. That map matters because EGFR-blocking drugs work dramatically in this subgroup, and resistance eventually follows.
plos-pone-0001326:
Grapes and wine form a large worldwide market, and the cultivated grape, Vitis vinifera, could become a model for fruit tree genetics. Riccardo Velasco and colleagues produced a draft genome sequence for a heterozygous grapevine variety, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Grapes are highly heterozygous, meaning their two genome copies differ at many positions, which complicates whole-genome shotgun sequencing.

The authors present a high quality draft consensus sequence despite that challenge. A consensus merges the two differing copies into one reference. Their sequence opened grape genomics to gene discovery for disease resistance, fruit quality, and breeding.
plos-pone-0001426:
Peter Kroth and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on sugar handling in a tiny sea alga. Diatoms are single celled algae that fix about a fifth of the world's carbon. Their cells arose through a merged past, so their chemistry is more complex than that of green algae. The team used the full genome to build a model.

Their model maps how this diatom makes, stores, and burns sugars. By comparing it with other algae, they flagged routes that seem unique to diatoms. Those routes may help explain why diatoms thrive in the sea. The model gives labs a base for tests on carbon flow in the oceans.
plos-pone-0001526:
Sophie Desset and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how fruit flies silence jumping DNA in the germ line. Small RNAs guard the genome by hushing these mobile parts. The team studied a locus that directs the hush of two such parts in body cells, not just germ cells. They asked which paths run that hush.

They show the locus works through both a Piwi based path and a second, free path. Two paths to one hush give the cell a backup. Germ line guards keep the next brood's genome sound. This body cell case broadens where such guards are known to act.
plos-pone-0001626:
Koleka Mlisana, Sara C. Auld, Anneke Grobler, and their co-authors measured anaemia in people with very early HIV infection for a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Anaemia, a low level of red blood cells or haemoglobin, is common in AIDS and is linked to worse illness and higher death rates. Far less was known about blood changes in the first weeks of infection with HIV-1 subtype C.

The study followed women who did not yet have HIV alongside women in acute and early infection, tracking how haemoglobin levels changed. The full text gives the blood values, the share of women who became anaemic, and how those patterns shifted over time. Knowing when anaemia starts in early infection can help clinics plan testing and care for people who have just caught the virus.
plos-pone-0001826:
Ke Zen and co-authors identified a molecule that helps breast cancer cells cross vessel walls in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Endothelial E-selectin plays a pivotal role in interactions between breast cancer cells and endothelial monolayers during metastasis. The counterreceptor on the cancer cell, and its role in transendothelial migration, were unknown.

The team reports that CD44v4 is a major E-selectin ligand that mediates breast cancer cell transendothelial migration. The full text gives the binding and migration assays. Metastasis requires cancer cells to exit the bloodstream; blocking the molecular handle they use could slow that step.
plos-pone-0001926:
Hongbo Zhu and co-authors built a new way to compare how proteins touch, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Where two proteins meet, atoms form weak bonds that are not covalent. The pattern of those bonds sets how snug and specific the fit is. Labs had many ways to compare protein shapes and binding sites, but none for these contact patterns.

Their method lines up the weak-bond patterns at two interfaces so like patterns can be scored as alike or not. Aligned in this way, interfaces from unlike proteins can be matched. That helps predict how a new protein will bind, a core task in drug design and in basic cell science.
plos-pone-0002026:
Rongqian Wu and co-authors tested a hunger hormone as a shield against gut injury, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. When blood flow to the gut is cut and then restored, a pattern called ischemia-reperfusion, the harm can spread from the gut to distant organs. Immune cells along the gut's vast vessel surface drive a local, then body-wide, inflammatory response.

The hormone is ghrelin, best known for sparking appetite. As the title states, ghrelin attenuated injury both in the gut and in remote organs after this insult. A gut hormone that also calms storm-like injury could aid care in intensive units.
plos-pone-0002126:
David Hendrickson, Daniel Hogan, Daniel Herschlag, and co-authors mapped how tiny RNAs steer gene activity, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. MicroRNAs are short pieces of RNA that do not code for proteins. Instead, they guide a silencing complex to matching messenger RNAs, which can then be cut down or blocked from making protein.

The team set out to find, in a systematic way, which messenger RNAs one protein pulls in. That protein is Argonaute 2, and the search ran when a given microRNA was at work. They also tracked how the amounts of those messages change. Their approach helps replace guesswork about microRNA targets with direct lists drawn from cells.
plos-pone-0002226:
Nikolaus Steinbeis and Stefan Koelsch compared how the brain handles meaning in music and in language, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Music can plainly carry meaning, yet how it does so is unsettled. The team asked whether the meaning of a musical passage is represented in the brain much as the meaning of a sentence is.

They combined EEG, which times brain activity finely, with fMRI, which locates it. The two methods together gave evidence for neural representations that are partly shared and partly distinct. The study helps map where music and language meet in the mind, and where each keeps its own machinery.
plos-pone-0002326:
Christian Dobel, Christian Putsche, Pienie Zwitserlood, and co-authors recorded brain signals from people born unable to recognize faces, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Congenital prosopagnosia is a severe face perception problem present from birth, not caused by injury. People with it cannot recognize even familiar persons by face.

Using MEG, which tracks magnetic fields from the brain with fine timing, the team looked for early faults in face processing. They found dysfunction in the left hemisphere at early stages. A fault that early suggests the problem starts in the first steps of face analysis. It does not start in memory for people. That reshapes how the condition is classed.
plos-pone-0002426:
Work from Llop-Guevara and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Alba Llop-Guevara, Marc Colangelo, Derek K. Chu, and others. Its subject is in Vivo -to- In Silico Iterations to Investigate Aeroallergen-Host Interactions. Allergic asthma is a complex process arising out of the interaction between the immune system and aeroallergens.

Yet, the relationship between aeroallergen exposure, allergic sensitization and disease remains unclear. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002526:
In 2008, Wei and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Bin Wei, Zheng Chen, Xu Zhang, and others. Its subject is nitric Oxide Mediates Stretch-Induced Ca2+ Release via Activation of Phosphatidylinositol 3-Kinase-Akt Pathway in Smooth Muscle. Hollow smooth muscle organs such as the bladder undergo significant changes in wall tension linked to filling and distension.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002626:
Michael Klompas led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was automated identification of acute hepatitis b using electronic medical record data to facilitate public health surveillance. The catalog record names Michael Klompas first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Automatic identification of notifiable diseases from electronic medical records can potentially improve the timeliness and completeness of public health surveillance. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002726:
Rajkumar Sasidharan led a team whose 2008 PLOS ONE article deals with transmembrane protein oxygen content and compartmentalization of cells. Authorship is credited in the record to Rajkumar Sasidharan and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Recently. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state. The description here rests only on the title, the author record, and the abstract text held for the entry, with no claims added beyond those sources.
plos-pone-0002826:
Jenee N. Smith led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was SdiA, an n -Acylhomoserine lactone receptor, becomes active during the transit of salmonella enterica through the gastrointestinal tract of turtles. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Jenee N. Smith, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. LuxR-type transcription factors are typically used by bacteria to determine the population density of their own species by detecting N-acylhomoserine lactones (AHLs). Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002926:
Maria Camats, Sonia Guil, Mariette Kokolo and co-authors studied how the helicase p68 shapes H-Ras splicing in 2008. H-Ras RNA can be spliced two ways, making either the p21 or the p19 protein, depending on whether a piece called IDX is kept. The p68 protein was known to reduce IDX inclusion.

Published in PLOS ONE, the study shows p68 also alters the activity of other splicing factors that act on the same RNA. Splicing is how one gene yields several proteins. The results add detail on how a single helicase can steer that choice in a cancer-linked gene.
plos-pone-0003026: Stephen Beres, Ricardo Sesso, Sergio Pinto and colleagues reported the genome sequence of a Lancefield group C Streptococcus zooepidemicus strain in PLOS ONE in 2008. The strain caused epidemic nephritis, a kidney disease outbreak, and the subtitle calls the work new information about an old disease. The catalog record gives title, authors, and year, with no further abstract detail. The article presents the full genome of that outbreak strain as a base for studying how this animal-associated streptococcus infects people.
plos-pone-0003126:
Yara C. Blanco, Alessandro S. Farias, Uta Goelnitz and co-authors test a support treatment for cerebral malaria in this 2008 PLOS ONE study. Cerebral malaria brings nerve signs, seizures and coma, and it shares some traits with stroke. Even so, few studies had looked at new supportive care for the disease. Hyperbaric oxygen, given under pressure, had shown success in other settings.

The title states the central finding: hyperbaric oxygen prevented early death in mice with experimental cerebral malaria. Readers find a test of a non-drug support idea for a severe form of malaria. The work points to care that might buy time alongside standard treatment.
plos-pone-0003226:
Kwok M. Ho, Matthew Knuiman, Judith Finn and colleagues build a survival model for critically ill patients in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Long-term survival outcome of critically ill patients is important for assessing new treatments and for making treatment decisions. The team developed a prognostic model for estimation of long-term survival, called PREDICT. It was a retrospective linked data cohort study.

Readers get a tool aimed beyond hospital discharge, at long-term outlook. Families and clinicians often need that longer view when weighing intensive care. A validated model can support those hard conversations with data instead of guesswork alone.
plos-pone-0003326:
Scot E. Dowd, Randall D. Wolcott, Yan Sun and colleagues sequence bacteria from diabetic foot ulcers in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Ulcers on the feet and legs of people with diabetes are linked with chronic infections. Such ulcer infections are too often followed by amputation. There is little knowledge of the ecology of such infections, or of how to control or clear this type of chronic infection.

Using bacterial tag encoded FLX amplicon pyrosequencing, the team show the polymicrobial nature of chronic diabetic foot ulcer biofilm infections. Readers learn these wounds host mixed groups, not single germs. That mix explains why antibiotics aimed at one species often fail in such ulcers.
plos-pone-0003426:
Israel Hershkovitz and colleagues found ancient tuberculosis traces in this 2008 paper. They studied bones from a Neolithic settlement in the eastern Mediterranean. The settlement dated to about nine thousand years ago. Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the TB germ, was thought to have evolved beside humans for ages.

The team pulled out and characterized DNA of that germ from the remains. Finding it in such old bones backs the long shared history. TB leaves no home outside its human host, unlike many germs. This molecular proof pushes confirmed TB deep into prehistory. Few finds tie a named germ to a dated human settlement so directly.
plos-pone-0003526:
Lucina Q. Uddin and co-authors scanned self-face recognition in autism for this 2008 study. Autism involves less interest in social exchange and stronger self-focus. Earlier theories stressed social impairments in the disorder. The team asked how the brain handles self versus other faces.

Using brain imaging, they watched participants recognize their own faces. Neural patterns for self and other could then be compared. Where those patterns diverge may mark autism's social gap. The study gives a brain-level view of self representation. Face reading is core to social life, which is why its gaps matter.
plos-pone-0003626:
Elena R. Álvarez-Buylla, Álvaro Chaos, Maximino Aldana, and colleagues published this modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It asks how a flower takes shape as its genes switch on and off. The team built a model of the gene network that guides flower formation.

In their model, random noise could push the network toward stable flower forms, not just blur them. That runs against the older view of growth as a fixed, preset program. The study presents flower form as the product of a network that can use chance and still stay stable.
plos-pone-0003726:
Galit Tzur, Asaf Levy, Eti Meiri, and colleagues published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Human embryonic stem cells can renew themselves and can also turn into any body tissue. Small RNAs called microRNAs help steer that choice by tuning gene activity after genes are read.

The team tracked microRNA patterns as the cells differentiated toward endoderm, the layer that forms the gut and related organs. They also probed what those microRNAs do in the process. The patterns show small RNAs at work in one of the embryo's first big decisions.
plos-pone-0003826:
Daniel Mietchen, Bertram Manz, Frank Volke, and colleagues published this animal study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Below freezing, ice crystals threaten the structure and function of cells. Insects in seasonally cold places have evolved many strategies to reorganize their tissues against the cold.

The team assessed cold adaptation in insect larvae inside the living animal. They used magnetic resonance imaging and spectroscopy to watch tissues handle the cold without cutting them open. The in vivo view shows the tricks larvae use to survive deep cold through a hard winter. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008.
plos-pone-0003926:
Jianfeng Zhou, Wenhong Li, Hiroyasu Kamei, and co-authors compared a growth-control gene in fish in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns IGFBP-2, a protein that binds growth factors. It helps govern growth, development, reproduction, and aging. High levels of it also appear in many advancing cancers.

Teleost fish carry two copies of the gene, unlike most other vertebrates. The team compared the proteins those copies make and how each is used. Form and basic function stayed much the same after duplication. Gene use, though, had drifted apart between the two copies over time. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004026:
Francisco J. Quintana, Avishai Mimran, Pnina Carmi, and co-authors described a new immune control route in 2008. HSP60 is a heat shock protein that shapes T cell responses. It can signal through a receptor or serve as an antigen. The protein rises in stressed and inflamed tissues.

Their PLOS ONE article reports regulatory T cells target HSP60 itself. These anti-ergotypic cells react to the presented stress protein. That reaction forms another loop for calming immune responses. Understanding the loop may help treat autoimmune disease. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004126:
Kristin Field and colleagues published this feeding study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines casein hydrolysates, broken-down milk proteins used in foods for their nutrition and useful properties. Their bitter taste often limits how much makers can add to products meant for people.

Earlier evidence hinted that other animals also avoid eating them, but few species had been tested. The team offered animals a choice between foods with and without the hydrolysates. They found that plant-eating species avoided them, while omnivores did not. The result matters for food design and for understanding how taste guides diet across species.
plos-pone-0004226:
Yong Zhao and colleagues published this diabetes study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Type 1 diabetes is caused by the immune system destroying the pancreas's insulin-making beta cells. Controlling that autoimmunity is essential to any real treatment. Regulatory T cells, the immune system's peacekeepers, play a pivotal role in holding self-attack in check.

The team used human cord blood stem cells to modulate these regulatory T cells. They report that the treated cells reverse the autoimmune diabetes in nonobese diabetic mice, the standard model of the disease. The approach aims at the cause of type 1 diabetes, not just its blood sugar.
plos-pone-0004326:
Martin Schweizer, Markus Henniger, and Inge Sillaber published this stress study in PLOS ONE in 2009. In many depressed patients, stressful life events help trigger the illness. In rats, chronic mild stress can produce depression-like states, and the procedure is a standard animal model. Whether it works the same way in mice was less certain.

The team examined chronic mild stress in mice, looking at anhedonia, the loss of pleasure that is a core symptom, and at activity. They report an anomalous anxiolysis, a paradoxical calming, alongside the expected effects. Mixed results like these warn against assuming one species' model fits another.
plos-pone-0004426:
Health is more than one number, and Alessandra Andreotti, Nadia Minicuci, Paul Kowal, and co-authors set out to draw fuller health profiles in PLOS ONE in 2009. They drew on the World Health Survey, run by the World Health Organization in seventy countries between 2002 and 2004. The survey gathered data meant to be compared fairly across peoples.

The team applied a method called the Grade of Membership model to that survey. Instead of forcing each person into one class, the model lets each person partly belong to several health profiles at once. That gives a richer, multi-sided view of how health, risk factors, and outcomes cluster in real populations. Such profiles can guide health policy across very different countries.
plos-pone-0004526:
Two diseases that look alike can be told apart quickly with a combined DNA test, report Maria Isabel Queipo-Ortuno, Juan Colmenero, Pilar Bermudez, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The diseases are tuberculosis outside the lungs and focal complications of brucellosis, another bacterial infection. They are hard to differ by symptoms alone, and both cause much illness and death in many countries.

The team developed a multiplex real-time PCR assay, a test that detects several targets at once. It picks up Mycobacterium tuberculosis and the brucellosis bacterium in a single run on a patient's sample. A fast, sure answer matters because the two diseases need different drugs. The test shortens the guesswork that delays the right treatment.
plos-pone-0004626:
Doctors and health workers do not always see the same sickness in the same child, a study by John Wagai, John Senga, Greg Fegan, and co-authors shows in PLOS ONE in 2009. Case management guidelines use a limited set of clinical features to guide assessment and treatment of common childhood diseases in poor countries. The whole system rests on workers recognizing those features correctly.

Using video records of clinical signs, the team assessed agreement among experts. They also assessed whether Kenyan health workers could identify the signs shown. Disagreement at this basic level means children with the same illness can receive different care. The findings point to where training and guidelines need strengthening, in the first minutes of a sick child's assessment.
plos-pone-0004726:
Chandrajit Chatterjee and Ram Sarkar proposed a step wise math method to model and forecast malaria cases, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Malaria stays one of the worst health problems in the world today. Case counts shift with age, sex, social life, weather, and how the disease spreads in a place.

A good forecast must weigh those drivers and the spread pattern at once. The team built a staged curve fitting method for that task. Better forecasts help clinics stock drugs and staff in time. They also help target spray and net campaigns where cases will rise. The work also raises clear questions that targeted studies can now address.
plos-pone-0004826:
José Igual and colleagues asked whether compensatory mitigation for marine bycatch suffices for long lived seabirds, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Following the polluter pays principle, it was proposed that the local long line fishing industry fund eradication of terrestrial predators at seabird breeding colonies. That would compensate for bycatch caused by fishing activity under a mitigation scheme debated by managers and conservation groups.

Models test if predator removal offsets birds lost at sea. For slow breeding species, gains may arrive too late. Buying years to extinction is not recovery. Direct bycatch reduction remains essential. The results give future studies a clearer base for comparison and follow up.
plos-pone-0004926:
The Wnt signal tells cells when to grow and when to specialize. Its key messenger is a protein called beta-catenin. When beta-catenin builds up unchecked, it helps drive many cancers. Geng Wu and co-authors studied one control on it in PLOS ONE in 2009. They examined the Wnt co-receptor LRP6. They asked how it blocks the enzyme GSK3.

Once Wnt switches LRP6 on, the receptor gains phosphate tags. Those tags sit on repeating motifs in its tail. The study shows the tagged motifs directly inhibit GSK3. So beta-catenin escapes destruction, and the growth signal stays on. The work details a control switch at the heart of development and cancer.
plos-pone-0005026:
Tinnitus is ringing in the ears with no outside source. Its causes remain incompletely understood. Some people blame electromagnetic fields for their symptoms. Michael Landgrebe and colleagues examined a possible link in PLOS ONE in 2009. They asked whether tinnitus and electromagnetic hypersensitivity are associated. They also asked whether the two share a mechanism.

The data hint at overlapping pathways. People reporting electromagnetic sensitivity showed particular tinnitus patterns. That is not proof of a shared cause. It is a first step toward testing one. The work treats both conditions seriously without overstating the evidence. Such care is rare in a field full of strong claims.
plos-pone-0005126:
Aptamers are DNA strands that grip targets like antibodies. Some fold into four-stranded knots called G-quadruplexes. Tao Li, Erkang Wang and Shaojun Dong improved them in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their strategy was grafting. Proven pieces were combined into new designs. Some G-quadruplex aptamers bind hemin and act as DNA enzymes.

The grafting produced aptamers with better binding. It also produced DNAzymes with higher activity. Mix-and-match design beats random search here. The recipe is general, not tied to one target. Biotech gains better molecular tools. Sensors, diagnostics and research reagents all use aptamers. A design shortcut shortens their development. The work shows rational design catching up with selection.
plos-pone-0005226:
Even when a person rests quietly, the brain produces slow, organized waves of activity. Those waves, seen in functional brain scans, are thought to reflect the brain's built-in networks. He and colleagues uncovered the modular layout of that resting activity in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The analysis sorted spontaneous activity into modules, groups of regions that work together. Mapping that layout is one of the hard problems in neuroscience, since it must be drawn from noise-like signals. A trusted map of resting networks helps researchers spot what changes in brain disease.
plos-pone-0005326:
Genes that appear and disappear together across many genomes usually work together. A phyletic vector records, for one gene, the pattern of presence and absence across species. Li and colleagues matched those patterns to detect biochemical pathways in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Their probabilistic matching weighs how closely two genes' patterns align. Closely similar vectors flag genes that likely share a pathway. The method turns genome catalogs from many species into pathway maps, without any wet-lab work for each new organism. Each new genome sequenced makes these maps sharper, since more species means more rows in the table and a clearer view of which genes keep the same friends across time.
plos-pone-0005426:
Akihiko Ozawa, Richard Speaker, and Iris Lindberg described a human enzyme in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Cells often attach fatty tags to proteins after the proteins are made, and those tags change what the proteins do. Yet the enzymes that attach one kind of tag were still poorly known.

The authors found and described an enzyme that adds a short fat chain to a protein building block. They tested what speeds it up, what slows it down, and what it needs to work. The careful profile fills a gap in basic knowledge about how cells mark and control their proteins.
plos-pone-0005526:
Daniela Nitsch and co-authors built a method to find disease genes in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Gene hunts often narrow a disease to a stretch of chromosome that still holds dozens of genes. Only a few of them can be tested in the lab.

Their method uses networks of known gene links to rank the genes in such a stretch. Genes tied to similar diseases or pathways rise to the top of the list. Ranking well saves years of lab work and helps families learn the cause of a disease sooner.
plos-pone-0005626:
Peter Daley and co-authors ran a pilot study on preparing sputum for tuberculosis tests in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Looking at sputum under a microscope is a main way to diagnose tuberculosis, but it misses many cases. Treating the sputum first can make the germs easier to see.

The team compared two quick preparation methods, each taking under an hour. They measured how much each method added to the accuracy of the smear test. Cheap gains in accuracy matter most in the poor settings where tuberculosis is commonest. Microscopy is still the front-line test in most poor countries, so gains there reach the most patients.
plos-pone-0005726:
Rhona McDonald and colleagues profiled a remarkable protein from horse sweat in 2009. Horses are odd among mammals for sweating a protein-rich fluid to cool down. The main protein, latherin, acts like a soap, helping sweat spread through the oily coat.

The team read latherin's full amino acid chain from its gene. The chain is much the same in horses from four far-apart regions, a sign its job is finely tuned. Latherin also shows up in horse saliva. Knowing its makeup helps explain how horses cope with heat and hard work, a matter of real care in racing and sport.
plos-pone-0005826:
Gail Rattinger and Lisa Bero examined in 2009 whether drug company funding tilts head-to-head trials of diabetes drugs. When a sponsor pits its drug against a rival's, results tend to favor the sponsor. The drugs studied, thiazolidinediones, are among the costliest oral options for type 2 diabetes.

The team looked for factors tied to favorable results and conclusions in such trials. Design choices, like doses chosen for the rival drug, can stack the deck quietly. Documenting those factors helps doctors read industry trials with care. It also supports rules for fairer comparative testing.
plos-pone-0005926:
Eosinophils are white blood cells best known for fighting parasites and driving allergy. In 2009, Fanny Legrand, Virginie Driss, Gaëtane Woerly and colleagues found something unexpected on these cells in humans. Their PLOS ONE paper reports a working receptor complex, built from CD3 and a gamma-delta T cell receptor, on the eosinophil surface.

That kind of receptor was thought to belong to T cells alone. Finding a distinct, working version on eosinophils widens what these cells can do in the body's first line of defense. The result invites a fresh look at allergy and infection, where eosinophils may sense threats in ways no one had credited to them.
plos-pone-0006026:
The microbes in the gut help digest food, but they also talk to the immune system. Joshua Uronis, Marcus Mühlbauer, Hans Herfarth and colleagues asked in 2009 whether changing that microbial mix changes cancer risk. Their PLOS ONE paper studies colitis-linked colorectal cancer, a cancer that grows out of long gut inflammation, as in Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.

Shifting the gut community shifted how prone the animals were to that cancer, the title reports. A result of this kind makes the microbiome a possible lever for prevention, not just a bystander. It also sharpens the question for patients with gut inflammation: which microbes guard them, and which ones raise their risk over time.
plos-pone-0006126:
Circles of DNA float free of the chromosomes in every eukaryotic cell. Zoya Cohen and Sara Lavi asked in 2009 where those circles come from. Their PLOS ONE paper shows extrachromosomal circular DNA forming in a mammalian cell-free system without any DNA replication, testing a pool of circles built from repeated chromosomal sequences.

Circular DNA has been tied to genomic instability, aging and a backup way of lengthening telomeres. A formation route that skips replication changes how each of those links is read. The cell-free system strips the process to its core parts, letting the team name what circle making truly requires.
plos-pone-0006226:
Bacteria that shrug off methicillin pose a lasting threat in hospitals. Ida Autiero, Susan Costantini, and Giovanni Colonna modelled that resistance as a whole-system problem in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Living systems stay functional under attack, a property called robustness, and resistance is one form of it.

A systems biology model treats the bacterium as a network rather than a single drug target. Networks show where several weak points might be hit together. The approach can suggest drug combinations that a one-target view would miss. It also explains why resistance survives single-drug pressure so well.
plos-pone-0006326:
Averaging millions of cells into one measurement hides how individual cells differ. Alan Diercks, Heather Kostner, and Adrian Ozinsky present a new method in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Their real-time PCR approach reads several genes at once in many single-cell samples. Decoding multicellular complexity requires procedures that beat those averaged limits.

Simultaneous multiplexed detection lets each cell report several genes, not just one. Cell populations can then be split into real subgroups rather than blurred. Heterogeneity matters in immunity, cancer, and development. The method gives labs a practical route to single-cell detail.
plos-pone-0006426:
Maria Karanika and co-authors drew on a meningitis registry for a 2009 PLOS ONE study of sick children. Meningitis in childhood still kills many patients in many countries. Doctors need fast ways to tell which germ is causing acute bacterial meningitis. The team analyzed clinical symptoms and lab findings recorded in the registry.

The goal was to find signs that point to the likely pathogen before full test results arrive. Early clues can speed the choice of the right treatment. Registry data let the authors test these clues across many real cases. The work supports quicker, better-targeted care for a dangerous disease of childhood.
plos-pone-0006526:
Roberta Pastorino and co-authors studied immune genes and multiple sclerosis in Sardinia for PLOS ONE in 2009. The human leukocyte antigen complex on chromosome 6 has been unambiguously associated with multiple sclerosis. The region's features are especially complex, making fine mapping hard. Sardinia's population has a distinct genetic history that can help.

The team studied association between protective and deleterious HLA alleles and MS in central east Sardinia. Some alleles raise risk while others lower it. An island population with high MS rates is a powerful place to separate those effects. The results refine which immune genes matter in this disease.
plos-pone-0006626:
Anna Barnes, Edward Bullmore, and John Suckling measured slow brain recovery after mental effort in PLOS ONE in 2009. In functional magnetic resonance imaging, the brain's response to experimental manipulation is almost always assumed to be independent of endogenous oscillations. The team tested that assumption. They examined endogenous human brain dynamics following cognitive effort.

Their title reports those dynamics recover slowly following effort. In other words, the brain's background state takes time to settle. Experiments that ignore this carryover may misread task effects. The finding matters for the design of nearly all brain imaging studies.
plos-pone-0006726:
Henrik Walter and colleagues asked how long emotion regulation effects last in the brain in PLOS ONE in 2009. People can voluntarily calm their reactions to unpleasant scenes. Brain imaging shows the amygdala quiets during such regulation. The amygdala is a hub for threat and emotion. Little was known about whether the quieting survives after regulation stops.

The study tracked the temporal dynamics of voluntary emotion regulation. Participants regulated, then stopped, while brain activity was recorded. The key question was sustainability of the neural effect. Lasting effects would mean a short effort buys longer calm. Brief effects would argue for different training designs. The findings inform therapies built on emotion regulation skills.
plos-pone-0006826:
