Iraad F. Bronner and his team read gene use across a set of brain diseases in PLOS ONE in 2009. The diseases are the tauopathies, marked by bad tau protein in the brain. The set holds Alzheimer's disease and Pick's disease. It also holds two more: progressive supranuclear palsy and frontotemporal dementia. The four look much alike in the clinic and in the lab. That likeness has long slowed work on all of them.

Full scans of gene use told the four apart. The scans also found paths of cell work that all four share. Marks that split look-alike diseases can sharpen diagnosis. Shared paths hint that one drug might help more than one disease. The scan gives the field a map it had lacked.
plos-pone-0006926:
Zheng Kou, Yongdong Li, Zuohua Yin, and colleagues reported a bird flu survey in PLOS ONE in 2009. They sampled wild birds across fourteen provinces of China. The target was the highly pathogenic H5N1 influenza virus. Sampling ran from April 2004 to August 2007.

H5N1 had emerged in Asia in 1996 and later spread to Europe and Africa. The authors note that monitoring and data analysis in mainland China were not yet sufficient. Their survey gathered field evidence on where the virus appeared in wild birds. Such surveys help health officials track a virus that threatens poultry, wildlife, and people.
plos-pone-0007026:
Shuming Zou, Hiroyasu Kamei, Zubin Modi, and colleagues charted growth factor genes in zebrafish in PLOS ONE in 2009. Insulin-like growth factors steer development, growth, and lifespan. Most vertebrates, humans included, carry one IGF-1 gene and one IGF-2 gene. Zebrafish turned out to be different.

The team found and characterized four distinct IGF genes in this fish. They traced how the genes were duplicated and how they diverged. They also found new roles in building the body's midline and the notochord. Extra gene copies let one fish split old jobs in new ways.
plos-pone-0007126:
Alice Mado Proverbio, Serena Mariani, Alberto Zani, and colleagues probed how the brain stores names in PLOS ONE in 2009. A long debate asks whether distinct meaning domains sit in distinct brain systems. Patients with naming problems sometimes lose one class of words only. Brain imaging had not settled the map. The team used paired words as their test.

They compared a proper name, Barack Obama, with a matching common noun phrase, President Elect. Brain responses, recorded as ERPs, differed between the pair. Different storage for names and descriptions supports the domain view. It also shows how identity and role are coded apart.
plos-pone-0007226:
Anna-Karin Roos, Fredrik Eriksson, James A. Timmons, and colleagues studied DNA delivery through skin in PLOS ONE in 2009. Electric pulses can push molecules into living cells, a method called electroporation. It had become popular for delivering DNA in living tissue for gene therapy and vaccines.

The authors test skin electroporation in detail. They measure effects on transgene expression, how long delivered DNA persists, and the local tissue environment. Their results matter for designers of DNA vaccines and gene treatments who need both strong expression and acceptable local tissue damage levels.
plos-pone-0007326:
Angela M. C. Rose, Sibylle Gerstl, Ali E.-H. Mahamane, and colleagues evaluated rapid meningitis tests during an outbreak in Niger in 2009. The Pastorex test is a main rapid diagnostic for meningococcal disease in Africa's meningitis belt. Earlier evaluations used heated, centrifuged spinal fluid under good lab conditions, which field clinics often lack.

The authors test two rapid diagnostics for Neisseria meningitidis serogroup A in the field. The 2006 outbreak setting shows real-world performance. Their PLOS ONE results matter because quick, accurate diagnosis guides vaccination campaigns during fast-moving meningitis outbreaks.
plos-pone-0007426:
Sébastien Ballesteros, Elisabeta Vergu, and Bernard Cazelles published a modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how influenza A changes over time. Flu epidemics return again and again, and the usual explanation was steady, gradual drift in the virus. Newer evidence hinted that change in its main surface protein might instead come in bursts. The authors used simple mathematical models to sort this out.

Their models show how gradual genetic change can still produce a punctuated pattern at the level that matters for immunity. Long quiet stretches are broken by sudden jumps in the surface protein. That pattern helps explain why flu can slip past immune defenses built against earlier strains. The work links small steady changes to the big epidemic cycles people actually experience.
plos-pone-0007526:
Alfredo Mendoza-Vargas and colleagues published a genome-wide mapping study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on E. coli, the most studied bacterium in science. Despite decades of work, a major share of its transcription start sites remained unknown. Those sites mark where reading of a gene begins. Without them, the circuits controlling gene expression stay partly hidden. The team set out to map them across the whole genome.

Their survey identified start sites, promoters, and the binding sites of transcription factors at genome scale. The results enrich RegulonDB, the reference database for E. coli regulation. A fuller map means researchers can model the bacterium's control systems with fewer gaps. Even a model organism, it turns out, still holds basic secrets. This study fills in many of them at once.
plos-pone-0007626:
John Horner and Mark Goodwin published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the dome-headed dinosaur Pachycephalosaurus. Some dinosaurs changed shape dramatically as they grew, through extended youth and late growth spurts. With few individuals preserved, the stages of that transformation are hard to find. The team studied skulls across the growth series of this Upper Cretaceous plant-eater. The domes told an extreme story.

The skull's shape changed so much with age that young and old look like separate species. Late-stage growth did most of the reshaping. That warns paleontologists: some named species may be juveniles of known ones. Counting dinosaur diversity demands care about growth, not just form. The study is a landmark in reading dinosaur lives from their bones. It turns a strange dome into a biography.
plos-pone-0007726:
Haishan Li and C. David Pauza published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests two immune-regulating compounds on a special class of human T cells. The compounds are a natural prostaglandin, called 15d-PGJ2, and a diabetes drug, rosiglitazone. Both are predicted to calm autoimmune disease.

The target cells, Vdelta2 T cells, play a role in autoimmunity in animals and people. Before this study, how the compounds affect them was unknown. The authors measured the cells' responses in the lab. The results help judge whether these drugs could treat autoimmune disease safely.
plos-pone-0007826:
Hua Zhang and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It links patterns of tiny RNAs to outcomes in children with leukemia. MicroRNAs are short molecules that tune gene activity. They play critical roles in cancers, including adult leukemia.

Their role in pediatric acute leukemia was less clear. The authors measured microRNAs that were abnormally expressed in young patients. Certain patterns tracked with clinical prognosis. Others predicted relapse in the central nervous system, a feared event. If the patterns hold up, a small blood test could flag children who need stronger treatment early.
plos-pone-0007926:
Rodrigo Calado and colleagues reported a family study of severe liver disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. They looked at faults in the genes that build telomerase, an enzyme that keeps the ends of chromosomes at a safe length. Such faults were already known to harm bone marrow.

In the families studied, the same kind of fault tracked with a wide range of grave liver problems. When telomeres grow too short, cells that divide often suffer first, and the liver proved no exception. The work widens the list of ills tied to worn chromosome ends and gives doctors a genetic clue when liver failure runs in a family.
plos-pone-0008026:
Angelique Gougelet and colleagues tested an antibody against stubborn blood cancers in PLOS ONE in 2009. Lymphoma and myeloma cells often resist both drugs and radiation. High levels of the signal IL-6 track with that resistance, so blocking IL-6 looked like a way to soften the cells.

Cancer cell lines treated with the antibody stayed just as hard to kill. Neither drug response nor radiation response improved. A clear no is still useful: it steers teams away from a costly dead end and toward other ways of breaking resistance in these cancers.
plos-pone-0008126:
Tao Huang and colleagues forecast drug effects from gene activity watched over time in PLOS ONE in 2009. Side effects often surface late, after years of costly drug work, or even after a drug reaches patients. An early warning drawn from the first hours of gene response could save both money and health.

Profiles of gene activity across time carried enough signal to predict how bodies would answer a drug, including foreign compounds. The forecasts were built on patterns, not single genes. Drug teams could use such a screen to drop risky candidates while dropping them is still cheap.
plos-pone-0008226:
Declan P. McKernan and colleagues studied gut immunity in animal models in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Irritable bowel syndrome is often viewed as a stress-related disorder. It involves faulty communication among the brain, gut, and immune system. Stress is known to alter innate immune responses. Yet little work had linked that fact to bowel symptoms.

The team measured toll-like receptor messages in the colonic lining of two animal models. These receptors sense microbes and trigger immune defenses. Expression rose selectively in models relevant to the syndrome. The result supports a role for innate immunity in irritable bowel complaints.
plos-pone-0008326:
Huabin Zhao, Binghua Ru, and Emma C. Teeling traced a vision gene in mammals in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mammals spread into many light environments, from bright savanna to dark caves. That spread is linked to adaptive changes in their visual systems. Rhodopsin is the light-sensitive protein used for dim-light vision. Its properties help set what an animal can see at night.

The authors studied rhodopsin molecular evolution across mammals in low light habitats. Comparing gene sequences reveals how selection tuned the protein. Such changes show evolution acting at the molecular level. The work links ecology to the chemistry of sight.
plos-pone-0008426:
Nahuel Fittipaldi and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2010 on Streptococcus suis, a germ that harms pigs. They looked at pili, the thin hair-like parts on the cell surface. Those parts help the germ stick to host cells and spread in the body.

The team changed a gene for one pilus part, called the ancillary pilin. With that part gone, the pili still formed, but they were made of the main part alone. The result shows how the pilus is built, step by step. It also points to parts that drugs might block to weaken the germ.
plos-pone-0008526:
Yizhe Tang and co-authors build a new adenovirus for cancer gene therapy in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Safe and effective cancer medicines are still needed. Many patients have diseases that current treatments cannot cure. Adenoviruses can carry therapeutic genes into tumor cells. But a single virus type may infect too narrow a range of cancers. The team derive a triple mosaic adenovirus instead.

A mosaic virus mixes capsid parts from different adenovirus types. Mixing parts can broaden which cancer cells it enters. It may also evade immune defenses that block one type alone. The paper describes how the triple mosaic was made and tested.
plos-pone-0008626:
Reiko Sanokawa-Akakura and co-authors study amyloid toxicity in fruit flies in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Amyloid beta is the protein fragment that builds up in Alzheimer disease. FKBP52 is a large immunophilin, a protein that helps fold other proteins. Copper balance in cells also affects amyloid harm. The team use Drosophila, the fruit fly, to test these factors together. Flies offer fast genetics for brain disease models.

They find FKBP52 controls amyloid beta toxicity in the flies. Copper homeostasis, keeping copper at steady levels, also shapes that toxicity. Both factors may be targets for limiting amyloid damage. Fly work can reveal modifiers hard to find in mammals.
plos-pone-0008726:
Claudio Rolli, Thomas Seufferlein, Ralf Kemkemer, and colleagues watched tumor cells squeeze through tight spaces. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used tiny channels built in the lab. A cancer cell's inner skeleton, the cytoskeleton, gives it shape and stiffness. To invade tissue, a cell must soften and deform. How skeleton layout governs that squeezing was unclear.

Cells crawled through channels narrower than themselves while the team filmed them. Stiffer, well-organized cells struggled where softer ones slipped through. Speeds and shapes revealed which layouts favor invasion. The setup offers a clean way to test drugs meant to slow cancer spread.
plos-pone-0008826:
Qian Han, Haizhen Ding, Howard Robinson, and colleagues solved the structure of a fruit fly enzyme that makes brain signals. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme, DDC, finishes the making of dopamine and serotonin. It clips a piece off their precursor building blocks. Both finished chemicals steer mood, movement, and sleep. Knowing the enzyme's shape helps explain how it picks its targets.

The crystal structure shows the active site in fine detail. Tests then measured which related compounds the enzyme accepts. Shape and pickiness together reveal its working rules. The fly enzyme models the human version used in brain chemistry.
plos-pone-0008926:
Sinead Leahy and colleagues published the full genome of Methanobrevibacter ruminantium in PLOS ONE in 2010. The microbe lives in the rumen, the first stomach of cattle and sheep, where it makes methane gas. Methane warms the planet far more strongly than carbon dioxide does. Farm animals release large amounts of it through burping.

The team read the microbe's DNA letter by letter and mapped its genes. They looked for weak points that might let farmers or drug makers slow methane output. The genome points to surface proteins and enzymes that are found only in this kind of methane maker. Those targets could guide vaccines or feed additives that cut emissions from livestock.
plos-pone-0009026:
Min Ki Jee and co-authors pushed human fat stem cells back toward a younger state, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Stromal cells from fat tissue can become several cell types, but they are not full stem cells. The team combined low oxygen with a new antioxidant compound, called a DHP derivative. Both tricks mimic conditions that keep cells primitive.

Treated cells turned back the clock, a change called de-differentiation. They switched on markers of more primitive stem cells. Reprogrammed fat cells could one day supply repair tissue from a patient's own body. The recipe avoids viruses, which makes it attractive for future medical use.
plos-pone-0009126:
Pierre Becquart and co-authors surveyed rural Gabon for signs of past Ebola infection, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Zaire ebolavirus is the deadliest member of the Ebola virus family. How widely it circulates between the famous outbreaks was unclear. Gabon contains both regions with past epidemics and quiet forest areas.

The large survey ran for three years and covered 4,349 people in all. Blood tests found antibody proof of past infection in many of them. Immune cells that remember the virus were common as well. High silent immunity suggests the virus reaches these people more often than outbreaks show.
plos-pone-0009226:
Huaiping Zhu, Hong Qian, and Guangpu Li published this cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It concerns endocytosis, the process by which cells pull material inside. A protein called Rab5 acts as a switch for the early steps. Rabex-5 switches Rab5 on, and Rabaptin-5 helps in the same process.

Rabex-5 can activate Rab5 through two distinct pathways. One route also creates positive feedback, where active Rab5 boosts its own activation. The team found that this feedback switches on only after a delay. That timing detail shapes how cells start forming the vesicles that carry cargo inward.
plos-pone-0009326:
Youri Timsit and Péter Várnai published this DNA study in PLOS ONE in 2010. DNA inside cells is twisted into supercoils, and that twisting shapes many cell functions. The overall form of a supercoiled molecule depends on local contacts where DNA segments lie side by side. Those contacts affect both the physics and the biology of the molecule.

The authors examine helical chirality, the handedness built into DNA's twist. They argue it links local interactions between segments to the molecule's global shape. A clear link between the small scale and the large would help predict how DNA folds. That folding decides which genes are reachable and when.
plos-pone-0009426:
Dalia Denapaite and co-authors published this genome study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Streptococcus mitis lives quietly in the human mouth and throat. It is the closest relative of Streptococcus pneumoniae, a major killer. Comparing the harmless cousin with the pathogen asks what makes one a commensal and the other a threat.

The team sequenced strain B6, a form unusually resistant to many antibiotics. Its genome runs about 2.15 million letters and encodes some 2,100 genes. A resistant commensal is a reservoir of resistance genes living beside us. The genome gives researchers the full text for asking what separates neighbor from pathogen.
plos-pone-0009526:
Louise Harrington and co-authors tested a drug in rats with lung hypertension in PLOS ONE in 2010. In that disease, pressure in the lung's vessels climbs. The right side of the heart must push harder and can swell and fail. Rats kept in low oxygen develop a like condition. The team gave them a drug called GW0742, which activates a receptor named PPAR beta delta.

The drug relaxed the lung vessels in treated rats. It also limited the swelling of the right heart. Few good treatments exist for this disease in people. A drug that both eases pressure and guards the heart is a lead worth pursuing.
plos-pone-0009626:
Eric McCollum and co-authors evaluated HIV testing of children in Malawi hospitals in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many sick children in high prevalence areas are never tested for HIV. Staff shortages are a main barrier. The program shifted routine testing tasks to less costly, trained health workers. Two versions of that model were piloted in an urban hospital. The team reviewed how each performed.

Task shifting improved the program's outcomes, with more children tested and enrolled in care. That gain came without adding scarce doctors. The study backs a staffing strategy that many poor health systems can copy. It shows that who does a task can matter as much as the test itself.
plos-pone-0009726:
After spinal cord injury, nerve fibers usually fail to regrow. Yuxuan Wang and colleagues tested designer DNA strands that might lift that block. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The block comes partly from myelin, the coating around nerve fibers.

Myelin carries inhibitor proteins that stop axons, the long fibers of nerve cells, from growing. The strands, called aptamers, were built to block those inhibitors. With the inhibitors opposed, axons grew better in the tests. The approach points toward new ways to repair injured cords. Regrowing axons is a first step toward restoring lost movement.
plos-pone-0009826:
When cells face stress, they send chemical signals that can end in cell death or growth. Raphael Devillard and colleagues traced one such signal pathway in mouse cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The pathway runs through sphingolipids, fatty molecules that double as signals. A key enzyme, type-2 neutral sphingomyelinase, helped drive the response. The team linked it to both apoptosis, orderly cell death, and proliferation, cell multiplication. Stress signals can push a cell either way. Balancing those two outcomes matters in cancer and tissue repair. Mouse cells stand in for human cells in early tests.
plos-pone-0009926:
When the brain misreads a scene, two leading theories explain the error differently. Guido Hesselmann and colleagues weighed those theories against brain data. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. False inference means drawing a confident conclusion the evidence does not support.

Predictive coding says the brain constantly guesses the world and updates on errors. Evidence accumulation says it gathers proof until a threshold is crossed. Neuronal fluctuations, the noise in brain activity, helped tell the models apart. The debate shapes how scientists picture perception itself. Both theories still shape research on perception.
plos-pone-0010026:
The authors were William Hobbs, Richard Telford, H. John Birks, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study read lake mud in North America and Greenland. Tiny algae called diatoms leave shells in lake sediment. Their mix records the water and climate of past years.

By counting diatom groups in recent layers, the team measured how remote lakes changed in the twentieth century. They compared arctic lakes with alpine and forest lakes over the same years. The record helps separate climate effects from other forces acting on wild, far-off waters. Each layer adds a dated page to that history.
plos-pone-0010226:
The authors were Jing Xu, Jun-Ying Zhou, Wei-Zen Wei, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study asked why some cancer cells resist a death signal. The signal, called TRAIL, can trigger cancer cells to die by apoptosis. Many tumors resist it, and the mechanism behind that resistance was not fully understood when the team began.

The authors showed that a survival route inside cells, the Akt pathway, plays an important role. When Akt signaling is active, human cancer cells withstand TRAIL better. Blocking that survival route could make TRAIL-based treatment work on tumors that now shrug it off.
plos-pone-0010326:
Catarina Lira-Medeiros, Christian Parisod, Ricardo Fernandes and others examined mangrove plants for PLOS ONE in 2010. Their focus was epigenetic change, meaning chemical marks that alter gene activity without altering the DNA code itself. One such mark adds a methyl group to a DNA base. Plants can pass these marks to their offspring. Stress from salt, heat, or living things may set them off.

The team studied a mangrove species that grows in sharply different natural settings. They compared marks across plants from those contrasting homes. If marks differ where conditions differ, marks may help plants cope locally. That idea matters as coasts change fast under climate pressure. Mangroves protect shorelines, so how they adapt is worth knowing.
plos-pone-0010426:
Jaakko Pohjoismäki and co-workers examined how heart muscle DNA is organized across life and disease for PLOS ONE in 2010. Heart cells carry many copies of a small mitochondrial genome. Adult heart copies form tangled structures, including doubled and branched forms. Why the heart keeps its DNA this way was unclear. The team compared organization, copying, and counts across development and pathology.

Changes over a lifetime could explain why some heart diseases emerge late. A maintenance style fit for youth may fail with age or illness. Mitochondrial DNA faults are tied to several heart conditions. Mapping the normal pattern is needed before faults can be spotted. This study supplies that map for the human heart.
plos-pone-0010526:
Junsong Sun and colleagues coaxed a complex hydrogen-making enzyme to mature in a foreign host for PLOS ONE in 2010. Hydrogen gas is a major candidate biofuel. Microbes make it with hydrogenase enzymes, intricate machines built around nickel and iron. These enzymes are complex and easily wrecked by air. Building them in easy lab hosts had been a bottleneck for biofuel work.

The team got the enzyme expressed and matured outside its native microbe. That step matters because engineering better enzymes needs a workable host. A nickel-iron enzyme that can be produced and tweaked opens design space. Clean hydrogen from biology remains a long-term prize. This study removes one specific obstacle on that road.
plos-pone-0010626:
Jasper van den Boorn and colleagues combined three treatments against melanoma in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Melanoma that has spread is hard to treat with standard drugs. Yet the cancer is visible to the immune system, which gives immunotherapy a chance.

One drug, monobenzone, removes skin pigment and exposes pigment cells to attack. Two helper compounds, imiquimod and CpG, then rally immune cells. Together the trio shrank tumors and extended survival in the mice. Turning the pigment system into a target may offer a new route for patients who run out of options.
plos-pone-0010726:
Tanja Musch and colleagues showed how certain drugs force cancer cells to grow up, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some tumor cells keep stem-like traits that help them resist treatment. Nucleoside drugs, which mimic DNA building blocks, can push such cells to mature instead of killing them outright.

After drug treatment, key stem cell factors inside the cells were destroyed. The destruction ran through caspase enzymes, usually known for dismantling dying cells. As the factors fell, the cells lost their stem-like behavior. Forcing maturity is a gentler attack plan than poisoning, and it may work where standard drugs fail.
plos-pone-0010826:
Laura Kananen and fellow Finnish researchers published this study in PLOS ONE in 2010. They asked whether hard experiences in childhood leave a lasting mark on telomeres, the caps that protect the ends of chromosomes and shorten with age and stress. Their data came from a large national health survey carried out in Finland at the start of the century.

The team measured telomere length in blood cells from adults with anxiety disorders and matched adults without them. Telomeres did not differ across the whole group, yet older patients with anxiety showed clearly shorter telomeres. Childhood hardship was also tied to shorter telomeres in adulthood, in patients and controls alike. Kananen and colleagues suggest early stress can echo in the body for decades, which matters for how doctors think about anxiety and aging.
plos-pone-0010926:
E Besray Unal, Attila Gursoy and Burak Erman published this drug design study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Peptide drugs, short chains of amino acids, can block disease proteins with fewer side effects than many small chemicals. But no set way existed to design such a blocker from scratch for a chosen target. Their method, VitAL, needs no examples of known peptides to learn from.

The algorithm builds a peptide step by step, docking residue pairs along a chosen path across the target protein's surface, using a simplified model to find the binding site first. Unal and colleagues present a fully computational route from a protein structure to a candidate inhibitor. If it generalizes, de novo peptide design could shorten the search for treatments against proteins that resist conventional drugs.
plos-pone-0011026:
Berna Atik, S Claiborne Johnston and Deborah Dean published this stroke risk study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Narrowed neck arteries are seeded with plaques that can trigger stroke, and plaques often harbor Chlamydia pneumoniae, a respiratory bacterium. The team had earlier linked the bacterial burden in plaques to inflammatory signals, and now examined an inflammation-mediating enzyme called Lp-PLA2.

They studied tissue from patients having plaque-removal surgery, staining it for the enzyme, immune cells, the bacterium, and inflammatory markers, alongside blood measurements of enzyme level and activity. Atik and colleagues test whether infected plaques are also the plaques richest in this enzyme. The question matters because Lp-PLA2 is both a drug target and a blood test used to judge cardiovascular risk.
plos-pone-0011126:
Touchon and Rocha studied bacterial immune systems in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many bacteria carry CRISPR, a stored record of past virus attacks used for defense. In common gut bacteria, the authors found these systems were unusually small, slow to change and narrow in scope.

The team also mapped counter systems that viruses use against CRISPR. Together the results show a stripped down form of immunity, tuned to a stable gut setting. That economy is of interest for gene editing, which borrows CRISPR tools. It also helps explain how gut bacteria and their viruses coexist over long periods.
plos-pone-0011226:
Horney, Moore, Davis and colleagues surveyed North Carolina during the 2009 flu pandemic for PLOS ONE in 2010. A new H1N1 vaccine had just become available. The team asked who planned to take it, who followed advice to keep distance when ill, and where people got their information.

Answers revealed what drove pandemic behavior in that population. Trust and information sources shaped vaccine intent and daily choices. Health agencies can use such findings to craft clearer messages in the next outbreak. Building public trust before a crisis, the study implies, is as vital as the vaccine itself.
plos-pone-0011326:
Mizuno, Hosogi, Park and colleagues studied wheat crosses in PLOS ONE in 2010. Breeding tetraploid wheat with a wild relative can produce hybrids that sicken and die, a barrier called hybrid necrosis. The team linked that death to a reaction like the hypersensitive response plants use against germs.

In effect, the hybrid's own defense alarm fires without any germ present. That explains why some crosses fail despite healthy parents. Breeders can use this knowledge to avoid fatal combinations in advance. It clears a path for bringing useful wild traits into wheat without wasting seasons on doomed crosses.
plos-pone-0011426:
Alexander Seewald and co-authors measured in 2010 how much genetically identical worms still differ from one another. A cage of isogenic roundworms shares the same DNA, yet individuals vary in stress response and lifespan. The team used a glowing reporter that marks a stress protein known to predict longevity and stress resistance in these worms.

They clustered the two-dimensional glow patterns to turn worm-to-worm variation into firm numbers instead of impressions. Quantifying variation among genetic twins isolates the share of difference that DNA cannot explain. That share is where environment, chance, and cell noise leave their marks. The method gives biologists a sharper tool for a deep question: how much of an animal's fate is written in its genes, and how much is decided by everything else?
plos-pone-0011526:
Taku Kashiyama and co-authors compared in 2010 the two calcium channels that frogs use to trigger muscle contraction. Muscles contract when calcium floods out of internal storage through ryanodine receptor channels. Frogs carry two forms, alpha and beta, side by side in the same fibers. The team tested them in a muscle cell line, asking whether the pair is mere backup or a division of labor.

The two receptors produced distinct intracellular calcium signals, differing in shape and timing. One cell can thus tune its calcium messages with fine control by choosing which channel speaks. Calcium is a universal signal, so its dialect matters in heart, brain, and gland cells too. The frog's two-channel system is a clean model of how a cell gets many messages out of one ion.
plos-pone-0011626:
Ta-Chien Chan and co-authors built a daily flu warning system in PLOS ONE in 2010. Public health teams need to spot unusual rises in flu-like illness early, before an epidemic takes hold. Any alert carries uncertainty, so a useful system must weigh how likely a true outbreak is, not just count cases.

Their model combines place and time in a Bayesian framework, which handles uncertainty openly. It watches daily illness reports across areas and flags abnormal patterns with a stated level of confidence. Health officials using such a system can act sooner while knowing how much trust to place in each alert.
plos-pone-0011726:
Todd Brusko and co-authors engineered human regulatory T cells with chosen targets, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Regulatory T cells calm immune responses, and boosting them could treat autoimmune disease and transplant rejection. Broadly boosting them, however, risks suppressing the whole immune system, including useful defences against infection.

By transferring T cell receptor genes into these cells, the team created regulators aimed at a specific antigen. Targeted peacekeepers could settle the immune attack where it occurs without a blanket shutdown. The approach points toward tailored cell therapy for autoimmunity and transplantation.
plos-pone-0011826:
Jessica Bogs and co-authors probed what makes H5N1 bird flu so deadly, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Highly harmful bird flu viruses grow out of mild forerunners. They stand apart from all other flu viruses by a polybasic cut site in their surface protein, found in subtypes H5 and H7. That site was long treated as the whole key to their deadliness.

The team tested the power of a low-harm virus to cause grave disease, and found harm factors that sit beyond that famed cut site. The added culprits round out the picture of this flu's deadliness, and they inform risk checks on new strains.
plos-pone-0011926:
Yaolong Chen and colleagues audited in 2010 how well trial results are reported in the abstracts of five leading Chinese medical journals. Abstracts of randomized controlled trials matter because many readers judge, and sometimes act on, a trial from its abstract alone. Little was known about reporting quality in these journals.

The audit checked whether the abstracts carry the details readers need, such as how patients were assigned and what the main results were. Gaps in an abstract can mislead even when the full trial was done well. The findings give editors a concrete checklist of what to demand before a trial abstract reaches doctors' screens.
plos-pone-0012026:
Matthias Negri, Maurizio Recanatini, and Rolf Hartmann studied in 2010 an estrogen-making enzyme by watching it move. The enzyme, 17β-HSD1, catalyzes the final step in making estradiol, the strongest estrogen, making it an attractive target for breast cancer treatment. In solution, such enzymes exist as a shifting ensemble of shapes, not one fixed pose.

By investigating the enzyme's dynamic motion, the team gained insight into its kinetics and how ligands bind. A moving target binds drugs differently than a frozen diagram suggests. Motion-aware design could yield blockers that fit the enzyme as it actually behaves in the body.
plos-pone-0012126:
Xiao Chang, Shuai Liu, Yong-Tao Yu, and co-authors mapped gene activity over time in an antibiotic-making bacterium, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The bacterium's full genome had been read a few years earlier, and a custom chip let the team watch nearly all its genes at once. They wanted to see how genes group into working modules as the cell grows and produces.

They identified sets of transcript units that rise and fall together, and charted how those sets are organized across the genome. A module map turns a flood of gene data into a readable wiring diagram. Since this bacterium makes a useful antibiotic, understanding its switches may help raise yields in industrial production.
plos-pone-0012226:
Gábor Firneisz, Tímea Varga, Gabriella Lengyel, and co-authors measured an enzyme in the blood of patients with fatty liver disease, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fatty liver tied to insulin resistance is now extremely common and quietly progresses toward serious liver damage, yet finding it early usually takes scans or biopsy. The enzyme they measured, DPP-4, is already famous in diabetes care, where blockers of it are standard drugs.

Comparing patients with diabetes, patients with fatty liver, and healthy controls, they tested whether the enzyme's blood activity tracks insulin resistance and liver disease. A blood marker would let doctors screen for fatty liver during routine diabetes visits. That matters because the disease is silent for years while still reversible.
plos-pone-0012326:
Martina Wengenroth, Maria Blatow, Martin Bendszus, and co-authors scanned the hearing cortex of people with Williams syndrome, in PLOS ONE in 2010. This rare genetic condition is famous for an unusual love of music and sound, alongside intellectual disability and a friendly social style. The team sought the brain basis of that musicality in the auditory cortex, the strip that first processes sound.

They found the auditory cortex leans leftward in these individuals, matching an all-at-once, holistic way of hearing rather than a detail-by-detail one. Linking a gene condition to both a brain asymmetry and a way of perceiving gives music cognition a rare concrete anchor. It may also inform teaching methods that work through sound for these learners.
plos-pone-0012426:
Aurore Liénard, Isabelle Merckaert, Yves Libert and colleagues followed young doctors after a communication course, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Talking well with patients is a core medical skill, and training courses can teach it. The open question was whether skills practiced in training survive the move to real wards, where time pressure and habit push back.

The team observed residents during real clinical rounds after the program. Many trained skills did transfer to the workplace, though unevenly. Knowing that transfer happens, and where it fades, helps schools design follow-up coaching rather than one-off courses. Better doctor-patient talk improves trust, safety, and how well patients follow treatment.
plos-pone-0012526:
Tomoharu Osada, Hideki Ogino, Toshiaki Hino and colleagues found a chemical tagging step required for nuclei to fuse after fertilization in mice, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. After sperm meets egg, the two parental nuclei must break their envelopes and mingle their genomes. That mingling needs fast rearrangement of chromatin and proteins, driven by chemical tags.

The team showed that polyADP-ribosylation, a fast tag added to proteins, is required for the pronuclei to fuse properly. Without it, development stalls at the first step. The discovery adds a concrete mechanism to the biology of conception and may inform fertility research.
plos-pone-0012626:
Ashworth, Teng, Kaufeld and co-authors traced a kidney problem to a protein called cofilin-1. The kidney's filter cells, podocytes, grip the filter with tiny feet full of actin fibres. Those fibres must shift as pressure changes, and cofilin helps remodel them.

Their 2010 work, spanning zebrafish, mice and human samples, showed that switching cofilin-1 off leads to protein leaking into urine. Protein in urine is an early sign of kidney failure, so the mechanism matters for patients. The study ties a small cell protein to a common disease sign.  Further patient samples would test how general the effect is.
plos-pone-0012726:
Cai, Huang, Feng and co-authors built a thirty-five gene signature for a common lymphoma. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma splits into subtypes that behave differently, and survival varies just as much. Sorting subtype and predicting survival both shape each patient's treatment plan directly.

Their 2010 work found one gene set that does both jobs at once, instead of needing two separate tests. A single readout that classifies and forecasts is simpler for clinics to run. It also hints the two tasks share deeper biology than their separate histories suggest.
plos-pone-0012826:
Sun, Pager, Luo and co-authors blocked hepatitis C copying with pieces of the virus's own core protein. The virus needs a host enzyme, DDX3X, to run its life cycle, and its core protein binds that enzyme. Their 2010 study cut the core into peptides and tested which pieces interfere.

Some core-derived peptides stopped the genome of the common 1b type from copying, by acting on DDX3X. Using the virus's own parts as blockers is a neat route to new antivirals. The host enzyme angle may also resist viral escape mutations better.
plos-pone-0329426: Galvez-Hernandez and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for a review on AI in primary health care. The planned review covers tools that serve whole organizations and systems, not single patients. Examples include scheduling, records, and population health tasks. As a scoping review protocol, it sets the search and sorting rules in advance. Clinics need such a map before buying system-level AI.
plos-pone-0331726:
Sayeeda Tarannum and colleagues studied why staff in a specialist tuberculosis hospital in Bangladesh did or did not wear N95 respirator masks, which guard against catching the disease from patients. The team trained twenty-eight doctors, nurses, and support workers in fitting, wearing, and storing the masks, supplied each person with two months of masks. They watched and interviewed staff before and after the training.

At the start, nearly all nurses wore masks while no doctors or support workers did, a gap the study set out to explain. Interviews dug into how staff judged their own risk and what helped or blocked daily mask use, from comfort and supply to habit and workplace norms. The authors aim to guide protection programmes that fit how hospital staff actually behave.
plos-pone-0333726:
Richa Giri led a survey of citrus groves across Nepal. The target was the germ behind citrus greening. The disease is the worst threat to citrus crops in the world. The team took more than a thousand leaf samples from thirteen districts. A gene test flagged infected trees. Five samples were read in full to trace the strain's kin.

One in four samples tested positive. The disease is thus spread wide in Nepal. The strain matched the Asian form of the germ. Its closest kin came from India. The team urges clean young trees for new groves. They also back strict control of the insect that carries the germ.
plos-pone-0342726: Kolen and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on poor nutrition in people who lost a leg. These patients lost a major lower limb due to blood vessel disease. The title states the finding in strong terms: undernutrition is alarmingly common in this group. The team followed patients forward in time. Hungry patients heal slower, so this warning argues for routine nutrition checks after amputation.
plos-pone-0342926:
Mohajon and colleagues assessed a floating solar plant design for a wetland in Bangladesh in a 2026 study. Floating panels save scarce land, but owners need to know how fast output fades and whether the plant pays over its life. The design uses a ring-shaped float that lets some light pass through to water life below.

Checks supported the float's balance and buoyancy, and a light model tested whether water plants could still grow beneath. A learning model forecast how output and energy yield would decline over twenty-five years under local weather. Cost over the plant's life was worked out as well. Together, the checks frame floating solar as workable where land is tight.
plos-pone-0344826:
Ihor Kendiukhov reports an unusual experiment in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. An automated loop of AI programs proposed hypotheses. It then tested one hundred and forty-one of them. The subject was what AI models of cells actually learn. These models read single-cell gene activity. They are widely used in biology. The question was simple. Does the geometry inside them reflect real biology? Or is it just a training artefact?

Several patterns held up well. Gene neighbourhoods had genuine mathematical shape. Curved distance measures found regulatory gene pairs better. Two independently trained models agreed on the overall shape of gene space. Yet the strictest checks told a narrower story. Solid signal concentrated in immune tissue. The paper, negatives included, calibrates how much trust these models have earned.
plos-pone-0345426:
Pierre Lovinfosse leads a multi-center check of a scan meant to spot hidden rejection in transplanted kidneys without a biopsy. Silent rejection can damage a new kidney while blood tests still look calm, so clinics rely on scheduled biopsies. The scan tracks sugar use in the kidney, compared against a back muscle, and earlier small studies had raised hopes for it.

Across several centers and close to two hundred stable recipients, scan values overlapped heavily between normal kidneys and those with borderline or silent rejection. The scan measure did not track tissue damage scores, while older donor age did predict abnormal tissue. Lovinfosse and colleagues conclude the scan should not be used to rule out silent rejection, a clear negative result that can save clinics wasted effort.
plos-pone-0346626:
Iñigo Palacios-Martínez and colleagues censused two hundred thirty-two winter roosts of western jackdaws across the Iberian Peninsula to see who shares the night. Most roosts were shared with other species, mainly other crows, starlings, and cattle egrets, averaging nearly three species per site. Shared roosts held significantly more jackdaws than jackdaw-only ones.

Proximity to towns and landfills encouraged sharing, while high elevation, wide temperature swings, and forest cover discouraged it. Some companions, such as wood pigeons, came with higher jackdaw numbers, while glossy ibises and dense starling crowds came with fewer. Jackdaws dominated numerically in over half the shared roosts, but that dominance depended on who else showed up, painting roosts as negotiated communities.
plos-pone-0347426:
Nilima Thombre and co-workers build a tablet that swells hugely in the stomach so its drug can leak out slowly where it absorbs best. The test drug treats stomach ulcers but passes through the body poorly. Their 2026 study mixes the drug into a super-porous sponge-like gel made by foaming, then tunes the recipe with a structured set of trials.

The best version released nearly all its drug and swelled to about three times its size in tests. X-ray checks in living subjects showed it floating and staying in the stomach for up to twelve hours. Checks also confirmed the drug stayed stable inside the mix. Longer stomach time could mean fewer doses and steadier relief for ulcer patients.
plos-pone-0348126:
Graham Pluck and colleagues created a quick test of vocabulary knowledge for Thai speakers. Judging stored, learned knowledge matters in brain science, but most tests are built for English. Their forty-two item task simply asks people to tell real Thai words from invented ones. Responses from six hundred sixty-two Thai speakers, collected online, were used to polish the test in the 2026 study.

Scores lined up well with verbal fluency and other Thai language measures, rose with age and education as expected, and barely budged when people retook the test, showing stability without practice effects. The authors offer it as a fast way to estimate earlier cognitive ability in Thai patients.
plos-pone-0348426:
Nayiar Shahid and co-authors checked whether a family of cancer drugs can block the cell doorways that other cancer drugs need in order to work. The blockers, called tyrosine kinase inhibitors, are often combined with older drugs built from nucleosides, the letters of DNA. Those partner drugs enter cells through dedicated transporters, and earlier hints suggested the newer drugs jam the doors.

In engineered human cells carrying one transporter each, every drug tested jammed both main transporters, and one also jammed a third. Yet the jamming happens at strengths above those reached in patients, and losing the transporters did not change how one drug affected cell survival. The authors conclude that, at normal doses, this clash is unlikely to undermine combination cancer treatment.
plos-pone-0348726:
Sri Idaiani and colleagues drew on a large household survey of more than nineteen thousand adults across Java, Indonesia, to study how hard life events relate to poor mental health. Events such as loss, illness, or losing work were scored by how much stress they usually cause, and answers were compared with standard checks for depression and anxiety symptoms.

People who had lived through moderately stressful events had about three times the odds of depression, and the link grew much stronger for the most stressful events. Similar patterns held for anxiety. Education, household wealth, and living in a town or city softened the risk somewhat. The authors say support after major life events should account for these social differences.
plos-pone-0349026:
Zekun Zhou and Shuo Yang built a giant map of medical knowledge to rank possible drugs for type two diabetes, and, crucially, to explain each suggestion in plain steps. Their graph merges five databases spanning Western and traditional Chinese medicine, holding a quarter million entities linked by millions of relationships, with genes as bridges. Four learning models read the map to predict missing links.

One model consistently handled the trickiest many-to-many links best and drove the final predictions. On top of the predictions sits an explanation engine that searches for the strongest chain of reasoning, scoring paths by length, importance, and experimental backing. The authors argue that doctors and researchers will only trust machine-suggested drugs when the machine can show its work, and they built the system to show it.
plos-pone-0349226:
Silvers and colleagues evaluated a nurse training program in northern Laos in a 2026 paper. The program runs at a children's hospital in Luang Prabang, a city in a country where many young children still die from treatable illness. The team reviewed course plans, surveyed past visiting nurse mentors, and spoke with former program leaders about the first five years.

Mentors reported that local nurses had grown stronger in hands-on care since training began. They also stressed that teaching had to fit Lao culture and daily hospital life. A train-the-trainer approach, varied teaching methods, and materials built for local needs stood out as reasons the program worked.
plos-pone-0349526:
Brennan Keiser, Stacy Shaw Welch, and co-authors published a 2026 protocol for a trial bringing nurse-led pain care to rural adults with chronic pain. Rural communities carry heavy pain burdens yet often get by on medication alone, including risky opioids. The planned trial will recruit four hundred fifty adults from rural health systems and randomly assign them to usual care or to six months of virtual nurse care management.

The nurse program bundles talk therapy for pain, care coordination, and instructor-led online group exercise. The main measure is a combined score of pain intensity and how much pain interferes with life and activity, with mood, sleep, function, and opioid use also tracked. As a hybrid design, the trial will judge implementation, reach, fidelity, and staying power alongside effectiveness.
plos-pone-0349826:
Deena Fremont and co-authors pooled studies in 2026 on blood salt disturbances in people with eating disorders. Low potassium and sodium are among the medical dangers of these illnesses, and how common they are, and what harm follows, needed a single accounting.

Twenty studies covering more than twenty-five thousand people, mostly young women, were combined. Anorexia nervosa dominated the evidence. People with eating disorders had higher odds of salt abnormalities than healthy controls, and rates varied by diagnosis. Most studies looked backward at records, which limits firmness. Still, the pooled figures justify routine blood checks in eating disorder care.
plos-pone-0350026:
Wei Xiong and co-authors built a forecasting and decision system to help power companies predict what their distribution networks will cost and where money is best spent. Shifting loads and supply uncertainties strain older planning methods. Their 2026 model, named TransGrid-CostOpt, fuses deep learning with load forecasting, multi-goal optimization, and a learning-based decision module fed by several data sources.

On two public load datasets, the system beat traditional and recent rival methods, with overall performance gains the authors put between fifteen and thirty percent. Removing single modules hurt results, and the forecasting and decision parts proved most important. The authors present the framework as adaptable to fast-changing electricity markets, where cost control and reliable forecasts must advance together.
plos-pone-0350326:
Ritva Torppa and colleagues measured how well seventy-nine Finnish toddlers and preschoolers can name words from a category on demand, a skill called verbal fluency. Children had one minute to list animals or clothes while researchers counted correct words, groupings, and switches between groups. Parents also reported how much music the children made at home and in lessons.

Every part of the skill grew with age across the two-to-five span, though different parts matured at different speeds. Children with more informal music making at home, singing and playing outside formal lessons, performed better. Lessons themselves showed no such link in this small sample. The results sketch a normal path for early word retrieval and hint that everyday home music, not just training, rides along with stronger language growth.
plos-pone-0350426:
Medical residents in Syria train inside a health system strained by years of conflict. Mohammad Al-Jawad and colleagues surveyed residents across six Syrian regions in spring 2025 about burnout, using a modern assessment tool, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

The questionnaire covered exhaustion, distance from patients, shrinking sense of achievement, plus job satisfaction, coping habits, and workplace problems. Burnout in doctors worldwide often passes half of those surveyed, and the authors expected Syrian rates to run high under wartime pressure. Their goal was a careful count with a sharper instrument than older studies used, so training hospitals can target the worst drivers.
plos-pone-0350626:
Su Youn Nam and Junwoo Jo followed nearly three million Korean adults to see how weight change over four years relates to later stomach cancer risk. Weight and stomach cancer have a tangled relationship that may differ by sex, age, and smoking. Their 2026 study used national health exam data from 2009 and 2013, sorting people into twenty-five weight-change paths and tracking cancer cases through 2017.

Staying in the first obesity band was tied to higher cancer risk across most groups. In contrast, men, smokers, and younger adults who gained modestly from normal weight to overweight showed slightly lower risk. Dropping from obesity to overweight lowered risk in women before menopause, while patterns after menopause differed. The authors conclude that the meaning of a weight change depends heavily on who is changing.
plos-pone-0350726:
What China's foreign ministry spokespeople say at daily briefings builds an image of China and its rivals. Feng Pan, Weixiao Li, and Tao Li analyzed a large text collection of briefing answers given during a public health crisis, in this 2026 PLOS One language study.

Spokespeople used cooperative talk to stress China's stance and joint efforts, and sharper talk to push back at criticism led by the United States. The pattern mostly fits a known framework of praising one's own side and blaming others, but it bent with circumstances. The authors trace the shifts to diplomatic beliefs, geopolitics, and traditional Chinese culture, and suggest the old framework needs a flexible update.
plos-pone-0350826:
Maha Bashri and Sameera Ahmed examine, in a 2026 study, whose voices dominate news coverage of climate change and whose get left out. They focus on reporting in American and British newspapers around COP26, the United Nations climate summit held in Glasgow, Scotland.

Their content analysis finds that politicians, scientists, and activists from wealthy northern countries receive most of the attention. Indigenous people and minority communities, who often face the worst climate harm, appear far less often. The authors connect this imbalance to power and access, and call for news coverage that includes a wider range of speakers.
plos-pone-0350926:
Sven Schwabe and Franziska Herbst mapped who provides suicide assistance in Germany, and who takes part. A court ruling in twenty twenty left the practice legal but unregulated. No official count of it exists. The team interviewed sixteen experts in twenty twenty-five. They spoke with scientists, officials, journalists, and members of right-to-die groups.

Five kinds of actors emerged from the interviews. Right-to-die organizations lead the list. Medical and lay assistants follow. Treating doctors play a part, and so do funeral directors. Relatives and friends complete the chain. The result is a whole informal system with no registry watching it. Any future law would have to govern this cast, and this study names it.
plos-pone-0351126:
Paula Barrué-García and colleagues describe a plan to build one combined nursing assessment for patients cared for at home instead of in a hospital ward. Hospital-at-home programs are growing, nurses visit only at intervals, and records there are patchy because nurses juggle many separate forms covering function, skin risk, falls, frailty, food, and sleep. Their planned instrument merges those checks into a single tool.

The study protocol lays out how the tool, named VALENF-HAD, will be assembled from existing validated measures and then tested for whether it is clear, consistent, and truly measures what it claims. No results are reported here. A single well-tested form could cut duplicated paperwork and missed risks, giving home nurses more of their visit time for the patient rather than the clipboard.
plos-pone-0351226:
China's Double World-Class program pours money into chosen university departments, and Jianqin Hang and Xing Ma asked what happens to the departments left out. Their 2026 PLOS One study used discipline-level data from Chinese universities between 2014 and 2023.

Two forces could act: reflected prestige helping neighbors, or drained resources hurting them. For Chinese-language core journals, unchosen fields published slightly less and slightly weaker work after the policy. For English-language journals, the same fields published notably more and better work. The split suggests prestige spilled over internationally while domestic resources tightened, a mixed verdict for a policy meant to lift whole universities.
plos-pone-0351626:
Shobha Islam and three colleagues build a mathematical model, published in 2026, that treats maths anxiety like a spreading infection among students. Their framework sorts students into those currently anxious and those not, then tracks how anxiety passes between them and fades over time.

The analysis finds a threshold value that decides the outcome. Below it, anxiety dies out. Above it, anxiety settles in for the long term. The system stays stable on either side of that line. Two factors push the threshold up most: how many students enter university and how fast anxiety spreads socially. The model suggests schools should focus on slowing that social spread and helping anxious students recover, rather than only drilling skills.
plos-pone-0351726:
Zhi-qiang Zhang and colleagues traced allergic rhinitis back to the bone marrow, where the white cells that drive the allergy are born. Eosinophils, the effector cells, answer to a receptor called CCR3. The team combined gene-data mining with mice engineered to lack CCR3 only in bone marrow cells, then gave the mice an allergen-driven rhinitis and tracked progenitor cells through marrow, blood, and nose.

The receptor's absence blunted the disease: fewer nasal symptoms, less tissue damage and inflammatory infiltration, and a smaller supply line of eosinophil progenitors leaving the marrow. A gene hub tied to the receptor's deletion also emerged from the data screens. Hay fever is usually treated in the nose; this study argues part of the disease is decided earlier, at the cell factory, and names a lever there.
plos-pone-0351926:
Mateus Ribeiro and co-authors describe in 2026 two new species in a small genus of stalked fungi found in northeastern Brazil. The genus is set apart by a cap like cover and a layered stalk, and naming inside it had rested mostly on looks. Specimens from a highland region were studied by shape and by three gene markers together.

Family trees placed the genus firmly apart from its close relative and grouped the two new species as sisters to a known pink species. Each new species differs from all known ones by a mix of shape and gene traits. The count of accepted species in the genus rises with the find.
plos-pone-0353126:
Pedro Fortes and colleagues explore in 2026 how people in Brazil interpret unusual experiences that stand out from everyday life, such as hearing a voice with nobody near. How such moments are judged can lead toward growth or toward distress and exclusion. One study checked and extended a question set on interpretations, and a second asked a large general sample about one experience each.

Most answers followed a smooth, single peaked pattern, suggesting shared ways of making sense across very different experiences. A fifth felt an immediate bad effect, yet about half judged the long term effect on life as positive. The authors highlight human resilience in framing the extraordinary.
plos-pone-0353726:
Mst Sumaiya Khatun and five co-authors catalogue a gene family that helps plants build lignin, in this 2026 PLOS ONE comparison of two model legumes. The CAD genes also support water-conducting tissue and defences against fungi and pests. Until now nobody had mapped the whole family across both Medicago truncatula and Lotus japonicus side by side.

The search found fifty-one such genes in the first species and thirty-five in the second, spread across several chromosomes. Their proteins share the same core building blocks, though the Lotus set looks more uniform in ancestry. Stress-response data show which family members switch on under drought and similar hardships, pointing breeders toward hardier legumes.
plos-pone-0354026:
Xiaojuan Chen and co-authors propose a lean computer method for scoring risk in the communication networks that carry power grid data. Grid operators need monthly warnings, but they often have little past data and cannot run heavy models. The new method trims weak measures, weighs the rest with a light attention step that favors measures tied to risk, and fits the score with a regression that resists overfitting.

On a year of small-sample data, the method cut average error by roughly a fifth against a standard fixed-weight approach and by a smaller margin against a heavier attention model. It also spotted key risk measures faster. Chen and colleagues present it as a practical early-warning tool that runs on modest hardware.
plos-pone-0354126:
Aekyoung Kim and co-authors argue that peak fertility raises women's interest in flashy luxury goods, and they explain the claim as a mating signal. Earlier work suggested women use luxury to set high standards and narrow the field of suitors. Kim's team proposes the opposite first step: visible luxury draws wide attention, which grows the pool of possible partners before any choosing begins.

Their account splits courtship into an attraction phase, where being noticed helps, and a selection phase, where standards filter the pool. Under this view, a fertility-linked pull toward showy goods fits both the new claim and the older findings. Kim and colleagues present the argument to sharpen debate among consumer researchers about why desire for luxury rises and falls.
plos-pone-0354526:
Yonas Abebe Tarefa and Abdul-Fatawu Abdulai map what research exists on technology-facilitated abuse of women and girls in sub-Saharan Africa, in this 2026 scoping review. Phones and social platforms have created new channels for harassment and control, yet the regional evidence had never been gathered in one place. From several hundred candidate articles across major databases, seventeen studies met their criteria.

The review identifies how technology enables abuse: anonymity for perpetrators, constant access to victims, surveillance used as coercive control, and harmful content that spreads fast and shames publicly. Victims reported psychological harm, damaged reputations, worse school performance, and obstacles to getting help, with depression among the longer-term effects. The authors say the evidence, though thin, already shows a serious problem, and they highlight how much research is still missing.
plos-pone-0354726:
Negin Kassiri and five colleagues published this 2026 study of nearly a thousand middle-aged industrial workers in Tehran, Iran. Factory noise damages hearing, and the team asked whether hearing loss also tracks with heart and blood vessel risk over the coming decade. Workers received hearing tests and standard cardiovascular risk scoring during routine occupational checkups.

Hearing loss patterns were described alongside predicted risk, and the authors kept the combined risk score out of models built from its own ingredients. Kassiri recommends weaving noise control, hearing checks, quitting support, and heart risk review into one surveillance habit.
plos-pone-0354826:
Elisabeth Bandak and colleagues outline in 2026 a ten week test of a kindergarten programme meant to bring more movement and joy in moving into daily life in Denmark. The programme was designed together with staff, leaders, and movement experts. Its parts mix formal setup, activity woven into existing routines, staff training, and inspiring materials.

Because this is a feasibility study, the focus falls on whether kindergartens can adopt the plan and whether the planned measures work. Mixed methods will check both. Findings will shape a refined version and guide a later, larger study of whether the programme truly changes children's activity.
plos-pone-0355226:
Ribal Karim and colleagues study in 2026 how stepping faster or slower than one's natural rhythm affects body and mood during walking in men and women. Healthy adults walked on a treadmill at their preferred pace and at paces a tenth faster and slower. Oxygen use, heart rate, effort ratings, and feelings were recorded across the sessions.

The fresh preferred pace used least oxygen, felt easiest, and gave the most positive mood compared with forced paces. Even a pace set from an earlier session cost more than the pace chosen that day. Women's hearts recovered faster after walking, but no other sex differences appeared in the main measures.
plos-pone-0355726:
Sho Matsushita and colleagues follow more than sixteen hundred independent older adults in Japan. They test whether a strong sense of coherence guards against losing independence or dying. Coherence means feeling that life is understandable and manageable. The trait is central to healthy aging theory, but hard outcome evidence was missing. Participants answered a short coherence scale at the start and were followed for roughly six years through care insurance and death records.

About one in thirteen participants lost independence or died during follow-up. Each step down the coherence scale raised that combined risk by about a quarter, and the death-only link looked similar in size. Matsushita and colleagues argue that supporting older adults' sense of meaning and control could be a real lever for longer independent life.
plos-pone-0355826:
Takao Arai and Hiroyasu Inoue published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on predicting which patents will be licensed. They use survival analysis, the statistics of time until an event, rather than a simple classifier. They compared old and new methods on over six hundred thousand American patents: classical regression, a plain neural network, a neural survival model, and fancier cure-rate versions assuming some patents never license.

All the deep learning approaches performed strongly, far ahead of classical regression at spotting the patents that did license. The standard neural survival model gave the best balance of simplicity and accuracy. The cure-rate extensions added almost nothing in practice, despite one statistically detectable edge, and survival framing itself beat static classification only modestly. The real gains, they conclude, come from deep learning's grip on complex patent features, not from modeling time or hidden subgroups, so users can keep the simpler model.
plos-pone-0356426:
Di Wang and seven colleagues test a simple index built from routine blood fats and sugar, in this 2026 study from a hospital in Harbin, China. They ask whether it tracks how badly the heart's arteries are narrowed. Just over eight hundred sixty patients with coronary heart disease who underwent angiography were sorted into mild, moderate, and severe narrowing using a standard scoring system. The index, which combines triglycerides and glucose, is thought to reflect insulin resistance.

Index values differed significantly between severity groups, and as a continuous measure the index was clearly associated with the extent of narrowing. After adjustment for age, sex, diabetes, and blood pressure, however, the step-by-step rise across index quartiles weakened and lost statistical significance. The authors conclude the index is positively tied to stenosis severity and may flag atherosclerosis burden, a reading best used alongside fuller clinical assessment.
plos-pone-0356726:
Phatchanat Klaihmon and colleagues examined NECTIN2, a cell-surface protein that helps cells stick together, in triple-negative breast cancer, the subtype with the fewest treatment options. Their 2026 laboratory study first checked public tumor data, then silenced the protein's gene in two aggressive breast cancer cell lines and watched how the cells behaved.

Tumors carried more NECTIN2 than healthy tissue, and patients with more of it relapsed sooner. Silencing it in the highest-expressing cell line sharply cut the cells' ability to migrate and invade, an effect partly reversed by restoring a partner protein that reshapes the cell skeleton. In the second cell line, silencing changed little. The contrast marks NECTIN2 as a candidate drug target worth testing, with effects that may depend on the tumor's makeup.
plos-pone-0357026:
Mi Ok Song and So Young Yun built a virtual reality program that trains nursing students to prevent and manage patient falls. They tested it on eighteen final-year students. Their 2026 usability study followed a standard software development cycle. It measured whether students finished the scenarios. It also measured how usable the system felt, how sick the headsets made them, and how present they felt inside the simulation.

Every student completed the program. Usability scored in the acceptable range. Motion sickness stayed mild, and the sense of being there scored high. Falls are a leading hospital harm that students rarely get to practice handling live. So a convincing simulator offers rehearsal without risk. The authors propose extending the tool to new graduate nurses.
plos-pone-0357126:
Javaria Baig led a team of eight authors asking adults how they feel about their own smiles, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. How people see their teeth shapes confidence more than any clinical chart. The team ran a cross-sectional study of how adults judge the look of their own teeth, how satisfied they are with their smile, and the factors linked to both.

Baig's findings tell dentists what patients actually care about, which often differs from the clinical ideal of perfect alignment. A dentist chasing textbook symmetry may miss the one flaw that bothers the patient daily. Cosmetic dentistry is a large market, and evidence on patient priorities can steer it toward need rather than sales. The study also flags social factors that shape smile satisfaction, useful for public dental health planning.
plos-pone-0357726:
Nila Ravindran and colleagues published a 2026 scoping review in PLOS ONE on the toll caring takes in medicine: compassion fatigue, secondhand traumatic stress, and vicarious trauma among doctors. Caring for seriously ill patients can exhaust doctors emotionally, but newer work suggests the damage runs deeper, into beliefs and work identity. The team searched five databases plus an AI-assisted source for a quarter-century of literature, then analyzed qualifying studies through a theory of personhood.

From nearly nineteen thousand initial records, just over a hundred studies survived full screening. Across them, the three conditions overlapped heavily, sharing moral, cognitive, relational, and identity features that reshape what doctors believe about themselves and their work. The review maps what worsens and what softens these strains, and what help exists. Hospitals, they argue, should treat the cost of caring as an identity problem, not merely tiredness, when designing support.
plos-pone-0357826:
Azhar Al-Busaidi and three colleagues published a materials study in PLOS ONE in 2026. They worked on a way to keep sea life from fouling surfaces such as ship hulls and sensors. Their coating used tiny rods of zinc oxide laid over polymers molded with fine surface patterns.

Al-Busaidi's team tested how well the coated surfaces resisted fouling growth. The mix of nano-scale texture and the oxide's own effects kept surfaces cleaner than plain material. Coatings like this could cut the fuel ships waste dragging growth through the water, and reduce the harsh chemicals now used to scrub hulls. Marine sensors that stay clean also keep sending good data for longer.
plos-pone-0358126: van Aert and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on whether research findings hold up when repeated. They took a statistical view of what counts as a successful repeat study. Their extended analysis drew on the SCORE data set, a large record of replication attempts. Clearer yardsticks for success help science tell solid findings from lucky ones.
plos-pone-0358226:
Lucia Martina Scalise leads a team of eight testing whether CT scans can stand in for digging into cremation urns, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Ten urns from the Bronze Age cemetery of Vicofertile near Parma, Italy, were scanned whole, then carefully excavated in the laboratory so the two pictures could be compared bone by bone. Cremated remains are fragile, and scanning promises answers without destruction, but image quality is often poor and materials blur together.

Where the scan data could be read, they held up well. Age classes of the dead, the burial's disturbance history, and heat damage such as fractures matched what physical analysis later found. The authors also trialed a simple segmentation routine for mapping where remains sit inside a vessel. Their verdict is measured: virtual examination is a genuine exploratory tool for urns that cannot be opened, provided its blind spots are respected.
plos-pone-0358326:
Anna Ohlson leads a team of eight grading sewage as a COVID-19 early warning system in Sweden, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Nineteen treatment plants, covering about forty-three percent of the population, reported virus levels in wastewater from mid 2023 through 2024. The team lined those curves up against officially reported cases, plant by plant, for Stockholm, and nationally, asking whether the sewage signal arrived earlier or tracked faithfully.

The tracking was faithful. Wastewater levels correlated strongly with reported cases, most tightly in Stockholm and the national aggregate. Tests of prediction showed solid accuracy, especially for ruling out rises. But the hoped for head start never appeared. Under weekly sampling and reporting, the sewage signal moved at the same time as case counts, not before them. The authors conclude wastewater earns its place as an independent mirror of circulation, valuable when clinic testing fades, rather than as a crystal ball.
plos-pone-0358426:
María Lloret Avellá and three colleagues count what it costs Spain's health system just to give leukemia drugs, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Older patients with acute myeloid leukemia who cannot face intensive chemotherapy receive a class of drugs by vein or under the skin, meaning repeated hospital trips. An oral version exists and works equivalently. The team priced everything except the drugs themselves, from preparation to transport, catheters, and infections, using a survey of thirty professionals at sixteen hospitals.

The non drug cost per patient came to roughly ten thousand euros for the intravenous route and over twelve thousand for the under skin route. The oral route cost barely thirteen hundred, a saving of nearly ninety percent. Fewer visits drive nearly all of the gap. The authors frame the switch as an organizational relief for crowded hospitals as much as a budget saving.
plos-pone-0359326:
Stefanie Wilhelm and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a prospective multicenter study, planned in advance and run at several hospitals. The topic is rebuilding the floor of the eye socket after injury, using a material called ultrahigh-molecular-weight polyethylene.

The outcomes tracked are patient-related, meaning results that patients themselves report, such as comfort, appearance, and daily function. Surgeons choosing implant materials need evidence about how people feel and function after surgery, not only how scans look. Eye and facial surgeons weighing this implant material are the main readers of the study.
plos-pone-0359426: Lu and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study proposing a new angle on motion sickness. They suggest a heart hormone, atrial natriuretic peptide, may ease the sickness. The proposed route runs through aldosterone, another hormone, which can raise fluid volume in the inner ear. Motion sickness blights travel and training for many people, so a hormone-based route could open new treatments.
plos-pone-0359626:
Faisal Adi Irawan, Ferry Efendi, and Praba Diyan Rachmawati published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Its title gives a young person's own words of protest at being labeled a glue kid. The study shares what street-connected adolescents in Indonesia's Merauke Regency say about their use of glue.

Glue sniffing is a cheap high among homeless and street-working youth, and the label glue kid adds stigma to harm. Hearing users' own experiences shows why the habit starts and what help would be accepted. Social workers and health outreach teams in Indonesia are the readers who meet these adolescents daily.
pmc-10635526:
Tang, Chen, Huang, and co-authors introduce SRplot, a free online platform for making charts and graphs from research data. Clear pictures help readers grasp complex results in papers. Many chart tools, though, demand coding skill, charge fees, or run on only one kind of computer.

SRplot answers those limits with a free site that is meant to be easy for anyone to use. Users can build publication-ready figures without writing code. For students and labs with small budgets, that lowers a real barrier between raw data and a chart that others can read at a glance.
pmc-13231426:
Gregory Cantrall, Gaurav Chauhan, and Steven Abel present a 2026 computer simulation study of long chain molecules, called polymers, inside crowded spaces like the inside of a cell. Real chains such as DNA are not evenly stiff along their length, so the team varied stiffness from section to section.
