Using a physics simulation method, they raised the pressure from surrounding crowders and watched the chains fold up. Large soft sections mostly drove the folding, while stiff sections helped chains stick to a nearby surface. The pattern of stiff and soft parts could even set the point where sticking begins. The results may guide the design of soft nano-scale materials.
pmc-13240226:
Liseth's team at Mayo Clinic combined CAR T cells with a cancer-killing virus to strengthen treatment of solid tumors. CAR T therapy often falters in solid tumors through fatigue and fading staying power. The team used vesicular stomatitis virus to wake the T cells' own native receptor. That waking happens next to the built-in synthetic receptor.

The pairing produced a subset of virus-primed CAR T cells with stronger killing behavior. Single-cell reads showed these cells grew in clones and switched on effector genes. Their active states and protein profiles differed from unprimed CAR T cells. Helper CD4 T cells proved pivotal in making the primed group, hinting at a new lever for tuning cell therapy.
pmc-13241426:
Moran's team at James Cook built a barramundi muscle cell line and watched its genes switch over. Barramundi is a prized farmed fish of the tropics with little cell data. Expression of key muscle regulators was tracked for fourteen days. Sampling covered the explant stage, early passages, and myoblast change.

Key genes switched on in patterns matching their known jobs in muscle growth. The cells duly changed form, proof of a true muscle line. Waves followed the culture's own shifts, including each passage. Moran offers the line as a base for studying fish muscle growth.
pmc-13241526:
Pei and co-workers in Japan alloyed a symmetric gold cluster with silver to make a chiral metal cluster atom by atom. Subnanometer clusters change their behavior sharply with each atom swapped. Starting from a carbon-centered cluster of six gold atoms, they added silver trifluoroacetate. The product holds four gold and six silver ions around the central carbon.

Calculations mapped the bonding between carbon, gold, and silver in the new cage-like structure. Using handed ligands, the team produced either mirror form of the cluster cleanly. Both forms glow red to near-infrared and show distinct chiroptical responses. The route etches gold out while silver moves in, opening a path to tailor-made light-emitting clusters.
pmc-13242426:
Maggie Yu and co-authors asked whether a sense of self-mastery shields people with multiple sclerosis from the effects of stressful life events. Their paper appeared in Quality of Life Research in 2026. They analyzed survey answers from 948 people with the disease across several countries. Stressful events were counted and weighted, mastery was split into low, middle, and high levels, and both were compared with quality of life and fatigue.

Among people with low or moderate mastery, heavier stress loads came with clearly lower mental quality of life. Stress also raised the odds of severe fatigue several-fold, mainly in the low-mastery group. Among high-mastery respondents, those links largely vanished. The snapshot design cannot prove cause and effect, and the authors call for follow-up over time. Still, they suggest that building mastery could soften the harm stress does to people living with multiple sclerosis.
pmc-13243326:
Natália Albino Pires and colleagues piloted a tablet app that uses heritage to stir autobiographical memory in older adults. Their study appeared in the Journal of Cross-Cultural Gerontology in 2026. Reminiscence therapy is known to work with music and crafts, but traditional dance and oral storytelling had barely been tried as triggers. The team built a selection protocol and a prototype, LONG-REMI, then field-tested them in six centers in Spain and Portugal.

Fifty-six adults aged sixty-five and over took part, some with mild or moderate cognitive decline and some without. Dance clips and traditional tales were matched to each person's background by the app's support tools. Both heritage forms evoked memories and sparked communication in both groups. The authors call the approach reproducible and ready for larger trials. Heritage, they argue, is not decoration: it is identity material that therapy can put to work.
pmc-13244626:
Jean Marie Annoni and colleagues ran a worldwide project in which people with aphasia set the research agenda for their condition. Their report appeared in Research Involvement and Engagement in 2026. Aphasia's burdens reach far past language into emotional and social life, yet researchers choose the questions. This initiative, started by a person with aphasia and three laypeople, involved more than one hundred patients from fourteen countries, working in many languages.

A three-phase process generated topics, refined them in national co-design sessions, and voted them into priorities, with eleven countries joining the vote. Inclusive methods, under a framework built for lay involvement, let people with severe language difficulty lead rather than attend. The agenda confirmed earlier findings and sharpened one demand above all: public awareness must rise. The authors present the project as proof that priority setting can be co-created across languages when access is designed in.
pmc-13245426:
Li and co-authors charted the yearly hormone cycle of an endangered turtle in this 2026 PeerJ study. The Beale's eyed turtle, found only in southeastern China, is critically endangered, yet its reproductive physiology was almost undocumented, a gap that hampers captive breeding. The team measured three sex hormones in blood from captive turtles across a full year using standard immunoassays.

Males showed two testosterone peaks, in spring and late summer, matching mating seasons and a pattern of sperm production after mating. Females peaked in estradiol in April, tied to egg-yolk formation for a single yearly clutch, with progesterone cresting around ovulation in June. The authors offer the profiles as a reference calendar for managing breeding of this rare species in captivity, while noting their small sample.
pmc-13246126:
Chen and co-authors studied a risky intensive-care maneuver after one of the most dangerous heart operations, in this 2026 Critical Care Explorations paper. Patients who develop severe lung failure after repair of an acute type A aortic dissection are often too unstable to turn face-down, the prone position that helps failing lungs. The team reviewed seventy-eight such patients at one heart center.

Fifty-eight patients were proned and twenty stayed on their backs. Oxygen levels in the proned group rose quickly, within hours, and patients turned within forty-eight hours of lung failure spent less time on the ventilator. No safety disaster emerged. The authors back early, protocol-guided proning for selected patients, with prospective trials to confirm.
pmc-13246926:
Delgado Casanova and colleagues followed a common breast-biopsy finding to see whether it really needs surgery, in this 2026 Breast Cancer Research and Treatment study. A radial sclerosing lesion is a benign, star-shaped scar-like area that mimics cancer on imaging; historically, surgeons removed such lesions to be safe. Their hospital reviewed four hundred nineteen lesions in three hundred ninety patients diagnosed by needle biopsy from 2020 to 2025.

Lesions that went on to repeat biopsy or surgical removal, sixty-three in all, turned up no cancer at all. Across the whole group, the estimated chance of cancer appearing at the lesion site within three years was zero. The authors support watching these lesions with imaging when biopsy sampling and imaging agree, sparing many women an operation.
pmc-13249026:
Monteiro and colleagues checked eye-measuring machines in patients with implanted helper lenses, in this 2026 research letter from Porto, Portugal. Two modern biometers map the eye's inner surfaces automatically before cataract surgery. An extra lens inside the eye, placed earlier to correct vision, can confuse that mapping, so the team reviewed one hundred such eyes.

Both devices misdrew the eye's surfaces in roughly a quarter of eyes, mistaking the implanted lens for the natural one. Errors shrank the measured chamber depth and inflated lens thickness, and one lens style caused most mistakes. One machine sometimes refused to guess, forcing manual checks. The authors warn surgeons to inspect every scan in these eyes.
pmc-13249926:
Goodwin and colleagues show that invisible structure steers how people hunt through a cluttered display, in a 2026 perception study. Across six online experiments, participants foraged for many copies of two target types among distractors, while the screen was visibly divided into segments holding equal numbers of objects. The divisions carried no hint about where targets hid, since targets were spread evenly.

Even so, searchers kept working inside one segment rather than hopping to the next, a systematic style the layout alone induced. That style cost speed but improved memory for where things had been. Stronger visual structure strengthened the effect. The authors warn that display design silently choreographs search behavior, in the lab and in everyday scenes.
pmc-13250026:
Anne McMunn and Jeroen Spijker introduce a 2026 journal collection on unpaid care in later life across Europe. People live longer now, but extra years are not always healthy years, so more older people need help from family and friends.

The editors argue for a life course view: what shapes who ends up giving care, and how heavily, is built across a whole working and family life. Women still give more care, and for longer, though the gap narrows among older couples. Carers also tend to be worse off money-wise. The collection's papers trace how jobs, partnerships, and money earlier in life lead into caring roles.
pmc-13250326:
Salam Melhem, Hadeel Bouzia, and Nour Moosa report a misleading belly pain case in this 2026 report. An eight-year-old boy had one day of worsening right-sided pain, and an ultrasound first suggested early appendicitis, a very common cause of such pain in children.

Keyhole surgery told a different story: a twisted, bleeding lump of the fatty apron inside the belly, near the upper colon, while the appendix was only mildly red. Surgeons removed the lump and the appendix, and lab tests confirmed the fatty tissue had twisted on itself with no appendicitis present. The boy recovered well. The authors back keyhole checks when scans disagree with symptoms.
pmc-13250626:
Yuhei Suzuki and co-authors describe a cancer returning after 24 quiet years in this 2026 case report. A 55-year-old woman had fluid around her right lung and swollen glands under her breastbone, found after a stem cell transplant for a blood disease.

At age 31 she had surgery and radiation for a windpipe cancer called adenoid cystic carcinoma, a slow type known for late returns. A needle sample taken through the airway proved the swollen gland was the same cancer back again, not her blood disease. Because this cancer grows slowly, speed of growth cannot rule it out, and the authors urge tissue checks whenever it is suspected.
pmc-13251226:
Angelika Bolte and co-authors crack a hidden genetic case in this 2026 study. Their patient, a Syrian child with severe developmental regression, had clear chemical signs of Sandhoff disease, a storage disorder, but standard gene tests found no cause.

Deep gene reading using long-read methods found the answer buried inside a gene called HEXB: a change deep in a non-coding stretch that switches on a false segment, breaking the gene's message. Both copies carried it, a pattern the team calls a candidate founder variant in the region. The case shows why hidden variants may be missed in Middle Eastern patients and hints at future splice-fixing therapies.
pmc-13252726:
Quan Zhou and colleagues link arm function, exercise, and thinking in older Chinese adults in this 2026 study. The group studied lives apart from their children, a fast-growing group as China ages, and their mental sharpness is a growing concern.

Data came from a 2018 national longevity survey covering 5,060 such adults, with an average age near 79. About 15 percent had cognitive impairment. Restricted upper limb function more than doubled the odds of impairment, while regular exercise lowered them. Exercise explained only a small slice of the arm-brain link, about six percent. The authors treat exercise as a minor pathway, not the main story.
pmc-13253826:
Marwa Abdeltawab Ahmed and colleagues test a nano form of a farm insecticide in a 2026 mouse study. Chlorpyrifos is known to harm male fertility, and its nano-emulsion form may enter the body more easily. Forty male albino mice got one of three daily doses, or none, by mouth for 35 days.

At the top dose, fertility fell to zero and sperm survival dropped from 74% to 43.1%. Testosterone fell from 4.2 to 1.8 nanograms per milliliter, while stress and DNA damage markers rose. Tissue checks showed shrunken tubes and harmed testis structure, which the authors link to oxidative stress, meaning cell damage from reactive oxygen.
pmc-13254226:
Lizhi Wu and co-authors review how microplastics combine with other pollutants in a 2026 paper. Microplastics are tiny plastic bits now found worldwide. On their own they can harm cells, immunity, and the brain, hormone, and reproductive systems. They can also carry other pollutants on their surfaces, changing those pollutants' effects.

The review covers combined effects with heavy metals, organic pollutants, plastic additives, antibiotics, and viruses, plus the mechanisms behind them. The authors urge future work on realistic exposure scenes, long-term effects, and combined exposure risks, to guide public awareness and policy on plastic pollution.
pmc-13254426:
Shuhong Mei and a large team model a frustrating stroke outcome in a 2026 multicenter study. Futile recanalization means a vessel reopens after clot removal, yet the patient still has major disability at 90 days. The study covered 350 stroke patients, with a model built in 260 and checked in 90 from another center.

In all, 152 patients, or 43.43 percent, had futile recanalization. Predictors were higher stroke severity, lower early CT score, high blood sugar at admission, poor backup blood flow, and longer time to reopening. Their scoring chart reached accuracy values of 0.84 to 0.86 in testing, with fair calibration.
pmc-13254726:
Peng and colleagues combined bulk, single-cell, and spatial data to position the chemokine-like factor CKLF as a driver of liver cancer growth. CKLF was more abundant in hepatocellular carcinoma tissue than in normal liver, and high levels tracked with later stage, distinct molecular subtypes, and shorter survival. The factor appeared in tumor cells and in infiltrating immune cells alike.

Laboratory tests supported a causal role: silencing CKLF slowed proliferation, movement, and colony growth in liver cancer cell models. Forcing the Ras pathway on partly reversed those effects, placing CKLF upstream of AKT and ERK signaling. The authors propose CKLF as both a prognostic marker and a drug target.
pmc-13256226: A short 2026 retraction notice in Open Forum Infectious Diseases withdraws an IDWeek conference abstract by Monirujjaman Biswas on acute viral hepatitis in hospitalized children in North India. The work covered clinical, blood-test, ultrasound, and cause-related findings. The journal says the abstract overlapped significantly with a previously published study, without giving credit to it. It also says the authorship cannot be verified. The notice gives no patient findings, so the retracted work is described here only by its subject and the reasons for withdrawal.
pmc-13257626:
Chen Chen and colleagues argue that history, not just chemistry, shapes magnesium hydrides used to store hydrogen. These materials offer high capacity from a cheap, abundant metal. Yet samples with the same label often behave very differently. Their 2026 Perspective blames hidden states written in by making and using the material.

Defects, leftover strain, unstable structures, and changed catalysts all steer how hydrogen enters and moves. That makes each sample's reaction path depend on its past, which the authors say explains the field's reproducibility troubles. They propose recording processing history as standard metadata. Designing around reaction pathways, they argue, beats hunting for better compositions alone.
pmc-13259126:
Yodthong Baimark and co-authors blend a shrimp-shell derivative into corn-based plastic to help it rot faster. Poly(L-lactic acid) is biodegradable in name but lingers far too long in soil and packaging waste streams. Their 2026 fix stirs in thermoplastic chitosan, plasticized with lactic acid itself.

A small chitosan dose made films stretch further before breaking and toughened them noticeably. Higher doses reversed those gains, so the sweet spot sat low. Wetter surfaces and far greater soil-burial weight loss followed as chitosan content rose. After a year underground, the richest blend lost dozens of times more mass than plain film, suiting single-use packaging.
pmc-13260226:
Lisa Linnenbrink-Garcia and co-authors wrote a 2026 review article making the case for many-sided motivation interventions built into everyday classrooms. Most earlier programs targeted one slice of motivation, such as showing students why a subject is useful, without changing the classroom context. The authors survey approaches to supporting student motivation, then argue for programs that combine several theories at once. They also introduce complex dynamic systems thinking as a guide for understanding motivation in schools.

Two programs that worked are described in detail. One targeted reading motivation and engagement in primary and middle school classrooms. The other targeted science motivation and engagement at middle school level. Both were embedded in normal teaching rather than delivered as add-ons. The authors close by weighing the practical challenges of such broad programs against their promise for lasting student engagement.
pmc-13261926:
Sarper İçen and Şefika Nurhüda Karaca Cengiz present a 2026 exploratory study of impulsivity and internet gaming disorder symptoms in teenage boys with ADHD. Adolescents with ADHD face elevated risk of problem gaming. It was unclear whether different sides of impulsivity, such as acting without planning, relate to different gaming symptoms.

The study recruited 45 male adolescents aged 12 to 17 from two psychiatry clinics in Türkiye. Most gamed over four hours daily, 73.3% on weekdays and 75.6% on weekends. Gaming symptom scores rose with non-planning impulsivity (ρ = 0.56), attentional impulsivity (ρ = 0.52), and motor impulsivity (ρ = 0.45). When all three were modeled together, only non-planning impulsivity stayed independently associated with symptom severity. Age showed no significant correlation with impulsivity or gaming severity. The authors frame these as exploratory links needing confirmation in larger samples.
pmc-13262826:
Ifeoma Jovita Nduka and co-authors model whether breast X-ray screening is worth its cost in Nigeria in a 2026 journal article. Mammography is the standard screening test, but Nigeria has no national screening program and use is low. The team simulated yearly and two-yearly screening for women from age 40 over a lifetime, from the health provider's viewpoint.

Yearly screening cost 238.60 US dollars per woman in their model and averted about 1.060 disability-adjusted life years, a measure of healthy years lost. Its cost per healthy year gained fell well below the study's pay threshold. The authors call yearly screening the best value among the options modeled, while warning the result depends on model assumptions and is not a final policy directive.
pmc-13263326:
Aiping Wu and co-authors publish a 2026 correction notice for their Scientific Reports article on liraglutide, a diabetes drug, and artery disease linked to high cholesterol. The original paper reported that the drug reduces adhesion between vessel-lining cells and white blood cells.

The notice fixes labeling mistakes made while assembling figures. Panels in Figure 6 carried the wrong condition labels and now show the correct ones for treated and untreated cells. Figure 8 also contained incorrect data, which has been replaced with data matching the main text. Readers can view the original, incorrect figures in the notice for the record. The article itself has been corrected.
pmc-13263626:
Olivia Klapec and colleagues lay out a randomized trial to settle whether fruit-flavored e-cigarettes help smokers quit better than the flavors regulators allow. Pod fruit flavors were restricted despite hints they aid switching. Their 2026 protocol recruits daily smokers with repeated failed quit attempts who want to switch.

Participants draw fruit, menthol, or tobacco pods for six weeks, plus a structured switching plan. Lab sessions first measure how rewarding each flavor feels against real cigarettes. Daily cigarette counts through the switch and at twenty-six weeks form the main outcome, verified by breath carbon monoxide. The design also tests whether reward explains any flavor advantage.
pmc-13263726:
Xiang-ting Shi and colleagues introduce a new primrose from Guizhou, Primula xingyiensis, and fit it into its section. Section Carolinella primroses are hairy, powder-free plants with bell-shaped calyces. Their 2026 description rests on the newcomer's gracile build and unusual flowers.

Slender stems, small leaves furred on both sides, and long-styled single-form flowers set it apart. Its corolla stretches seven to eight times the calyx length, a striking proportion. The authors supply distribution details, a conservation assessment, and a key to every known species in the section. The key turns the paper into a field tool, not just an announcement.
pmc-13264426:
João Castro Mendes and co-authors present a 2026 case report on a hip replacement that lasted well for 16 years despite a shaky start. The patient had a hip socket shaped wrong from birth and bad joint wear. Surgeons used a metal support ring, but part of it was left with poor bone cover.

The patient was a 59-year-old man treated in 2010. Surgeons packed ground bone from his own thigh bone head around the bare part of the ring. At 16 years he had no pain and full use of the hip. Scans showed the graft had joined the bone, with no loosening. The authors say such grafts can make up for weak first cover.
pmc-13264526:
Jennifer C Wong wrote a 2026 commentary on a mouse study of Dravet syndrome, a severe form of epilepsy that starts in early life. The condition also brings slow development, poor body temperature control, and bad sleep. Wong sums up work by Fadila and colleagues on how sleep and temperature link in this illness.

In the mouse model, core body temperature was lower than normal. Healthy mice cooled as they fell asleep, but the Dravet mice did not. Warmth helped healthy mice sleep, yet not the sick ones. Restoring the faulty gene in the brain, or stimulating a brain area that controls heat, brought back the warmth effect. Wong highlights the hypothalamus as a key site.
pmc-13264626:
Manar T Ali and colleagues published a 2026 study of Sphagneticola trilobata, an ornamental plant used in folk medicine. They compared the chemistry of its flowerheads and leaves for the first time in full. Oswald Spengler's The Decline of the West, Volume 1, appears in Charles Francis Atkinson's translation of 1926. Subtitled Form and Actuality, the volume states Spengler's bold scheme. Cultures, he argues, are organisms that pass through birth, growth, maturity, and decay. Each has its own soul and its own mathematics, art, and science.

The West, in his reading, has entered its late, hard phase of civilization. Spengler compares cultures side by side in vast tables of parallel ages. Critics call the method prophetic rather than scientific. The book was the most debated philosophy of history of its century. Atkinson's version carried the debate into English.
summers-history-witchcraft-1926:
Montague Summers was a Catholic priest and a firm foe of witchcraft. His History of Witchcraft and Demonology came out in 1926. Summers held, as few of his day did, that the witch cult was real. His book tells the tale with vast stores of fact.

Pacts with the Devil, sabbats, and spells fill the early parts. The great trials of Europe and the New World take up the rest. Summers cites trial rolls, old tracts, and church law in bulk. The book is a mine of tales, read best with a keen eye on its slant.
swift-gullivers-travels-1726:
Jonathan Swift published Gulliver's Travels in 1726, in the first edition text used here. The full title sends Gulliver into several remote nations of the world. Readers took it first as a true travel tale, then as fierce satire.

Gulliver visits Lilliput, where men are six inches tall and wars turn on eggs. In Brobdingnag he is tiny, and a huge king scorns England's pride and guns. Later trips reach a flying island and the wise horse Houyhnhnms and brutish Yahoos. Man looks worse at each stop, and pride takes the hardest knocks of all. Swift's prose stays cool while the charges grow more and more savage.
tawney-religion-capitalism-1926:
R. H. Tawney published Religion and the Rise of Capitalism in 1926, a classic of economic history. Tawney, an English historian and socialist, studies how Christian teaching met the new market world. Medieval bans on usury gave way as commerce grew. Puritan teaching, he argues, could both discipline greed and bless success.

The book is often called the English answer to Weber's Protestant ethic. Tawney writes with moral force and fine irony. He mourns a lost age when faith set limits on acquisition. His closing plea joins economics to ethics. The work remains a humane, learned critique of acquisitive society. It shaped British social thought for decades.
tilden-toxemia-explained-1926:
John Henry Tilden blamed nearly all illness on one cause, and Toxemia Explained of 1926 states his case in full. Tilden, a Denver doctor who had turned against drug prescribing, taught that waste the body fails to clear poisons the blood. That state, toxemia, then shows itself as many different diseases.

Rest, fasting, and right living form his cure, since drugs only mask the warning signs. Tilden walks readers through digestion, habits, and the slow build-up of enervation, his word for drained nerve energy. The book became a classic of natural hygiene, and its plain, stern advice still finds readers.
tob-0144-61626:
Volume four completes the Gutenberg set of The Secret Doctrine with further theosophical pieces. Blavatsky's scheme of cosmic cycles, root races, and hidden masters fills out its last corners here. Readers who have come this far meet the system at its most detailed and most demanding.

The extra writings answer objections, expand on symbols, and tie loose threads from the earlier volumes. Little in them makes sense alone; together they crown the largest occult system of the nineteenth century. Whether one accepts a word of it or not, the work's scale and influence are hard to deny. The full set rewards slow, patient reading.
tob-10626:
Unknown authors in the early centuries told the story of Adam and Eve after Eden in the Life of Adam and Eve. Versions survive in Latin, Greek, and other tongues. The work belongs to the pseudepigrapha, Jewish and Christian writings outside the Bible's canon.

After their expulsion, Adam and Eve repent in hunger and grief, with Adam standing forty days in the Jordan River. Satan tells his own fall, Eve laments her fault, and the book ends with Adam's death and burial. Tender and sad, it fills gaps Genesis leaves open and shaped later tales of the first parents.
tob-10826:
Henry Ridgely Evans spent his hours with ghosts professionally: he was a stage magician and a debunker of fraudulent mediums. Hours with the Ghosts visits haunted houses, spirit photographs, and slate-writing mediums, then looks for the tricks behind them. Entertainment and exposure proceed together, with one skeptical eyebrow raised.

Evans retells famous hauntings and séances in detail before explaining wires, confederates, and sleight of hand. He loves a good ghost story too much to be dull, and knows stagecraft too well to be fooled. Readers who like their spooks investigated, by a man who could perform the tricks himself, will enjoy his company.
tob-13326:
Edwin Arnold published The Light of Asia in 1879, an epic poem telling the Buddha's life in Miltonic blank verse. The sheltered prince Siddhartha, raised behind palace walls, encounters age, sickness, death, and a wandering ascetic: the four sights that drive his search. Enlightenment under the bodhi tree forms the climax.

Arnold's poem sold hundreds of thousands of copies and introduced the Victorian world to Buddhism more effectively than any scholarly treatise of its day. He presents the Buddha with Christian-era reverence, a framing modern readers will notice. As a cultural event, The Light of Asia genuinely lit a path for Western interest in Asia's religions.
tob-4026:
Benedictus de Spinoza wrote his Ethics in geometric form: definitions, axioms, propositions, and proofs, as if philosophy were Euclid. Its claim is the most radical of the seventeenth century. God and Nature are one substance, everything follows from that substance's nature by necessity, and human freedom lies in understanding necessity rather than escaping it.

Spinoza had been excommunicated from Amsterdam's Jewish community and published nothing under his name during his life; the Ethics appeared after his death. Emotions, bondage, and the intellectual love of God occupy its later parts. Patient readers find a serene, demanding system that modern philosophy keeps rediscovering.
tob-4126:
Reynold A. Nicholson's first book, in 1898, selected poems from the Divan of Shams-i Tabriz. The poems are Rumi's, named for Shams, the wandering friend whose love and loss remade Rumi into a poet. Nicholson, then a young scholar, chose lyrics of love-madness as the road to God.

English readers met Rumi the lyric poet here, decades before Nicholson's great Mathnawi translation. The versions are free but fervent, drunk on their subject in the right way. Checked from the 1919 printing, the selection still glows. It shows both poets at once: Rumi in Persian fire, Nicholson in English devotion.
tob-4226:
A. E. Waite played detective in The Book of Black Magic and of Pacts, published in 1898. He surveys the grimoires one by one: the Key of Solomon, the Grimorium Verum, the Grand Grimoire, and their kin. For each he asks what the rituals actually say, apart from the legends around them.

Waite prints rites of evocation and pact in detail, then judges them with a scholar-magician's dry scorn. His critical sorting shaped how the next century read the whole grimoire shelf. Verified from the 1919 edition, the book remains a sharp, skeptical guide through magic's darkest library.
toland-celtic-religion-druids-1726:
John Toland was an Irish free thinker. He wrote this study of Celtic faith and learning late in life, and it came out in 1726, after his death. The text here is from the 1815 printing. Toland was known for bold views on faith and church power.

He treated the druids as men of their time, not as priests of dark rites. With a cool eye he sifted old Greek and Roman reports from Welsh and Irish lore. His book was the first clear, sharp account of the druids in the age of reason.
tombazi-photographic-expedition-kangchen:
Nicholas Tombazi took a camera to the glaciers of Kangchenjunga and came back with a tale for the ages. His Account of a Photographic Expedition to the Southern Glaciers appeared in 1926. In it he tells what he saw on the Sikkim side in 1925.

At 15,500 feet he watched a wild man, as he took it, moving on the slope below him. He tells of the form, the gait, and the measured footprints left in the snow. His is the most detailed early yeti report from a trained observer. The book anchors the whole shelf of yeti lore.
twelfth-night-pg1526: Shipwrecked Viola serves her master Orsino disguised as a boy while secretly loving him, in this edition of Shakespeare's most perfect comedy. The countess Olivia falls for the disguise, Sir Toby torments the prig Malvolio, and Feste's songs stitch it all together. Love's sweet confusions, resolved in joy.
un-ga-res-26: Two working groups owe their start to Resolution 26, passed by the UN General Assembly in its first session in 1946. One group was to weigh the transfer of some tasks, work, and assets of the dying League of Nations to the new UN. The other was to study where the UN should build its lasting home. Every member state could sit on both groups.
un-ga-res-a-69-26:
Africa's ban on nuclear arms is backed in Resolution A/69/26, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Treaty of Pelindaba, signed in Cairo on 11 April 1996, made the whole African continent a zone free of nuclear weapons. The Security Council had hailed the signing the next day as a real gain for world peace and safety.

The text recalls Assembly votes of 1996 and 2001 on the treaty, and the stands of the African Union. Zones free of nuclear arms, it argues, raise safety most where strains run high, and it names the Middle East as such a place. The vote urges the treaty's full force and reach across Africa.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 26, from the first session in 1946, is a brief founding order. The Assembly set up two temporary committees open to every member state. One was a League of Nations Committee, to weigh the transfer of certain League duties, work, and assets. The other was a Permanent Headquarters Committee, to weigh the site of the United Nations' lasting home.

Resolution 69/26 of the General Assembly welcomes the African Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zone Treaty, the Treaty of Pelindaba, signed in Cairo in 1996 and in force since 15 July 2009. The Assembly calls on African states that have not yet signed or ratified to do so quickly. It thanks the nuclear-weapon states that have signed the treaty's protocols and urges them to ratify. It asks states parties to complete safeguards agreements with the International Atomic Energy Agency. Three conferences of states parties had met in Addis Ababa by 2014.
un-sc-res-1026:
Bosnia's peace deal had just been initialed when the Council met in November 1995. On 30 November 1995 it extended UNPROFOR until 31 January 1996. The force would hold the line pending the peace agreement's use. The Dayton deal had been initialed on 21 November. Bosnia, Croatia, and Yugoslavia were among its signers. The Council welcomed the Secretary-General's report on the next steps.

The Secretary-General had to keep the Council informed on the peace process. His reports would carry facts and advice on carrying out the deal. The short extension bridged an awkward gap. A NATO-led force was about to take over the military task. UNPROFOR's troubled three years were nearly over.
un-sc-res-126:
Kashmir's stalled settlement was reviewed by the Security Council on 2 December 1957. Gunnar Jarring, Sweden's representative, had traveled to the region under resolution 123 (1957) and reported on what blocked progress. Both India and Pakistan still accepted the plan for a free and impartial plebiscite on the future of Jammu and Kashmir. The Council thanked Jarring and voiced concern at the lack of movement.

The Council asked both governments to make no statements and take no steps that could worsen the situation. Each was to urge calm on its own people so that talks could go forward. The United Nations Representative for India and Pakistan was asked to propose further action to the parties. He was authorized to visit the subcontinent for that purpose. He had to report on his efforts as soon as possible. Demilitarization remained a key step toward any settlement.
un-sc-res-1526:
Terrorism financing is the battleground of Resolution 1526, adopted in January 2004. It tightened the sanctions system aimed at Al-Qaida and the Taliban, which listed people and groups whose money had to be frozen. A new team of experts was created to watch how states complied.

The text sharpens the list's rules, presses states to act against listed names at home, and gives the monitoring team a wider reach. Sanctions texts like this one run quietly in the background of counterterrorism for years. This one shows the machinery being rebuilt after early lists proved patchy and uneven.
un-sc-res-1626:
UNMIL was extended with an election surge on 19 September 2005. Liberia's presidential and legislative elections were set for October. State authority was spreading, with a new police service and fresh judges. The transitional government had just signed the GEMAP program on honest economic management. UNAMSIL in Sierra Leone was set to close on 31 December 2005.

The Council extended UNMIL's mandate for six months. Liberian parties were called to show full commitment to a democratic process free of violence. With troop contributors' consent, UNMIL could help guard the Special Court for Sierra Leone's premises once UNAMSIL left. A temporary rise in the mission's personnel ceiling was authorized to cover the elections. Extra staff would secure the vote and the weeks around it. The world was called to answer Liberia's continuing needs generously. GEMAP's swift start was welcomed as the path to lifting the sanctions of resolution 1521 (2003).
un-sc-res-1726:
Côte d'Ivoire's mission received a short extension at the end of 2006. On 15 December 2006 the Security Council kept UNOCI and its French support force until 10 January 2007. The Secretary-General had reported on the country that month. The Council restated its support for the impartial forces on the ground. It voiced serious concern at the stalled peace process. Elections had been delayed again that autumn.

The brief term covered the year-end while a new plan was weighed. An African Union backed roadmap had set fresh deadlines weeks earlier. The mission's troops held the zone between government and rebel areas. The Council stayed actively seized of the matter. A longer renewal with a revised mandate followed in January.
un-sc-res-1826:
Côte d'Ivoire returns in United Nations Security Council Resolution 1826, adopted on 29 July 2008. The Ouagadougou peace deal was slowly taking hold. A first round of presidential elections was set for 30 November 2008. Rights abuses, including sexual violence, still scarred daily life.

The text renews the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire and its French support force until 31 January 2009. The mission must give the election commission transport and other practical help. Ivorian forces and former rebels are urged to draw up one shared security plan for the vote. The Council also presses for faster voter listing, disarmament, and the return of state services.
un-sc-res-1926: Judge Thomas Buergenthal resigned from the International Court of Justice in 2010. His departure would take effect on 6 September that year. On 2 June 2010 the Security Council fixed the date to fill the vacancy. The election would be held on 9 September 2010. It would take place at a Council meeting and at a General Assembly meeting. The Assembly was then in its sixty-fourth session. The short text performs only that scheduling act.
un-sc-res-2026: Resolution 2026 stands in the Security Council's numbered output, preserved here as an official-record transcription from English Wikisource. The Council's decisions are the primary documents of its work, outliving the debates around them. This decision is kept whole: the facts as the members stated them and the steps they voted to take in response.
un-sc-res-226:
The Congo accused Portugal of hosting its enemies in 1966. Congolese leaders said Angola, under Portuguese rule, served as a mercenary base. Portugal replied that no mercenaries or camps existed there. On 14 October 1966 the Council took note of both statements. It then urged Portugal to match its own denial with action. Foreign mercenaries must not use Angola to meddle in the Congo's affairs.

All states had to keep out of the Congo's domestic business. The Secretary-General was told to watch how the resolution was used. The vote was unanimous. The text reflects the Congo's early years of coups and foreign plots. Mercenary bands based across its borders were a constant threat to the young state.
un-sc-res-26: How judges of the world court are picked gained a shared rule in Security Council Resolution 26, of 4 June 1947. The Assembly had adopted a stopgap rule in November 1946, if the Council would agree. Under it, a meeting held to elect court judges must sit on till each open seat is filled, by a full majority of votes in one or more rounds. The Council agrees to the rule and adopts it for its own such meetings too.
un-sc-res-326: The official series of Council decisions runs through Resolution 326, catalogued here for 1970. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-426:
One day after the Council created UNIFIL on paper, it gave the new force its legal shape. Resolution 425 had ordered Israel's withdrawal from southern Lebanon and called for a United Nations force there. The Secretary-General reported on 19 March 1978 on how to carry that order out. Resolution 426 was adopted the same day.

The Council approved the Secretary-General's report in full. It decided that the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon would be established on the terms set out in that report. The force was set up for an initial period of six months. After that, it would continue in operation if required, provided the Council so decided. The short text is the founding decision for UNIFIL. The force it created in March 1978 is still the basis of the United Nations presence in southern Lebanon.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Peace came to Bosnia on paper in November 1995. The Dayton talks had birthed a pact. The sides first signed their names to it on 21 November in Ohio. A formal rite would come later. UNPROFOR, the much-tried force in Bosnia, still held the field. Resolution 1026 passed with no dissent on 30 November 1995.

The force's term stretched to 31 January 1996, and no more by this grant. The pause let the Council plan the handover. The chief had to send word fast on how the pact would shift tasks. His report of 23 November fed the choice. The goal was a clean pass of the baton, as the pact set out. The force won warm praise for its hard years of work.

Kashmir's stalled settlement is the subject of Resolution 126, adopted on 2 December 1957 by ten votes to none with one Soviet abstention. A Swedish envoy, Gunnar Jarring, had traveled to India and Pakistan for the Council that spring and reported on his mission. Both governments still accepted the older UN plan: Kashmir's future decided by a free and impartial vote of its people.

The Council thanked Jarring for his careful work. It noted with concern that his report showed no real progress toward a settlement. Demilitarization of the state featured in the text as one of the steps on the way. The resolution kept the plebiscite framework formally alive even as the two countries' positions hardened into the pattern that still defines the dispute.

Belgrade's fresh start at the UN ran through this line of 2000. On 31 October, the Council adopted Resolution 1326 without a vote. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was now just Serbia and Montenegro. A decade of wars had shrunk it. Its president had fallen that same month. The state applied as a new member, not as heir to the old seat.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit it. The Assembly seated it the next day. The step settled a long legal fight in quiet fashion. The old federation's membership had passed to no heir on its own. Belgrade accepted a clean slate, and the world body moved on.

Switzerland, the great holdout, joined the UN by way of this line. On 24 July 2002, the Council adopted Resolution 1426 without dissent. It met twice in one day to do so. Swiss voters had backed joining in a national vote that March. Decades of strict neutrality had kept the country out until then.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit the Swiss Confederation. The Assembly seated it that September. The arrival closed the largest gap in the UN's claim to speak for all states. Switzerland kept its lasting neutrality all the same. It also kept its role as host of the UN's Geneva hub.

Sanctions on Al-Qaida and the Taliban are strengthened on 30 January 2004. The measures — asset freezes, travel bans, and an arms embargo on listed people and groups — dated from earlier resolutions. States, the Council found, needed clearer duties and better help in applying them.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council sharpened how the measures should be carried out and widened the sanctions committee's role in watching over them. A stronger monitoring arrangement is set up to help the committee track compliance and breaches. States are pressed to enforce the freeze and bans fully against everyone on the committee's list, and to report on the steps they have taken.

Resolution 1626, adopted on 19 September 2005, links Liberia's elections to safety for the Special Court for Sierra Leone. Liberia was preparing for October presidential and legislative votes, state authority was spreading, and a new economic management program had been signed. Next door, the UN Mission in Sierra Leone was due to end on 31 December 2005, leaving the court without its guard force.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the UN Mission in Liberia, UNMIL, until 31 March 2006. It lets UNMIL send up to 250 soldiers to Sierra Leone from November 2005 to guard the Special Court, with a matching short-term rise in UNMIL's ceiling. It also lets UNMIL rush more troops in to pull those guards and court staff out if a grave safety crisis hits. A drawdown plan for UNMIL is requested for March 2006.

A short extension for a peacekeeping operation in crisis is what Resolution 1726 delivers. Adopted on 15 December 2006, it concerns Côte d'Ivoire, where a civil conflict had split the country and stalled elections. The Council voiced serious worry about worsening conditions and the suffering and displacement of civilians.

Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, the Council extended the mandates of UNOCI, the UN operation there, and of the French forces backing it, but only until 10 January 2007. That brief window, less than a month, shows the Council buying time while a political deal remained out of reach. It also kept the matter under active review.

Côte d'Ivoire's long-delayed presidential election anchors Resolution 1826, adopted on 29 July 2008. The Ouagadougou Political Agreement of March 2007 had set a peace path, and the first round of voting was set for 30 November 2008. Voter identification and registration still lagged, militias had not fully disarmed, and rights abuses, including sexual violence, continued despite general improvement.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the UN Operation in Côte d'Ivoire, UNOCI, and the French forces supporting it until 31 January 2009, above all to back free and fair elections. UNOCI must help deliver security for the vote and logistics for the electoral commission. The Council urges faster progress on identification, disarmament, and restoring state authority nationwide. It will review the mandate and troop levels by January 2009, with a report three weeks before that includes benchmarks for a possible phased drawdown.

A judge from the United States chose to step down in 2010. Thomas Buergenthal had sat on the world court for a decade. His term still had time to run. Word of his choice reached the Council that spring. He would leave on 6 September 2010. Resolution 1926 passed on 2 June 2010.

The poll to fill his seat was set for 9 September 2010. Voters in the Council and the Assembly's sixty-fourth session would cast at the same hour. That joint poll is how court judges are always picked. The new judge would serve just the rest of the old term. Buergenthal had fled Nazi camps as a boy. He grew to shape world human rights law. The text marks his exit with the court's plain, set form.

Talks on reuniting Cyprus were moving into a more intensive phase at the end of 2011. Resolution 2026, adopted on 14 December 2011, concerns UNFICYP, the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus. Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot leaders were negotiating a settlement. The aim was a federation with two zones and two communities. Cyprus's government had agreed that the force should stay.

The Council extended UNFICYP's mandate until 19 July 2012. It urged both leaders to speed up the talks. The core issues had to be settled before a planned meeting in January 2012. The text also pressed for steps that build trust. More crossing points on the Green Line were one example. Renewed mine clearing in the buffer zone was another.

Mercenaries in Congo drew the Council's fire in the fall of 1966. Congo's envoy said Angola was their base. Angola was then ruled by Portugal. Lisbon's man swore no such camps stood there. Both tales were heard at the 1306th meeting. Resolution 226 passed with no dissent on 14 October 1966. The same day, Botswana won its seat vote.

Portugal was urged, on its own sworn word, to bar the use of Angola. No armed bands could train there to meddle in Congo's affairs. All states were told to keep out of Congo's home fights. The chief had to watch how the call was heeded. Congo's tale had a long tail: this text fed the chain of bans that the 1967 mercenary text would build on.

How judges of the International Court of Justice are elected is the only subject of Resolution 26, adopted unanimously on 4 June 1947. The General Assembly had adopted a rule for its election meetings the year before. Under that rule, a meeting continues until candidates win an absolute majority of votes for all the seats to be filled. The Council agreed to the Assembly's rule. It then adopted the same rule for its own election meetings. The resolution was sent to the General Assembly for its information.

Zambia complained in early 1973 about attacks by the illegal regime in Southern Rhodesia. Zambia said the Rhodesian actions included an economic blockade and military threats. South African forces were working with the regime, Zambia charged. The actions were hurting Zambia's security and its economy. Resolution 326 was adopted on 2 February 1973.

The Council condemned every act of provocation and harassment against Zambia. It also condemned repression inside Rhodesia, including recent collective punishments. South Africa's military and armed forces had to withdraw at once and in full. They were to leave Southern Rhodesia and the border with Zambia. Britain, as the ruling power, was told to make sure that happened. Britain also had to bring the illegal regime's actions to an end.

Southern Lebanon gained a UN force in the spring of 1978. On 19 March, the Council adopted Resolution 426. Twelve members voted yes, none voted no, and two held back. China took no part in the vote. Days before, Resolution 425 had demanded that Israel pull out of the south.

The text backs the Secretary-General's report on how the force would work. It sets up the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon for six months at first. The Council could renew it later if need be. The force, known as UNIFIL, had three tasks. It would confirm the Israeli pull-out, restore peace, and help Beirut regain control of the south.
whitehead-religion-making-1926:
Alfred North Whitehead published Religion in the Making in 1926, based on his Lowell Lectures. Whitehead treats religion as a human response to a vision of truth. He traces religion from tribal rites and ritual to more rational, universal forms. Solitude, he argues, stands at the heart of mature faith.

He asks how religion can stay honest in an age of science. Dogmas, he says, are formulas that point beyond themselves and must not harden. The book became a source text for process theology. Whitehead links God to the lure toward value in the world. It is a brief, humane work of religious philosophy.
widger-s-quotations-from-the-project-gut: David Widger gathers choice quotations from a Project Gutenberg text. The best lines are set out here for browsing at leisure. Wit and wisdom come in small, pleasing doses. A reader's companion to a classic work.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol26:
The Journal of Discourses closes with Volume XXVI, printed at Liverpool in 1886 after more than thirty years. Twenty-six volumes hold sermons from 1854 onward, the longest such record of the Latter-day Saint movement ever made. Brigham Young's generation and its heirs speak across the whole run, caught in shorthand and fixed in print.

The final volume keeps the familiar form: doctrine, counsel, and defense from the senior elders of the church. With it, an archive ends that historians of American religion use daily, since nothing else preserves a faith's pulpit so fully. The set stands complete, a church's own voice across three decades.
